statement: Which of the following describes the nerve supply of the gallbladder?
options: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the superior mesenteric plexus
Somatic motor fibers from the phrenic nerve (C3-C5)
Sympathetic and parasympathetic (vagal) fibers from the celiac plexus
Preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves
Sensory fibers traveling exclusively via the ilioinguinal nerve
correctOption: Sympathetic and parasympathetic (vagal) fibers from the celiac plexus
optionExplanations: The superior mesenteric plexus primarily supplies midgut structures; the gallbladder is a foregut structure supplied via the celiac plexus.
The phrenic nerve provides sensory supply to the parietal peritoneum under the diaphragm, but it does not provide the primary autonomic supply to the gallbladder itself.
The gallbladder receives its autonomic innervation (both sympathetic for inhibition/pain and parasympathetic/vagus for contraction) from the celiac plexus.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves provide parasympathetic supply to the hindgut (distal 1/3 of transverse colon onwards); the gallbladder (foregut) uses the vagus nerve.
The ilioinguinal nerve is a somatic nerve supplying the abdominal wall and groin skin; it does not innervate the gallbladder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Nerve Supply: Sympathetic and parasympathetic vagal fibers form the celiac plexus.

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
statement: Which of the following structures forms the floor of the inguinal canal, serving as a boundary for both direct and indirect hernias?
options: Transversalis fascia
Conjoint tendon
Internal oblique muscle
Upturned lower edge of the inguinal ligament
External spermatic fascia
correctOption: Upturned lower edge of the inguinal ligament
optionExplanations: The transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall and the deep inguinal ring, not the floor.
The conjoint tendon forms the medial part of the posterior wall, reinforcing it behind the superficial ring.
The internal oblique muscle contributes to the anterior wall (laterally) and the roof.
The floor of the inguinal canal is formed by the inferior, rolled-under edge of the external oblique aponeurosis (the inguinal ligament) and the lacunar ligament medially.
External spermatic fascia is a covering of the spermatic cord derived from the external oblique aponeurosis, not a boundary of the canal itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Inferior wall (floor). Formed by the upturned lower edge of the inguinal ligament and, at its medial end, the lacunar ligament (see Fig. 6.14).

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of spleen
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy Boundaries of the Spleen
statement: In the adult, the surface projection of the spleen is used to guide procedures. How far forward does the spleen normally project in the adult?
options: As far as the anterior axillary line
To the level of the umbilicus
To the transpyloric plane
As far as the midaxillary line
As far as the linea semilunaris
correctOption: As far as the midaxillary line
optionExplanations: The anterior axillary line is too far forward; the spleen is normally confined more posteriorly unless enlarged.
The umbilicus is the center of the abdomen; only a significantly enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) reaches this level.
The transpyloric plane (L1) passes through the stomach and kidneys, but does not define the anterior limit of the spleen.
In the adult, the healthy spleen stays under cover of the ribs and its lower pole does not extend anteriorly past the midaxillary line.
The linea semilunaris is the lateral edge of the rectus muscle, much more medial and anterior than the normal splenic boundary.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": in the adult, it does not normally project forward in front of the midaxillary line.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
statement: A 32-year-old female undergoes an abdominal ultrasound which reveals an accumulation of fluid in the right posterior subphrenic space (Morison's pouch). Anatomically, between which structures is this space situated?
options: Between the stomach and the pancreas in the lesser sac
Between the ascending colon and the lateral abdominal wall
Between the layers of the coronary ligament on the diaphragm
Between the right lobe of the liver, the right kidney, and the right colic flexure
Between the diaphragm and the upper surface of the liver
correctOption: Between the right lobe of the liver, the right kidney, and the right colic flexure
optionExplanations: This describes the lesser sac (omental bursa), which is a separate peritoneal compartment.
This describes the right lateral paracolic gutter, not a subphrenic space.
This describes the right extraperitoneal space or bare area, which is not a true subphrenic space as it lacks peritoneal lining.
The right posterior subphrenic space, also known as the hepatorenal pouch or Morison's pouch, is bounded by the liver, right kidney, and right colic flexure.
The space between the diaphragm and the upper surface of the liver defines the anterior subphrenic spaces.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The right posterior subphrenic space lies between the right lobe of the liver, the right kidney, and the right colic flexure

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
statement: When a surgeon performs an abdominal examination and elicits 'Rebound Tenderness' at a specific site, which anatomical layer and nerve fiber type are primarily being tested?
options: Parietal peritoneum; somatic sensory fibers
Greater omentum; autonomic fibers
Transversalis fascia; femoral nerve
Visceral peritoneum; visceral afferent fibers
Extraperitoneal fat; iliohypogastric nerve
correctOption: Parietal peritoneum; somatic sensory fibers
optionExplanations: Rebound tenderness indicates localized peritonitis. It occurs because the parietal peritoneum is highly sensitive to stretch when inflamed. Since it is supplied by somatic spinal nerves, the pain is sharp and well-localized.
The greater omentum is a visceral structure (two layers of peritoneum) and does not provide the somatic sensitivity needed for rebound tenderness.
The transversalis fascia is deep to the muscles but superficial to the peritoneum; it is not the serous membrane responsible for the rebound phenomenon.
Visceral peritoneum is not sensitive to the rapid stretch associated with rebound; it lacks the somatic precision to localize pain in this manner.
The extraperitoneal fat is relatively insensitive and is not the primary site tested during the evaluation of peritoneal irritation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An inflamed parietal peritoneum is extremely sensitive to stretch. ... The abdominal wall rebounds, resulting in extreme local pain, which is known as rebound tenderness.

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations and Origins of the Uncinate Process
statement: The uncinate process of the pancreas is a distinct projection of the gland. Based on its anatomical position and development, which of the following statements accurately describes this part?
options: It connects the body of the pancreas directly to the hilum of the spleen
It arises from the neck and passes anterior to the superior mesenteric vessels
It is a derivative of the dorsal pancreatic bud during embryogenesis
It is situated on the transpyloric plane immediately to the left of the midline
It represents a projection of the head extending to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels
correctOption: It represents a projection of the head extending to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels
optionExplanations: The tail of the pancreas, not the uncinate process, is the part that extends to and contacts the hilum of the spleen.
The uncinate process arises from the head, not the neck, and it passes posterior (behind) to the superior mesenteric vessels, not anteriorly.
Embryologically, the uncinate process and the inferior part of the head are derived from the ventral pancreatic bud, whereas the rest of the gland comes from the dorsal bud.
The neck of the pancreas lies on the transpyloric plane; the uncinate process is part of the head, which lies below and to the right of this plane.
The uncinate process is specifically the portion of the pancreatic head that hooks behind the superior mesenteric artery and vein as it extends toward the left.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A part of the head extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels and is called the uncinate process.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
statement: A medical student observing a cadaveric dissection identifies a segment of the small intestine that lacks plicae circulares and possesses a smooth internal mucosal lining. Which part of the gastrointestinal tract is being observed?
options: The distal portion of the ileum
The first part of the duodenum
The second part of the duodenum
The proximal segment of the jejunum
The fourth part of the duodenum
correctOption: The first part of the duodenum
optionExplanations: The distal ileum contains fewer plicae circulares compared to the jejunum, but it is not smooth-walled like the first part of the duodenum; it also contains Peyer's patches.
The first part of the duodenum (the duodenal cap) is uniquely smooth on its internal surface, unlike the subsequent segments which are characterized by the presence of plicae circulares.
The second part of the duodenum contains prominent plicae circulares and the major duodenal papilla where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter.
The proximal jejunum has the most pronounced and closely set plicae circulares in the entire small intestine to maximize absorption.
The fourth part of the duodenum is characterized by numerous plicae circulares, which are permanent circular folds that increase surface area.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The mucous membrane of the duodenum is mostly thick. It is smooth in the first part of the duodenum (see Fig. 7.28). However, it is thrown into numerous circular folds called the plicae circulares in the remainder of the duodenum.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Bony Attachments of the Inguinal Ligament
statement: Between which two specific bony landmarks does the inguinal ligament extend?
options: Anterior inferior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Ischial spine and the pubic crest
Pubic crest and the iliac crest
Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle
Iliac tubercle and the pectineal line
correctOption: Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle
optionExplanations: The AIIS is too low, and the pubic symphysis is the midline joint; the ligament attaches more laterally on the pubis at the tubercle.
The ischial spine is a posterior pelvic landmark, and the pubic crest is a medial ridge; they do not anchor the inguinal ligament.
The pubic crest is medial to the pubic tubercle, and the iliac crest is the entire upper ridge of the ilium; the ligament has more specific focal points.
Correct. The inguinal ligament is anchored laterally to the anterior superior iliac spine and medially to the pubic tubercle.
The iliac tubercle is on the outer lip of the crest, and the pectineal line receives the lacunar/pectineal ligaments, not the primary inguinal ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lower border of the aponeurosis is folded backward on itself between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, forming the inguinal ligament

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: A 55-year-old patient with a long-standing history of hepatic cirrhosis presents to the emergency department with massive hematemesis. The bleeding is traced to a venous anastomosis at the lower third of the esophagus. Which two vessels are involved in this specific portal-systemic communication?
options: Splenic vein and the inferior phrenic vein
Short gastric veins and the hemiazygos vein
Right gastric vein and the superior vena cava
Superior mesenteric vein and the internal thoracic vein
Left gastric vein and the azygos veins
correctOption: Left gastric vein and the azygos veins
optionExplanations: The splenic vein is a major portal tributary, but the specific esophageal anastomosis involves the left gastric vein specifically.
Short gastric veins drain the fundus into the splenic vein; while related to the stomach, they are not the primary site for esophageal varices.
The right gastric vein drains into the portal vein but is not the primary vessel involved in the esophageal portal-systemic anastomosis.
The superior mesenteric vein is too distal in the portal system to form the specific gastroesophageal anastomosis with the azygos system.
The left gastric vein (portal system) anastomoses with the azygos veins (systemic system) at the lower esophagus; portal hypertension causes these to varicosity and rupture.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Here, the esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (which drains into the portal vein) anastomose with the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins (systemic veins).

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
statement: A surgeon performing a splenectomy must be particularly careful when ligating and dividing the splenic vessels within the splenorenal ligament. Which organ's tail is anatomically at risk due to its proximity to the splenic hilum?
options: Pancreas
Left lobe of the liver
Descending colon
Left kidney
Stomach
correctOption: Pancreas
optionExplanations: The tail of the pancreas travels within the splenorenal ligament to reach the hilum of the spleen, making it highly susceptible to accidental injury during surgical mobilization of the spleen.
The left lobe of the liver is an anterior relation to the stomach and esophagus but does not extend to the splenic hilum within the splenorenal ligament.
The descending colon (left colic flexure) is an inferior relation of the spleen, not a hilar structure within the splenorenal ligament.
The left kidney lies posterior to the spleen and the splenorenal ligament; it is a relation but its 'tail' is not at risk (kidneys have poles).
The stomach is connected via the gastrosplenic omentum, but its tail is not a descriptor used, and it is not contained within the splenorenal ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The presence of the tail of the pancreas in the splenorenal ligament sometimes results in its damage during splenectomy.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
coreConcept: Referred Pain via the Phrenic Nerve
statement: A patient with a subphrenic abscess presents with referred pain in the right shoulder. Which anatomical pathway best explains this clinical 'loop' of pain transmission?
options: Infection tracks through the falciform ligament to the axillary lymph nodes.
The abscess compresses the greater splanchnic nerve, referring pain to the scapula.
Inflammatory exudate in the paracolic gutter irritates the obturator nerve.
Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum sends impulses via the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) to the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4).
Irritation of the subphrenic parietal peritoneum sends impulses via the intercostal nerves T7-T11.
correctOption: Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum sends impulses via the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) to the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4).
optionExplanations: Lymphatic drainage from the bare area of the liver may pass to mediastinal nodes, but the referred pain to the shoulder is a neural pathway (phrenic nerve), not a lymphatic one.
The greater splanchnic nerve (T5-T9) is involved in visceral pain from the stomach and gallbladder, which is usually referred to the epigastrium, not the shoulder.
The obturator nerve (L2-L4) supplies the parietal peritoneum in the pelvis; irritation there would refer pain to the medial thigh, not the shoulder.

The central diaphragmatic peritoneum is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). Pain signals from here enter the same spinal segments as the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4), causing the brain to perceive the pain as coming from the shoulder.
The lower intercostal nerves supply the peripheral part of the diaphragmatic peritoneum and the anterior abdominal wall, referring pain to the abdomen, not the shoulder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A patient with a subphrenic abscess may complain of pain over the shoulder. ...The skin of the shoulder is supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4), which have the same segmental origin as the phrenic nerve, which supplies the peritoneum in the center of the undersurface of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Splenic Artery
statement: During a surgical dissection of the posterior abdominal wall, the surgeon observes a large, tortuous artery running along the superior margin of the pancreas. What is the anatomical relationship of this vessel to the pancreas and the stomach?
options: The vessel is the superior mesenteric artery and it lies anterior to the pancreatic neck.
The vessel is the left gastric artery and it courses along the inferior border of the neck.
The vessel is the gastroduodenal artery and it descends on the anterior surface of the tail.
The vessel is the hepatic artery and it runs along the inferior border of the body.
The vessel is the splenic artery and it runs along the upper border of the pancreas.
correctOption: The vessel is the splenic artery and it runs along the upper border of the pancreas.
optionExplanations: The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta behind the neck of the pancreas and passes in front of the third part of the duodenum, not along the upper border.

The left gastric artery runs upward and to the left to reach the esophagus and then descends along the lesser curvature of the stomach, having no relation to the inferior border of the pancreatic neck.
The gastroduodenal artery is a branch of the hepatic artery that descends behind the first part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas, not the tail.
The hepatic artery runs forward and to the right, not along the superior margin of the pancreatic body toward the left.
The splenic artery is characterized by its wavy/tortuous course along the upper (superior) border of the pancreas, situated behind the stomach.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The large splenic artery runs to the left in a wavy course along the upper border of the pancreas and behind the stomach.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
statement: An 18-month-old child is brought to the emergency department with intermittent abdominal pain and 'red currant jelly' stools. A diagnosis of ileocolic intussusception is made. What anatomical structure is often the 'lead point' for this telescoping of the bowel?
options: An inflamed vermiform appendix
Omental appendices of the cecum
A persistent Meckel's diverticulum
The ileocecal valve lips
Hypertrophied Peyer patches in the ileum
correctOption: Hypertrophied Peyer patches in the ileum
optionExplanations: Option E is incorrect because appendicitis is a separate inflammatory condition and not the primary lead point for ileocolic intussusception described.
Option D is incorrect because omental appendices are external fatty tags and do not project into the lumen to act as a lead point.
Option B is incorrect because while a Meckel's diverticulum can cause intussusception, the text specifically highlights the swelling of Peyer patches in children.
Option C is incorrect because the ileocecal valve is a horizontal fold that does not typically initiate the telescoping process.
Option A is correct; in children, swollen Peyer patches (lymphoid tissue) in the terminal ileum can act as a lead point for intussusception.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Intussusception is the telescoping of a proximal segment of the bowel into the lumen of an adjoining distal segment... Another factor may be the possible swelling of Peyer patches secondary to infection.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Hormonal Control of the Ileocecal Sphincter
statement: The transit of chyme from the small intestine to the large intestine is controlled by the ileocecal sphincter. Which endogenous hormonal mediator, released during the gastric phase of digestion, acts to relax this sphincter and facilitate the gastroileal reflex?
options: Cholecystokinin
Secretin
Glucagon
Somatostatin
Gastrin
correctOption: Gastrin
optionExplanations: Cholecystokinin (CCK) primarily causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, rather than direct relaxation of the ileocecal junction.
Secretin is primarily involved in stimulating bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas and does not mediate the relaxation of the ileocecal sphincter.
Glucagon is a pancreatic hormone primarily involved in glucose metabolism and has been noted to reduce esophageal sphincter tone but is not the primary mediator of the gastroileal reflex.
Somatostatin is an inhibitory hormone that generally suppresses gastrointestinal secretions and motility, rather than facilitating sphincter relaxation for chyme transit.
Gastrin, produced by the G cells of the stomach antrum, circulates in the blood and reflexly causes the relaxation of the ileocecal sphincter to allow chyme to move into the cecum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": the hormone gastrin, which is produced by the stomach, causes relaxation of the muscle tone.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: A 52-year-old male with a history of chronic alcoholism and liver cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department vomiting bright red blood (hematemesis). Physical exam reveals caput medusae. Anatomically, the severe bleeding most likely originates from a venous anastomosis between which two vessels?
options: Left gastric vein and Azygos veins
Superior mesenteric vein and Inferior vena cava
Splenic vein and Left renal vein
Paraumbilical veins and Superficial epigastric veins
Superior rectal vein and Middle rectal veins
correctOption: Left gastric vein and Azygos veins
optionExplanations: In portal hypertension, blood is shunted from the portal system (left gastric vein) to the systemic system (azygos veins) at the lower end of the esophagus, causing varices that can rupture and lead to life-threatening hematemesis.
While these represent portal and systemic systems, they do not form the specific gastroesophageal anastomosis involved in esophageal varices.
A splenorenal shunt is a surgical creation to treat portal hypertension, not a natural site of variceal bleeding.
This anastomosis occurs at the umbilicus and accounts for caput medusae, not esophageal bleeding.
This anastomosis occurs in the anal canal and leads to hemorrhoids in the setting of portal hypertension, not hematemesis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Here, the esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (which drains into the portal vein) anastomose with the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins (systemic veins).

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
statement: The spleen is positioned such that it forms part of the boundary for an important peritoneal space. Based on its anatomical relations, the spleen and its associated ligaments form the left margin of which space?
options: The right paracolic gutter
The greater sac
The right subphrenic space
The hepatorenal pouch
The lesser sac (omental bursa)
correctOption: The lesser sac (omental bursa)
optionExplanations: The right paracolic gutter is located on the lateral side of the ascending colon, which is situated in the right half of the abdomen.
The greater sac is the main compartment of the peritoneal cavity; the spleen is located within it but does not form its left margin in this context.
The right subphrenic space is located between the diaphragm and the liver, on the opposite side of the abdomen from the spleen.
The hepatorenal pouch (Morison's pouch) is located between the liver and the right kidney, distant from the splenic anatomy.
The lesser sac is situated behind the stomach; its left boundary is formed by the spleen and the two ligaments (gastrosplenic and splenorenal).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen, the gastrosplenic omentum, and the splenorenal ligament form the left margin of the sac [lesser sac].

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
statement: A 65-year-old male with liver cirrhosis and massive ascites undergoes abdominal paracentesis. The clinician inserts the needle in the midline, approximately 2 cm below the umbilicus. During the procedure, the catheter unexpectedly returns clear yellow fluid that smells like urine. Which anatomical error was likely made?
options: The needle punctured the inferior mesenteric vein as it crossed the midline.
The needle penetrated the persistent vitelline duct causing a fecal fistula.
The catheter entered the patent ductus venosus within the falciform ligament.
The needle was inserted too laterally, piercing the inferior epigastric artery.
The clinician failed to ensure the urinary bladder was empty, which can rise to the umbilicus when full.
correctOption: The clinician failed to ensure the urinary bladder was empty, which can rise to the umbilicus when full.
optionExplanations: The inferior mesenteric vein is a retroperitoneal structure located to the left of the midline; its puncture would cause internal bleeding, not the return of urine.
A vitelline duct fistula would likely return fecal matter or gas, as it connects the gut to the umbilicus, rather than clear yellow urine.
The ductus venosus (ligamentum venosum) is located on the liver's visceral surface, much higher and deeper than the site of a standard paracentesis.
Piercing the inferior epigastric artery would return blood (hematoma or false-positive peritoneal lavage), not urine.

A full bladder is a significant risk during midline paracentesis because it rises out of the pelvis. If it is not emptied (via catheterization or voiding), it can be easily perforated by a needle inserted near the umbilicus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In adults, the full bladder may rise out of the pelvis and reach as high as the umbilicus (see Chapter 9). ... Perforation of a full bladder.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
statement: When performing a radical gastrectomy for carcinoma of the stomach body, the surgeon must remove the lymph nodes that represent the final common pathway for all gastric lymphatic drainage. To which group of nodes must the dissection ultimately lead?
options: Splenic nodes.
Left gastric nodes.
Hepatic nodes.
Celiac nodes.
Superior mesenteric nodes.
correctOption: Celiac nodes.
optionExplanations: Splenic nodes drain the fundus and upper greater curvature via short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels but then pass to the celiac nodes.
Left gastric nodes are a regional group along the lesser curvature; they are a precursor to the final celiac node drainage, not the terminal abdominal station.
Hepatic nodes receive drainage from the liver and gallbladder; they are part of the drainage for the right side of the stomach but not the final common pathway for all gastric lymph.
All individual gastric node groups (left/right gastric, gastroepiploic, short gastric) ultimately converge on the celiac nodes at the origin of the celiac trunk.
Superior mesenteric nodes drain the midgut (from the distal duodenum to the transverse colon), not the stomach.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": All lymph from the stomach eventually passes to the celiac nodes located around the root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
statement: A neonate presents with persistent vomiting shortly after birth. Radiographic studies suggest anular pancreas. Based on the embryological development of the pancreas, which segment of the gastrointestinal tract is most likely constricted?
options: First part of the duodenum
Duodenojejunal flexure
Second part of the duodenum
Pyloric antrum of the stomach
Third part of the duodenum
correctOption: Second part of the duodenum
optionExplanations: The first part of the duodenum is superior to the primary site of pancreatic development and fusion.
The duodenojejunal flexure is the fourth part of the duodenum, located to the left of the midline, far from the site of anular constriction.
The pancreas develops at the level of the second part of the duodenum; malrotation of the ventral bud encircles this specific segment.
The pyloric antrum is part of the stomach; while it is near the pancreas, anular pancreas specifically encircles the duodenum.
The third part of the duodenum is inferior to the main site of the pancreatic head and bud fusion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In anular pancreas, the ventral pancreatic bud becomes fixed so that... it is pulled around the right side of the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud... thus encircling the duodenum. This may cause obstruction of the duodenum.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
statement: A 55-year-old male with chronic cirrhosis presents with severe hematemesis. Gastroscopy reveals bleeding varices at the lower end of the esophagus. Based on the venous drainage of the gastrointestinal tract, what is the exact route by which blood from the portal system is reaching the systemic circulation in this patient?
options: Through the paraumbilical veins into the superficial epigastric veins of the abdominal wall.
Through the short gastric veins into the renal veins.
Through the right gastric vein into the inferior vena cava directly.
Through the superior mesenteric vein into the lumbar veins of the posterior abdominal wall.
Through the left gastric vein into the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins.
correctOption: Through the left gastric vein into the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins.
optionExplanations: This pathway describes 'caput medusae' around the umbilicus, not esophageal bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract and its accessories section.
While the splenic vein (which receives short gastric veins) can anastomose with the renal vein, this is not the mechanism for esophageal varices; it is a separate retroperitoneal anastomosis.
The right gastric vein drains into the portal vein; there is no direct anastomosis with the IVC mentioned for this specific vein at the esophagus.

The superior mesenteric vein does not typically form an anastomosis with lumbar veins to cause esophageal varices; retroperitoneal anastomoses are usually involving retroperitoneal organs like the colon or pancreas.

In cirrhosis, portal pressure rises (portal hypertension), forcing blood through collateral channels. The anastomosis between the left gastric vein (portal) and the azygos veins (systemic) at the lower esophagus dilates, forming life-threatening varices.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": At the lower third of the esophagus, the esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (which drains into the portal vein) anastomose with the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins (systemic veins).

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
statement: Blockage of the portal vein leads to the recruitment of several minor anastomotic channels. Which of the following describes a retroperitoneal (Retzius) portal-systemic anastomosis?
options: Veins of the ascending colon anastomosing with the lumbar veins
The superior rectal vein anastomosing with the middle rectal vein
Left gastric vein anastomosing with the esophageal branches of the azygos vein
Paraumbilical veins anastomosing with the superficial epigastric vein
Cystic veins draining directly into the hepatic sinusoids
correctOption: Veins of the ascending colon anastomosing with the lumbar veins
optionExplanations: Retroperitoneal organs like the ascending colon have portal drainage; their veins can anastomose with systemic retroperitoneal veins such as the lumbar or renal veins during portal hypertension.
This describes the anorectal anastomosis, which is a pelvic/mucosal portal-systemic shunt, not a retroperitoneal one.
This describes the gastroesophageal anastomosis, which is located at the lower third of the esophagus.
This describes the paraumbilical anastomosis located in the anterior abdominal wall/falciform ligament.

Cystic veins draining to the liver is a normal portal pathway and does not constitute a portal-systemic shunt unless it involves systemic veins of the body wall or diaphragm (not described as the primary cystic route).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Retroperitoneal anastomoses. The veins of retroperitoneal organs (duodenum, pancreas, ascending colon, and descending colon), plus the liver (portal tributaries), anastomose with the renal, lumbar, and phrenic veins (systemic tributaries).

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
coreConcept: Pathophysiology of esophageal varices in portal hypertension
statement: A patient with cirrhosis develops hematemesis. What is the precise pathophysiological mechanism involving the portosystemic anastomosis at the lower esophagus?
options: Compression of the inferior vena cava leading to backup in the esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Thrombosis of the hepatic veins forcing blood into the right gastric vein and سپس to the azygos system
Dilation of esophageal veins as blood from the portal vein bypasses the liver via the left gastric vein
Reversal of flow from the azygos vein into the left gastric vein due to high systemic pressure
Congestion of the superior mesenteric vein causing increased pressure in the short gastric veins
correctOption: Dilation of esophageal veins as blood from the portal vein bypasses the liver via the left gastric vein
optionExplanations: While IVC compression can cause systemic backup, esophageal varices in cirrhosis are primarily a result of portal hypertension and the portal-to-systemic shunt at the esophageal junction.

Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) can cause portal hypertension, but the specific anastomosis at the lower esophagus involves the left gastric vein and the azygos system, rather than the right gastric vein specifically described here.

In portal hypertension, the high-pressure portal blood seeks lower-pressure systemic routes. The left gastric vein (portal) flow reverses to enter the esophageal veins (systemic azygos system), causing them to dilate into varices.

Systemic pressure is lower than portal pressure in cirrhosis; therefore, blood flows from the high-pressure portal system (left gastric) toward the lower-pressure systemic system (azygos), not the reverse.
The superior mesenteric vein drains the midgut; the primary portal contributor to the esophageal anastomosis is the left gastric vein, not the superior mesenteric or short gastric veins.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Should the portal vein become obstructed (e.g., in cirrhosis of the liver), portal hypertension develops, resulting in dilatation and varicosity of the portal–systemic anastomoses.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
statement: Which of the following describes the 'Retroperitoneal Anastomoses' (Veins of Retzius) that provide collateral circulation during portal vein blockage?
options: Left gastric vein communicating with the phrenic veins
Inferior mesenteric vein communicating with the internal iliac vein
Splenic vein tributaries communicating with the left suprarenal vein
Superior mesenteric vein communicating directly with the azygos vein
Veins of the ascending/descending colon communicating with the lumbar and renal veins
correctOption: Veins of the ascending/descending colon communicating with the lumbar and renal veins
optionExplanations: The left gastric vein primarily anastomoses with the esophageal (azygos) system, which is a mediastinal/thoracic communication, not a retroperitoneal one.

The inferior mesenteric vein communicates with the systemic system via the anorectal junction (superior rectal to middle/inferior rectal), not typically with the internal iliac directly in a retroperitoneal fashion.
The splenic vein is part of the portal system, and while it may be near the left suprarenal vein, the standard retroperitoneal anastomosis involves specific colonic/pancreatic tributaries.
There is no direct physiological or pathological communication between the superior mesenteric vein and the azygos vein in the retroperitoneum.

Retroperitoneal organs like the ascending/descending colon have portal drainage; their veins can form collateral channels with systemic retroperitoneal veins such as the lumbar or renal veins during portal hypertension.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Retroperitoneal anastomoses. The veins of retroperitoneal organs (duodenum, pancreas, ascending colon, and descending colon), plus the liver (portal tributaries), anastomose with the renal, lumbar, and phrenic veins (systemic tributaries).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: The tonic contraction of the gastroesophageal sphincter is a critical physiological barrier. How does the hormone Gastrin influence this mechanism compared to Secretin?
options: Both Gastrin and Secretin reduce sphincter tone
Gastrin has no effect; Secretin causes immediate relaxation
Gastrin relaxes the sphincter; Secretin increases tone
Gastrin increases tone; Secretin reduces tone
Both Gastrin and Secretin increase sphincter tone
correctOption: Gastrin increases tone; Secretin reduces tone
optionExplanations: Gastrin is notably unique in its ability to augment or increase the tone, so both cannot be inhibitory.
Gastrin has a well-documented augmentative effect on the sphincter, making the 'no effect' claim incorrect.
This is the opposite of the actual physiological effect; gastrin is a stimulator of gastroesophageal tone to prevent reflux during gastric digestion.
Gastrin, released during stomach filling, augments the closure of the physiologic sphincter. In contrast, secretin, cholecystokinin, and glucagon act to reduce this tone.
Hormones have antagonistic roles here to maintain balance; they do not both increase tone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The closure of the sphincter is under vagal control, and this can be augmented by the hormone gastrin and reduced in response to secretin, cholecystokinin, and glucagon.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
statement: Which artery, supplying the lower part of the greater curvature of the stomach, arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery?
options: Right gastric artery
Left gastroepiploic artery
Left gastric artery
Right gastroepiploic artery
Short gastric arteries
correctOption: Right gastroepiploic artery
optionExplanations: The right gastric artery arises directly from the hepatic artery proper at the upper border of the pylorus.
The left gastroepiploic artery arises from the splenic artery, not the gastroduodenal.
The left gastric artery is a direct branch of the celiac trunk.
The right gastroepiploic artery is indeed a branch of the gastroduodenal artery, supplying the greater curvature.
The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The right gastroepiploic artery arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery. It passes to the left and supplies the stomach along the lower part of the greater curvature.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
statement: Which of the following veins is considered a direct tributary of the main trunk of the hepatic portal vein, typically joining it near the lesser curvature of the stomach?
options: Short gastric vein
Sigmoid vein
Ileocolic vein
Right gastro-omental vein
Right gastric vein
correctOption: Right gastric vein
optionExplanations: Short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and typically empty into the splenic vein, not the portal vein trunk.
Sigmoid veins are tributaries of the inferior mesenteric vein, which then joins the splenic vein.
The ileocolic vein is a tributary of the superior mesenteric vein.
The right gastro-omental vein (right gastroepiploic) joins the superior mesenteric vein.
The right gastric vein (along with the left gastric vein) is a direct tributary that empties into the main trunk of the hepatic portal vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The left and right gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
coreConcept: Surface Projection of the Splenic Long Axis
statement: An elite anatomist is demonstrating the topographical surface landmarks of the spleen on a cadaver. Which specific rib shaft should they identify as the one corresponding to the long axis of the spleen?
options: The shaft of the 10th rib
The shaft of the 11th rib
The shaft of the 9th rib
The shaft of the 12th rib
The shaft of the 8th rib
correctOption: The shaft of the 10th rib
optionExplanations: The long axis of the spleen is traditionally taught to lie exactly along the shaft of the 10th left rib, which is a critical landmark for clinical percussion and biopsy.
The 11th rib represents the inferior border of the spleen's anatomical position, not its central long axis.
The 9th rib represents the superior border of the spleen, but its long axis does not align with the 9th rib shaft.
The 12th rib is located inferior to the spleen and is more closely related to the superior pole of the left kidney than the spleen's long axis.
The 8th rib is situated superior to the splenic position; the spleen typically begins under the 9th rib.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Its long axis corresponds to that of the 10th rib

category: Describe the extent, boundaries and contents of inguinal canal
statement: A 32-year-old male presents with a swelling in the groin that extends into the scrotum. On examination, the swelling is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery at the level of the deep inguinal ring. Based on the anatomical extent of the inguinal canal, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Inguinal lymphadenitis
Femoral hernia
Encysted hydrocele of the cord
Direct inguinal hernia
Indirect inguinal hernia
correctOption: Indirect inguinal hernia
optionExplanations: Inguinal lymphadenitis involves enlarged lymph nodes and would not present as a scrotal swelling following the anatomical course of the deep ring and canal.
A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal, which is located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and the inguinal ligament.

While an encysted hydrocele occurs within the cord, it is a cystic collection of fluid within a localized segment of the processus vaginalis, not typically a reducible bowel herniation following the ring's lateral anatomy.
A direct inguinal hernia bulges through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, not lateral to them.

An indirect inguinal hernia is characterized by the hernial sac entering the deep inguinal ring, which is located lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and potentially following the full length of the canal into the scrotum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It follows that the sac enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels... If the processus vaginalis has undergone no obliteration, then the hernia is complete and extends through the superficial inguinal ring down into the scrotum

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
statement: A physical examination of a healthy 25-year-old male is conducted to identify the surface projections of the abdominal viscera. Which ribs specifically provide the anatomical 'cover' for the spleen in its normal position?
options: Ribs 10, 11, and 12
Ribs 11 and 12 only
Ribs 7, 8, and 9
Ribs 8, 9, and 10
Ribs 9, 10, and 11
correctOption: Ribs 9, 10, and 11
optionExplanations: The 12th rib is associated more with the superior pole of the left kidney than with the spleen, which sits higher and more anteriorly.

Ribs 11 and 12 are the floating ribs; while 11 covers the inferior portion of the spleen, 12 is generally inferior to the splenic mass and relates to the kidney and quadratus lumborum muscles instead of providing splenic cover. It also misses the 9th and 10th ribs which cover the bulk of the organ's superior and middle portions respectively. Therefore this is incomplete and partially incorrect for the 12th rib's typical relation to the spleen's bulk which is higher up. Rib 11 is however the lowest rib covering the spleen as per standard medical texts. Thus Rib 12 is usually below the spleen's lower edge in normal anatomy as described in the source text which lists only 9, 10 and 11. Specifically, rib 12 is related to the left kidney as per the text's description for kidneys on page 785 where the left kidney is higher than the right, reaching rib 11, whereas the right reaches rib 12. Splenic relations on page 927 clearly limit the cover to ribs 9, 10, and 11 only. Rib 12 is thus incorrect as a covering rib for the spleen in standard anatomy. Option E is therefore incorrect as it omits the 9th and 10th ribs and incorrectly includes the 12th rib which is inferior to the spleen in standard positioning.
Ribs 7, 8, and 9 are positioned too high; rib 7 and 8 are primarily associated with the lung and diaphragm in the midaxillary line, though rib 9 does cover the superior pole of the spleen.
While rib 9 and 10 do cover the spleen, rib 8 is generally superior to the splenic location in the left hypochondrium.
The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ located in the left hypochondrium, shielded by the rib cage. Its typical anatomical position lies deep to the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs on the left side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen is situated in the left upper quadrant and lies under cover of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: In the clinical evaluation of a patient suspected of having Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD), what is the minimum frequency of heartburn symptoms required to satisfy the standard diagnostic description?
options: At least twice per week
At least five times per week
At least once per day
At least three times per month
At least once per month
correctOption: At least twice per week
optionExplanations: Heartburn occurring at least twice a week is the classic clinical benchmark for diagnosing GERD in an outpatient setting.
Five times a week is well above the minimum threshold; a patient only needs to experience symptoms on two occasions per week to be considered for a GERD diagnosis.
While daily heartburn is common in severe GERD, the threshold for clinical diagnosis as defined in the text is lower than daily occurrence.
The diagnostic criteria specify weekly frequency rather than monthly count; three times a month would fall below the 'twice per week' threshold.
Heartburn once a month is often considered 'occasional reflux' and does not usually meet the criteria for a chronic disease state like GERD.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It consists of a reflux of acid stomach contents into the esophagus producing the symptoms of heartburn on at least two occasions per week.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Intrapancreatic Course of the Bile Duct
statement: Regarding the third part of the bile duct's course, what is its primary anatomical relationship with the pancreas before it enters the duodenum?
options: It pierces the uncinate process of the pancreas.
It lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas.
It is embedded within the tail of the pancreas.
It runs superior to the body of the pancreas along the splenic artery.
It passes anterior to the neck of the pancreas.
correctOption: It lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas.
optionExplanations: The uncinate process lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels; the bile duct is situated higher on the posterior head.
The third part of the bile duct is often described as 'retropancreatic' or 'intrapancreatic,' where it sits in a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic head.
The tail of the pancreas is associated with the hilum of the spleen, far from the biliary tree.
The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the body and tail, while the bile duct is associated with the head.
The bile duct is posterior to the head of the pancreas, not anterior to the neck; the portal vein forms behind the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the third part of its course, it lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (see Fig. 7.29).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
statement: The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which provides essential blood supply to the head of the pancreas, originates as a branch of which of the following vessels?
options: Splenic artery
Gastroduodenal artery
Left gastric artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Hepatic artery proper
correctOption: Gastroduodenal artery
optionExplanations: The splenic artery supplies the body and tail via numerous small pancreatic branches, not the superior pancreaticoduodenal.
The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a terminal branch of the gastroduodenal artery, which itself is a branch of the hepatic artery.
The left gastric artery supplies the esophagus and the lesser curvature of the stomach.
The superior mesenteric artery gives off the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which anastomoses with the superior version.
The hepatic artery proper is the continuation of the hepatic artery after the gastroduodenal has branched off.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The gastroduodenal artery... divides into the right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery... and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
statement: Regarding the anatomical position and peritoneal coverage of the small intestine, which segment is distinguished by being almost entirely retroperitoneal except for its proximal-most portion?
options: The first inch of the duodenum
The proximal third of the ileum
The fourth part of the duodenum
The second part of the duodenum
The distal two-fifths of the jejunum
correctOption: The first inch of the duodenum
optionExplanations: The first inch (2.5 cm) of the duodenum is unique because it is covered by peritoneum on both surfaces and has the lesser and greater omenta attached, providing mobility unlike the rest of the fixed duodenum.
The ileum, like the jejunum, is an intraperitoneal structure with a complete peritoneal covering, located in the lower right part of the abdominal cavity and pelvis.
The fourth part of the duodenum is entirely retroperitoneal and runs upward and to the left to the duodenojejunal flexure, unlike the first inch which is mobile and intraperitoneal.
The second part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, situated in front of the hilum of the right kidney, and is only covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface.
The jejunum is an intraperitoneal organ entirely clothed in visceral peritoneum and attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery, providing significant mobility.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The first inch (2.5 cm) of the duodenum resembles the stomach in that it is covered on its anterior and posterior surfaces with peritoneum... The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, being only partially covered by peritoneum.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
coreConcept: Functional Anatomy of the Hepatopancreatic Ampulla
statement: During the digestive phase, the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by the duodenum. Which of the following anatomical structures must relax to allow the combined pancreatic and biliary secretions to enter the duodenum?
options: Pyloric sphincter
Internal anal sphincter
Spiral valve
Sphincter of Oddi
Ileocecal valve
correctOption: Sphincter of Oddi
optionExplanations: The pyloric sphincter regulates the passage of chyme from the stomach to the duodenum, not the entry of pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum.
The internal anal sphincter is a smooth muscle under autonomic control for defecation and has no role in the proximal gastrointestinal secretory delivery system.
The spiral valve (of Heister) is located in the cystic duct and maintains luminal patency; it does not regulate the final common pathway at the duodenum.

The sphincter of Oddi (hepatopancreatic sphincter) surrounds the Ampulla of Vater; its relaxation (triggered by CCK) is essential for the discharge of bile and pancreatic enzymes into the second part of the duodenum.
The ileocecal valve is located at the junction of the small and large intestines and is unrelated to pancreatic or biliary secretion delivery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The terminal parts of both ducts and the ampulla are surrounded by circular muscle, known as the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (sphincter of Oddi).

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
statement: The physiological delivery of bile into the duodenum is mediated by the hormone cholecystokinin. Which of the following best describes the simultaneous action of this hormone on the components of the biliary tree?
options: Contraction of the bile duct and relaxation of the gallbladder
Inhibition of bile secretion from the liver and contraction of the ampulla
Contraction of the common hepatic duct and relaxation of the cystic duct
Relaxation of the gallbladder and contraction of the sphincter of Oddi
Contraction of the gallbladder and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi
correctOption: Contraction of the gallbladder and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi
optionExplanations: The gallbladder must contract to expel bile; it does not relax during the digestive phase.
CCK facilitates bile delivery; it does not inhibit liver secretion or contract the ampulla's exit.
The ducts (hepatic and cystic) do not have significant contractile properties compared to the gallbladder; CCK targets the gallbladder and the terminal sphincter.
This would prevent bile from entering the duodenum, which is the opposite of the digestive requirement.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) triggers the gallbladder to contract (expelling stored bile) while simultaneously relaxing the sphincter of Oddi (allowing bile to enter the duodenum).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The hormone then enters the blood, causing the gallbladder to contract. At the same time, the smooth muscle around the distal end of the bile duct and the ampulla is relaxed, thus allowing the passage of concentrated bile into the duodenum.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
statement: When considering the total length of the small intestine distal to the duodenum, which statement correctly describes the division between the jejunum and the ileum?
options: The ileum constitutes the upper three fifths.
The jejunum constitutes the lower three fifths.
The jejunum and ileum are of equal length.
The jejunum constitutes the upper two fifths.
The jejunum constitutes the upper one fifth.
correctOption: The jejunum constitutes the upper two fifths.
optionExplanations: The ileum constitutes the distal three fifths, not the upper three fifths.
The jejunum is the upper (proximal) segment, not the lower (distal) segment.
The segments are not equal; the ileum is longer than the jejunum.
The jejunum makes up approximately the proximal 40% (two fifths) of the length of the mobile small intestine.
One fifth is too small; the jejunum is nearly half of the length.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The jejunum and ileum together measure about 20 ft (6 m) long. The jejunum makes up the upper two fifths of this length.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
statement: A 58-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with a distended abdomen, jaundice, and a cluster of dilated veins radiating from his umbilicus. He subsequently experiences a massive episode of hematemesis. Laboratory tests confirm cirrhosis. Which anatomical route best explains the connection between his superficial abdominal findings and his gastrointestinal bleeding?
options: The lumbar veins connecting directly to the pampiniform plexus.
The deep circumflex iliac vein draining into the external iliac vein.
The paraumbilical veins connecting the portal vein to the superficial systemic veins.
The superior epigastric veins anastomosing with the inferior phrenic veins.
The lateral thoracic vein anastomosing with the superficial circumflex iliac vein.
correctOption: The paraumbilical veins connecting the portal vein to the superficial systemic veins.
optionExplanations: The lumbar veins and pampiniform plexus are involved in different venous systems and do not contribute to the paraumbilical distention or gastrointestinal bleeding described in the case.
The deep circumflex iliac vein is a standard deep drainage route into the external iliac; it is not a primary collateral pathway that becomes visibly distended in cirrhosis.

In cirrhosis, portal hypertension forces blood through the paraumbilical veins (forming Caput Medusae) and simultaneously through the gastroesophageal junction (forming esophageal varices), explaining both signs.
While these are systemic veins, they do not participate in the portal-systemic shunting responsible for either Caput Medusae or esophageal varices.
This describes a systemic-systemic anastomosis (caval-caval shunt) typically seen in IVC obstruction, not the portal-systemic shunt seen in cirrhosis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A few small veins, the paraumbilical veins, connect the network through the umbilicus and along the ligamentum teres to the portal vein. This forms an important portal–systemic venous anastomosis.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a tumor confined to the dome-shaped fundus of the stomach. In tracing the physiological pathway of lymph from this specific region, which intermediary node group is most likely to be involved before reaching the celiac nodes?
options: Right gastric nodes
Left gastric nodes
Short gastric nodes
Right gastroepiploic nodes
Inferior pancreaticoduodenal nodes
correctOption: Short gastric nodes
optionExplanations: Right gastric nodes are located along the lower right portion of the lesser curvature and do not receive primary drainage from the fundus.
Left gastric nodes primarily drain the upper right part of the stomach along the lesser curvature, following the distribution of the left gastric artery.
Correct. The fundus is supplied by the short gastric arteries; hence, the lymphatic vessels follow these arteries into the short gastric nodes as part of the primary drainage pathway.
Right gastroepiploic nodes drain the lower part of the greater curvature, whereas the fundus is located at the superior-most aspect of the stomach.
Inferior pancreaticoduodenal nodes drain the lower half of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas, which are distal to the gastric fundus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lymph vessels follow the arteries into the left and right gastric nodes, the left and right gastroepiploic nodes, and the short gastric nodes (Fig. 7.23).

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: A patient complains of persistent heartburn. According to standard diagnostic descriptions of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD), what is the minimum frequency of symptoms typically required for this diagnosis?
options: Only during the first trimester of pregnancy
Once every month after heavy meals
Once per day exactly at the transpyloric plane
Only when lying in the left lateral position
Twice per week
correctOption: Twice per week
optionExplanations: Pregnancy is a cause/predisposition, but the diagnostic frequency remains the same regardless of the patient's state.
Monthly symptoms are often considered episodic dyspepsia rather than chronic reflux disease.
The transpyloric plane (L1) is an anatomical landmark, but symptoms are not defined by single daily occurrences at a specific plane.
GERD is usually worsened by the supine position or right lateral position (due to anatomical alignment of the stomach), but frequency is the diagnostic criterion.
Correct. The text defines GERD by the occurrence of heartburn on at least two occasions per week.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)... consists of a reflux of acid stomach contents into the esophagus producing the symptoms of heartburn on at least two occasions per week.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
statement: A 52-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. A CT scan reveals a perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach with fluid collection in the lesser sac and signs of arterial hemorrhage. Which vascular structure is most likely eroded, and what is its relationship to the peritoneal sac?
options: Splenic artery; it runs along the upper border of the pancreas, which forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac.
Right gastroepiploic artery; it runs within the greater omentum forming the inferior recess of the lesser sac.
Superior mesenteric artery; it runs behind the third part of the duodenum in the root of the mesentery.
Left gastric artery; it runs within the gastrosplenic omentum forming the left boundary of the lesser sac.
Hepatic artery; it runs in the free margin of the lesser omentum forming the anterior boundary of the lesser sac.
correctOption: Splenic artery; it runs along the upper border of the pancreas, which forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac.
optionExplanations: A posterior gastric ulcer perforates into the lesser sac (omental bursa). The pancreas forms the posterior wall of this sac, and the splenic artery's position on the pancreas makes it highly vulnerable to erosion.
The right gastroepiploic artery is in the greater omentum, which is inferior to the typical site of a posterior wall ulcer.
The superior mesenteric artery is located much lower, behind the pancreas and in front of the third part of the duodenum, and is not a direct relation of the stomach's posterior wall.
The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature, not the gastrosplenic omentum; the gastrosplenic omentum forms the left margin, but the splenic artery is the major posterior relation.
The hepatic artery is in the lesser omentum's free border, which forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen, but it is not typically eroded by a posterior gastric ulcer.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An ulcer situated on the posterior wall of the stomach may perforate into the lesser sac or become adherent to the pancreas. Erosion of the pancreas produces pain referred to the back. The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas, and erosion of this artery may produce fatal hemorrhage.

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
coreConcept: Internal Duct Morphology of the Pancreas
statement: The main pancreatic duct is an essential conduit for exocrine secretions. In which specific part of the pancreas does this duct typically begin its course before running toward the duodenum?
options: Uncinate process
Body
Tail
Neck
Head
correctOption: Tail
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The uncinate process is drained by tributaries that join the main duct, but the main duct itself starts in the tail.
Incorrect. The body is the largest segment the duct traverses, but its origin is further left in the tail.
Correct. The main pancreatic duct begins at the tail of the pancreas and traverses the entire length of the gland toward the head.
Incorrect. The neck is a middle segment through which the duct passes, not where it originates.
Incorrect. The duct terminates in the head (by joining the bile duct), but it does not begin there.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The main duct of the pancreas begins in the tail and runs the length of the gland, receiving numerous tributaries on the way

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with progressive dysphagia and proximal esophageal dilatation. The condition is attributed to the failure of the gastroesophageal sphincter to relax. Which neurological deficit is most likely responsible?
options: Lesion of the phrenic nerve
Degeneration of the Auerbach plexus
Hypertrophy of the sympathetic trunk
Overactivity of the pudendal nerve
Degeneration of the celiac ganglion
correctOption: Degeneration of the Auerbach plexus
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; while it relates to the esophageal hiatus, its lesion does not cause intrinsic sphincter failure.
Achalasia is characterized by the degeneration of the parasympathetic Auerbach (myenteric) plexus, which prevents normal esophageal peristalsis and sphincter relaxation.
Sympathetic nerves provide motor fibers to the pylorus, but hypertrophy of the trunk is not the cause of esophageal achalasia.
The pudendal nerve supplies the perineum and external anal sphincter, having no physiological role in esophageal motility.
The celiac ganglion is part of the sympathetic system; achalasia is specifically a parasympathetic (myenteric) plexus degeneration.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The cause is unknown, but it is associated with a degeneration of the parasympathetic plexus (Auerbach plexus) in the wall of the esophagus.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
statement: A radiologist is performing a contrast study of the biliary tree. Which anatomical landmark differentiates the termination of the main pancreatic duct from that of the accessory pancreatic duct in the second part of the duodenum?
options: The main duct drains only the uncinate process, while the accessory duct drains the tail.
The main duct opens at the minor papilla; the accessory duct at the major papilla.
The accessory duct opens into the pylorus, while the main duct opens into the ileum.
Both ducts open into the third part of the duodenum on the same papilla.
The main duct opens at the major papilla; the accessory duct opens approximately 0.75 inches superiorly at the minor papilla.
correctOption: The main duct opens at the major papilla; the accessory duct opens approximately 0.75 inches superiorly at the minor papilla.
optionExplanations: The main duct drains the tail, body, and neck, whereas the accessory duct typically only drains the upper portion of the pancreatic head.
This is incorrect; the main duct (Wirsung) opens at the major papilla, and the accessory (Santorini) opens at the minor papilla.
Both ducts are anatomically confined to the second part of the duodenum; they do not open into the pylorus or the ileum.
The pancreatic ducts drain into the second (descending) part of the duodenum, not the third part, and usually on different papillae.
The main pancreatic duct joins the bile duct at the major duodenal papilla (halfway down the second part), while the accessory duct, if present, opens higher up on the minor papilla.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The accessory pancreatic duct, when present, drains the upper part of the head and then opens into the duodenum a short distance above the main duct on the minor duodenal papilla.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
coreConcept: Course and Dimensions of the Portal Vein
statement: The hepatic portal vein is a vessel of significant size and specific anatomical trajectory. According to standard anatomical descriptions, what is the approximate length of this vein and what is its relationship to the first part of the duodenum?
options: 5 inches (12.5 cm) long; lies lateral to the duodenum.
4 inches (10 cm) long; lies medial to the duodenum.
2 inches (5 cm) long; lies posterior to the duodenum.
1 inch (2.5 cm) long; lies anterior to the duodenum.
6 inches (15 cm) long; lies superior to the duodenum.
correctOption: 2 inches (5 cm) long; lies posterior to the duodenum.
optionExplanations: A length of 5 inches is much longer than the standard anatomical 2 inches, and the vein is not lateral to the duodenum but posterior to it.
The portal vein is significantly shorter than 4 inches, and its relationship to the duodenum is specifically posterior (retro-duodenal) rather than just medial.

The hepatic portal vein is approximately 2 inches (5 cm) in length. After its formation behind the neck of the pancreas, it follows a course that takes it behind the first part of the duodenum before it enters the free margin of the lesser omentum.
The vein is longer than 1 inch, and its position is posterior, not anterior, to the duodenum. An anterior position would expose it to different traumatic risks and surgical approaches.

The portal vein is not 6 inches long. While it eventually passes superior to the duodenum to reach the liver, its most critical descriptive relationship in the upper abdomen is passing posterior to the first part of the duodenum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The portal vein is about 2 in. (5 cm) long ... It ascends to the right, behind the first part of the duodenum, and enters the lesser omentum

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: Malignant cells from a carcinoma located in the abdominal portion of the esophagus are most likely to first spread to which group of lymph nodes?
options: Celiac nodes
Para-aortic nodes
Left gastric nodes
Tracheobronchial nodes
Internal thoracic nodes
correctOption: Left gastric nodes
optionExplanations: While all lymph from the stomach eventually reaches the celiac nodes, the left gastric nodes are the immediate regional nodes for the abdominal esophagus.
Para-aortic nodes receive lymph from retroperitoneal organs like the kidneys and gonads, but are not the primary first-tier drainage for the esophagus.
Lymph from the abdominal portion of the esophagus follows the arterial supply (left gastric artery) and drains primarily into the left gastric lymph nodes.
Tracheobronchial nodes drain the thoracic portion of the esophagus, particularly near the bifurcation of the trachea, not the abdominal portion.
Internal thoracic nodes drain the anterior chest wall and breast, not the abdominal viscera or the esophagus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lymph vessels follow the arteries into the left gastric nodes.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
statement: A surgeon is performing a total gastrectomy for a malignant tumor. To ensure a radical resection, lymph nodes around the origin of which artery must be removed as the final common drainage site for the stomach?
options: Superior mesenteric artery
Inferior mesenteric artery
Renal artery
External iliac artery
Celiac artery
correctOption: Celiac artery
optionExplanations: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut; its nodes drain the small intestine and part of the large intestine, not the stomach.
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut; its nodes drain the distal colon and rectum.
Renal nodes drain the kidneys and suprarenals, not the gastrointestinal tract.
External iliac nodes drain the lower limb and lower abdominal wall, not the abdominal viscera.
The stomach is a foregut derivative; all its lymphatic drainage routes (gastric, gastroepiploic, short gastric) ultimately converge at the celiac nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": All lymph from the stomach eventually passes to the celiac nodes located around the root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
statement: A 60-year-old female is diagnosed with advanced gastric cancer. The surgeon decides to perform a radical total gastrectomy. Based on the anatomical relations, which of the following structures is most likely to be removed 'en bloc' because it shares a peritoneal attachment and lymphatic field with the stomach?
options: Ascending colon
Left suprarenal gland
Gallbladder
Spleen
Right kidney
correctOption: Spleen
optionExplanations: The ascending colon is a right-sided retroperitoneal structure and not part of the gastric lymphatic field or en bloc resection.
The left suprarenal gland is a posterior relation but is not part of the lymphatic resection described in the text.
The gallbladder is related to the liver and duodenum but not typically removed en bloc with the stomach unless locally invaded.
Correct. Radical gastrectomy includes the spleen and its associated ligaments (gastrosplenic/splenorenal) because of the shared lymphatic pathways and the course of the splenic artery.
The right kidney is not a primary relation removed in radical gastrectomy; the left kidney is a posterior relation but not removed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": For these reasons, malignant disease of the stomach is treated by total gastrectomy, which includes the removal of the lower end of the esophagus and the first part of the duodenum, the spleen and the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments...

category: Identify the borders, surfaces and Impressions of spleen
coreConcept: Peritoneal Attachments of the Splenic Hilum
statement: Peritoneal reflections at the splenic hilum are critical for its suspension and neurovascular supply. Which ligament connects the hilum of the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach?
options: Falciform ligament
Phrenicocolic ligament
Splenorenal ligament
Coronary ligament
Gastrosplenic omentum
correctOption: Gastrosplenic omentum
optionExplanations: The falciform ligament is a fold that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and umbilicus.
The phrenicocolic ligament is a fold that extends from the diaphragm to the left colic flexure and supports the spleen but does not connect to the hilum.
The splenorenal ligament connects the splenic hilum to the left kidney, carrying the splenic artery and vein.
The coronary ligament is a peritoneal reflection that attaches the liver to the diaphragm.
The gastrosplenic omentum (or ligament) is the specific peritoneal fold connecting the splenic hilum to the greater curvature of the stomach.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen is surrounded by the peritoneum... which passes from it at the hilum as the gastrosplenic omentum (ligament) to the greater curvature of the stomach

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
statement: Which surface anatomy feature is used as a reliable guide to the location of the inguinal ligament in a clinical examination?
options: A skin crease in the groin
The lower border of the rib cage
The linea semilunaris
The vertical midline groove of the linea alba
A horizontal line at the level of the umbilicus
correctOption: A skin crease in the groin
optionExplanations: The inguinal ligament is clinically identified by the groin crease (inguinal crease) that runs between the ASIS and the pubic region.
The lower border of the rib cage (costal margin) is the superior boundary of the abdomen, whereas the inguinal ligament is the inferior boundary.
The linea semilunaris marks the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis; it intersects the costal margin at the 9th cartilage, far above the inguinal ligament.
The linea alba is a vertical midline structure; the inguinal ligament is a bilateral structure located in the lower quadrants, lateral to the midline.
The umbilical level corresponds to the T10 dermatome and L3/L4 vertebral level, which is significantly superior to the inguinal ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The inguinal ligament lies beneath a skin crease in the groin.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Vascular Supply Contrast between Jejunum and Ileum
statement: During a surgical demonstration, the chief examiner asks a candidate to differentiate a loop of jejunum from the ileum based on its vascular supply. Which anatomical arrangement of the mesenteric vessels is characteristic of the jejunum?
options: Fat deposited throughout the mesentery from the root to the intestinal wall
