The psoas fascia is a posterior abdominal wall structure that is not part of the en bloc resection for gastric malignancy.
The right kidney is a posterior relation but its capsule is not removed as part of the standard lymphatic clearance for gastric cancer.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": For these reasons, malignant disease of the stomach is treated by total gastrectomy, which includes the removal of... the tail and body of the pancreas and their associated nodes...

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
statement: The neurovascular supply of the pancreas is complex, involving multiple sources. Which of the following statements regarding the autonomic innervation and arterial supply is correct?
options: The splenic artery provides multiple small pancreatic branches to the gland.
The tail of the pancreas is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.
Sympathetic fibers are derived from the lumbar plexus (L2-L4).
The gland is supplied exclusively by the superior mesenteric artery.
Parasympathetic vagal fibers are inhibitory to pancreatic exocrine secretion.
correctOption: The splenic artery provides multiple small pancreatic branches to the gland.
optionExplanations: The splenic artery, as it runs along the upper border of the pancreas, gives off numerous small branches (up to ten) to supply the body and tail.
The tail is supplied by the splenic artery, which is a branch of the celiac trunk.
Sympathetic fibers are derived from the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses, not the lumbar plexus which is somatic.
The pancreas receives blood from the celiac artery (via the splenic and superior pancreaticoduodenal) and the superior mesenteric artery (via the inferior pancreaticoduodenal).
Parasympathetic vagal fibers are secretomotor, meaning they stimulate pancreatic secretion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The splenic and the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (see Fig. 7.26) supply the pancreas... Pancreatic branches: As many as ten small pancreatic arteries may branch off the splenic artery and supply the pancreas.

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Pancreatic Neck and Portal Vein Formation
statement: A 55-year-old male is undergoing an exploratory laparotomy. The surgeon identifies a constricted portion of the pancreas situated directly anterior to the junction where the superior mesenteric and splenic veins unite to form the portal vein. Which part of the pancreas is the surgeon identifying?
options: Head
Neck
Uncinate process
Body
Tail
correctOption: Neck
optionExplanations: The head lies to the right of the superior mesenteric vessels and does not sit directly in front of the portal vein's origin.
The neck is defined as the constricted segment lying anterior to the superior mesenteric artery's origin and the formation of the portal vein.
The uncinate process is part of the head and lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels, not anterior to the portal vein formation.
The body of the pancreas is located to the left of the midline and the superior mesenteric vessels.
The tail is the far-left portion of the gland, located within the splenorenal ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The neck is the constricted portion of the pancreas and connects the head to the body. It lies in front of the beginning of the portal vein and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta (see Fig. 7.26).

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: Regarding the anatomical relations of the abdominal portion of the esophagus, which structure lies immediately posterior to it, separating it from the vertebral column?
options: The left crus of the diaphragm
The left lobe of the liver
The right crus of the diaphragm
The lesser sac of the peritoneum
The caudate lobe of the liver
correctOption: The left crus of the diaphragm
optionExplanations: The abdominal esophagus rests on the left crus of the diaphragm as it enters the abdomen and heads toward the cardiac orifice.
The left lobe of the liver lies anterior to the abdominal esophagus, not posterior.
While the esophagus passes through an opening in the right crus, it is specifically related to the left crus on its posterior aspect after entry.
The lesser sac lies posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum; the esophagus enters the stomach before reaching the main expanse of the lesser sac.
The caudate lobe is a part of the liver related to the inferior vena cava and lesser omentum, not directly posterior to the esophagus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The esophagus is related anteriorly to the posterior surface of the left lobe of the liver and posteriorly to the left crus of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
coreConcept: External Features of the Large Intestine
statement: The large intestine is characterized by specific external features that distinguish it from the small intestine. Which of the following is found only on the large intestine?
options: Mesentery that passes downward and to the right into the iliac fossa
A smooth external wall lacking any sacculations or folds
A continuous layer of longitudinal muscle around the entire circumference
Permanent internal folds known as plicae circulares
Fatty tags known as omental appendices (appendices epiploicae)
correctOption: Fatty tags known as omental appendices (appendices epiploicae)
optionExplanations: This description specifically applies to the mesentery of the small intestine, which is mobile and has a diagonal root.
The large intestine is sacculated into haustra, whereas the small intestine has a relatively smooth external appearance.
In the large intestine, the longitudinal muscle is collected into three bands (teniae coli), whereas in the small intestine, it is a continuous layer.
Plicae circulares are characteristic of the small intestine and are absent in the large intestine.
Omental appendices are unique to the colon and consist of small pouches of peritoneum filled with fat.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The small intestine has no fatty tags attached to its wall. The large intestine has fatty tags, called the omental appendices (appendices epiploicae; epiploic appendages).

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
coreConcept: Arterial supply and lymphatic drainage of the hindgut
statement: In a surgical procedure to remove a malignant tumor from the descending colon, the surgeon must ligate the main arterial supply to the hindgut. To ensure a complete lymphadenectomy, the ligation should occur at the origin of which vessel from the abdominal aorta?
options: Celiac trunk
Right colic artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Median sacral artery
Inferior mesenteric artery
correctOption: Inferior mesenteric artery
optionExplanations: The celiac trunk supplies the foregut, including the stomach and proximal duodenum, which is not relevant to the descending colon.
The right colic artery is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery and supplies the ascending colon.
The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut (duodenum to proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon).
The median sacral artery is a small terminal branch of the aorta that supplies the lower sacrum and coccyx.
The descending colon is part of the hindgut, which is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). Lymphatic drainage follows the arterial supply back to the nodes at the IMA origin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The inferior mesenteric artery is the artery of the hindgut and supplies the large intestine from the distal one third of the transverse colon to halfway down the anal canal. It arises from the abdominal aorta about 1.5 in. (3.8 cm) above its bifurcation.

category: Describe the clinical picture and anatomical basis for the blockage of porto-systemic anastomosis
statement: A 60-year-old patient with end-stage liver disease presents with internal varicosities halfway down the anal canal. The anatomical basis for this involves a portal-systemic shunt between which specific vessels?
options: Superior rectal vein and Middle rectal vein
Middle rectal vein and Inferior rectal vein
Superior mesenteric vein and Inferior rectal vein
Inferior mesenteric vein and Internal pudendal vein
Inferior mesenteric vein and Common iliac vein
correctOption: Superior rectal vein and Middle rectal vein
optionExplanations: The superior rectal vein is the portal component, while the middle and inferior rectal veins are systemic components (branches of internal iliac/pudendal), forming the shunt.
The middle and inferior rectal veins are both systemic vessels; an anastomosis between them is not a portal-systemic shunt.
The superior mesenteric vein does not drain the rectum; the rectum is part of the hindgut drained by the inferior mesenteric system.
While the internal pudendal vein is systemic, the direct portal participant is the superior rectal vein, not the trunk of the inferior mesenteric vein.
The inferior mesenteric vein is the origin of the superior rectal vein, but the shunt occurs specifically at the level of the rectal plexus, not the common iliac.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Halfway down the anal canal, the superior rectal veins (portal tributary) draining the upper half of the anal canal anastomose with the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic tributaries)

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
statement: The horizontal transpyloric plane, passing through the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1), serves as a critical surface landmark for which specific part of the pancreas?
options: The lower border of the uncinate process
The major duodenal papilla
The tail of the pancreas
The superior border of the head
The neck of the pancreas
correctOption: The neck of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The uncinate process and the lower part of the head lie below the transpyloric plane in the umbilical region.
The major duodenal papilla is located in the second part of the duodenum, which descends to the level of L2 or L3, well below the transpyloric plane.
The tail of the pancreas is located above the transpyloric plane and to the left as it ascends toward the splenic hilum.
The superior border of the head is near the plane, but the neck is the specific anatomical part formally described as occupying the transpyloric plane.
The neck of the pancreas is specifically identified as lying on the transpyloric plane, which is at the level of the L1 vertebra.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": This plane passes through the pylorus of the stomach, the duodenojejunal junction, the neck of the pancreas, and the hila of the kidneys.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
statement: A newborn infant is found to have a large midline protrusion of the abdominal contents into the base of the umbilical cord. The mass is covered by a translucent sac consisting of amnion and peritoneum. Which of the following best defines this congenital anomaly?
options: Paraumbilical hernia
Acquired infantile umbilical hernia
Exomphalos (Omphalocele)
Gastroschisis
Epigastric hernia
correctOption: Exomphalos (Omphalocele)
optionExplanations: Paraumbilical hernias are acquired adult hernias through the linea alba near the umbilicus, not congenital defects involving the cord.
Acquired infantile umbilical hernia occurs after birth due to a weakness in the umbilical scar and is covered by skin, not a translucent sac of amnion.
Exomphalos, or omphalocele, is a congenital defect where midgut contents remain in the umbilical cord, covered by a sac of peritoneum and amnion.
Gastroschisis is a defect lateral to the umbilicus with no covering sac; the contents are exposed directly to the amniotic fluid.
An epigastric hernia is an acquired defect in the upper linea alba involving extraperitoneal fat, unrelated to the umbilicus or the midgut return.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Congenital umbilical hernia, or exomphalos (omphalocele), is caused by a failure of part of the midgut to return to the abdominal cavity from the extraembryonic coelom during fetal life.

category: Describe the anatomical basis for Sigmoidoscopy, rectal prolapse, rectal examination, rectal cancer and hemorrhoids
coreConcept: Anatomical Junction of the Sigmoid Colon and Rectum
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the landmark where the sigmoid colon terminates and becomes the rectum during a gross anatomy session. At which anatomical location does this transition occur?
options: Where it crosses the left common iliac artery
At the level of the pelvic inlet
At the level of the pelvic floor
In front of the sacrum
At the level of the iliac crest
correctOption: In front of the sacrum
optionExplanations: The inferior mesenteric artery becomes the superior rectal artery as it crosses the left common iliac artery, but this does not define the muscular junction of the gut tubes.
The pelvic inlet marks the beginning of the sigmoid colon as a continuation of the descending colon, not its termination into the rectum.
The pelvic floor is the site where the rectum terminates and becomes the anal canal, not where the sigmoid becomes the rectum.
According to the provided anatomical text, the sigmoid colon is an S-shaped loop that hangs in the pelvic cavity and specifically joins the rectum at the position in front of the sacrum.
The iliac crest is significantly superior to the pelvic cavity; the descending colon becomes the sigmoid colon further down at the pelvic brim/inlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The sigmoid colon begins at the pelvic inlet, where it is a continuation of the descending colon (see Fig. 7.1). It hangs down into the pelvic cavity in the form of an S-shaped loop. It joins the rectum in front of the sacrum.

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
coreConcept: Referred Pain Mechanisms in the LUQ
statement: A patient with a suspected subphrenic abscess on the left side complains of referred pain in the tip of the left shoulder. Considering the anatomical position of the spleen, which nerve is mediating this referred pain due to irritation of the overlying peritoneum?
options: Left Obturator nerve
Left Subcostal nerve (T12)
Left Phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5)
Left Vagus nerve
Left Intercostal nerve (T10)
correctOption: Left Phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5)
optionExplanations: The obturator nerve supplies the pelvic peritoneum and the medial thigh, unrelated to the subdiaphragmatic space.
The subcostal nerve (T12) supplies the lower abdominal wall and skin, not the central diaphragmatic peritoneum responsible for shoulder referral.

The spleen lies just beneath the diaphragm; irritation of the central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum (innervated by the phrenic nerve) refers pain to the C3-C4 dermatomes on the shoulder via common segmental origins.
The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the viscera but does not mediate somatic pain or shoulder-referred pain from the parietal peritoneum.
Intercostal nerves supply the peripheral diaphragmatic peritoneum; T10 would refer pain to the umbilicus, not the shoulder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The phrenic nerves supply the central part of the diaphragmatic peritoneum... The skin of the shoulder is supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4), which have the same segmental origin as the phrenic nerve.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
statement: A surgeon is performing a total gastrectomy for a patient with extensive gastric carcinoma. Based on the anatomical distribution of the lymphatic system in the stomach wall, why is it necessary to remove the greater omentum and the spleen as part of a radical procedure?
options: The short gastric arteries provide the only route for portal-systemic anastomosis
Gastric cancer strictly spreads via the portal vein only
Because the stomach is primarily supported by the falciform ligament
The spleen is the primary site of acid-producing cells in the abdomen
The lymphatic vessels of the mucous membrane are in continuity across the stomach wall
correctOption: The lymphatic vessels of the mucous membrane are in continuity across the stomach wall
optionExplanations: Short gastric arteries are branches of the splenic artery; portal-systemic anastomosis occurs primarily at the lower esophagus and anal canal.
Gastric cancer spreads via lymphatics first (celiac nodes) and bloodstream (portal vein) only in late stages; radical surgery targets the lymphatic field specifically.
The falciform ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall, not the stomach to the spleen.
Acid-producing cells (parietal cells) are located in the fundus and body of the stomach, not the spleen.

The intramural lymphatic plexus is continuous throughout the stomach, meaning cancer can spread widely within the wall, requiring en bloc removal of regional nodes in the omenta and ligaments (gastrosplenic/splenorenal).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Because the lymphatic vessels of the mucous membrane and submucosa of the stomach are in continuity, it is possible for cancer cells to travel to different parts of the stomach, some distance away from the primary site.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
coreConcept: Anatomic formation of the superficial inguinal ring
statement: The superficial inguinal ring is anatomically characterized as a structural deficit in which specific layer of the anterolateral abdominal wall?
options: Scarpa’s membranous fascia
Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle
Fascia of the internal oblique muscle
Transversalis fascia
Aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis
correctOption: Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle
optionExplanations: Scarpa's fascia is a superficial membranous layer of the subcutaneous tissue; while it is continuous with the fascia of the scrotum (Colles’ fascia), it does not form the anatomic boundaries of the inguinal rings themselves.

The superficial inguinal ring is precisely defined as a triangular hiatus or defect within the aponeurotic fibers of the external oblique muscle, located superior and medial to the pubic tubercle, serving as the exit for the spermatic cord or round ligament.
The internal oblique muscle contributes to the roof of the inguinal canal and the formation of the conjoint tendon, but it does not possess a defect that constitutes the superficial inguinal ring.

The transversalis fascia is the layer responsible for the formation of the deep inguinal ring, not the superficial ring. It provides the internal spermatic fascia as a covering for the cord structures as they enter the canal.

The transversus abdominis aponeurosis joins with the internal oblique to form the conjoint tendon, reinforcing the posterior wall of the canal, rather than forming the superficial ring in the anterior wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular-shaped defect in the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle and lies immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Pancreatic Neck and Portal Vein
statement: A 65-year-old male with a history of heavy smoking presents with significant weight loss and jaundice. Imaging confirms a mass in the head of the pancreas. During surgery, the surgeon notes the tumor is involving the junction of the veins that form the portal vein. At which anatomical landmark of the pancreas does this union occur?
options: Superior to the body
Anterior to the uncinate process
Posterior to the neck
Posterior to the tail
Within the major duodenal papilla
correctOption: Posterior to the neck
optionExplanations: The splenic vein runs behind the body, but the union with the superior mesenteric vein occurs further to the right.
The uncinate process is posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels, but the actual 'union' to form the portal vein is higher, behind the neck.
The neck of the pancreas is the crucial surgical landmark as it sits directly anterior to the formation of the portal vein by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins.
The tail is related to the splenic hilum; the portal vein has not yet formed at this lateral position.
The major duodenal papilla is the site of ductal entry into the duodenum, not a site for major venous junctions.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The portal vein is about 2 in. (5 cm) long and forms behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

category: Describe the nerve supply of Peritoneum
statement: The parietal peritoneum is uniquely sensitive to specific modalities of stimuli compared to the visceral layer. Which of the following sets of stimuli is the parietal peritoneum primarily sensitive to?
options: Stretch and chemical irritation only
Only tearing and mechanical distention
Only high-intensity crushing and ischemia
Pain, temperature, touch, and pressure
Autonomic distension and dull aching sensations
correctOption: Pain, temperature, touch, and pressure
optionExplanations: While chemical irritation can trigger parietal pain (as in a perforated ulcer), the parietal layer is also sensitive to touch, temperature, and pressure, which this option excludes.
Tearing and distention are the primary stimuli for the visceral peritoneum, whereas the parietal peritoneum is sensitive to the same modalities as the overlying skin.
Crushing and ischemia are typical triggers for visceral pain in certain organs, but the parietal peritoneum possesses somatic innervation, making it sensitive to finer modalities.
The parietal peritoneum receives somatic sensory innervation from the spinal nerves (lower thoracic and L1), allowing it to perceive sharp pain, temperature changes, touch, and localized pressure.
Autonomic distension and dull sensations are characteristic of visceral afferent pathways, not the somatic pathways of the parietal peritoneum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The parietal peritoneum, like the parietal pleura, is sensitive to pain, temperature, touch, and pressure.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
statement: During a physiological assessment, a student is asked to describe the multi-step mechanism by which concentrated bile is released into the duodenum. What is the primary hormonal trigger and its corresponding effect on the biliary tree?
options: Secretin induces relaxation of the gallbladder and contraction of the sphincter of Oddi.
Glucagon stimulates the cystic duct to dilate and the gallbladder to fill.
Cholecystokinin induces contraction of both the gallbladder and the sphincter of Oddi.
Gastrin stimulates the liver to produce bile and the gallbladder to relax.
Cholecystokinin induces contraction of the gallbladder and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.
correctOption: Cholecystokinin induces contraction of the gallbladder and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.
optionExplanations: Secretin primarily stimulates the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas and bile ducts, rather than regulating gallbladder motility.
Glucagon actually reduces the response of the sphincter of Oddi and does not stimulate gallbladder filling or cystic duct dilation in this context.
If both contracted, bile could not be expelled into the duodenum; CCK must cause a coordinated 'squeeze and open' effect.
Gastrin primarily affects gastric acid secretion and relaxes the ileocecal sphincter, but is not the primary mediator of gallbladder contraction.
Cholecystokinin (CCK), released by the duodenal mucosa in response to fat, triggers a coordinated reflex: gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The hormone then enters the blood, causing the gallbladder to contract. At the same time, the smooth muscle around the distal end of the bile duct and the ampulla is relaxed, thus allowing the passage of concentrated bile into the duodenum.

category: Draw and label the cutaneous innervation and dermatomes of anterior abdominal wall and anterolateral Abdominal wall and describe the clinical correlates
statement: What is the embryological origin of the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall, which explains their segmental innervation by the anterior rami of the spinal nerves?
options: Neural crest cells
Ectodermal somites
Somatopleuric mesoderm
Endoderm of the yolk sac
Splanchnic mesoderm
correctOption: Somatopleuric mesoderm
optionExplanations: Neural crest cells contribute to the adrenal medulla and peripheral ganglia, but not to the muscular sheets of the abdomen.
Ectoderm forms the skin and nervous system; the somites are mesodermal structures. Somatopleuric mesoderm is the specific derived term for the wall's origin in the text.
This is correct; the somatopleuric mesoderm splits to form the layers of the abdominal wall and retains its original segmental nerve supply from the spinal cord.
Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract, whereas the wall's muscle is mesodermal.
Splanchnic mesoderm gives rise to the muscle and serous coats of the gut tube itself, not the skeletal muscles of the abdominal wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The muscles of the anterior abdominal wall are derived from the somatopleuric mesoderm and retain their segmental innervation from the anterior rami of the spinal nerves.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of spleen
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of Splenic Trauma and Rib Fractures
statement: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a high-velocity motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals exquisite tenderness in the left upper quadrant, and a radiograph shows fractures of the left 9th and 10th ribs. He is tachycardic (120 bpm) and hypotensive (85/50 mmHg). Based on the anatomical location, which of the following is the most likely source of his internal hemorrhage?
options: Rupture of the left kidney
Perforation of the descending colon
Laceration of the spleen
Tear of the left lobe of the liver
Rupture of the left suprarenal gland
correctOption: Laceration of the spleen
optionExplanations: While the left kidney is posterior to the spleen, fractures of the 9th and 10th ribs in the midaxillary line are more classically associated with splenic injury rather than the deeper, more medial kidney.
Perforation of the descending colon would lead to peritonitis and potentially air in the retroperitoneum, but would not typically cause such rapid, severe hemorrhagic shock as a splenic rupture.
The spleen's location under the 9th-11th ribs makes it highly vulnerable to laceration following fractures of these ribs, leading to massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage and shock.
The left lobe of the liver is in the epigastrium and slightly to the left, but the right lobe is the primary site for hepatic trauma; the left 9th/10th ribs are far more lateral to the liver.
The suprarenal gland is small and deeply retroperitoneal; while it can be injured, it is rarely the source of life-threatening hypotension compared to the highly vascular spleen in this scenario.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Fractures of the lower ribs or penetrating wounds of the thorax or upper abdomen are common causes of liver injury... laceration of the spleen. ...automobile accidents of the crushing or run-over type commonly produce laceration of the spleen.

category: Describe anterolateral Abdominal wall arteries, Veins and Lymphatics and related clinical correlates—Caput Medusae
coreConcept: Deep Arterial Supply of the Rectus Sheath
statement: Which artery is the primary supplier of the upper central portion of the anterior abdominal wall, descending behind the rectus abdominis muscle?
options: Inferior epigastric artery
Deep circumflex iliac artery
Superior epigastric artery
Lumbar artery
Superficial epigastric artery
correctOption: Superior epigastric artery
optionExplanations: The inferior epigastric artery supplies the lower central part of the wall and ascends to meet the superior epigastric.
The deep circumflex iliac artery supplies the lower lateral part of the wall, not the upper central part.
Correct. As a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, it enters the sheath to supply the upper central region.
Lumbar arteries supply the lateral part of the abdominal wall, not the central rectus sheath region.
The superficial epigastric artery is a cutaneous branch of the femoral artery, not a deep vessel descending behind the rectus muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior epigastric artery, one of the terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery... descends behind the rectus abdominis muscle, supplying the upper central part of the anterior abdominal wall.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
statement: A surgeon performing a pancreatic resection must carefully manage the vascular relations of the organ. At which anatomical location does the superior mesenteric vein typically unite with the splenic vein to form the portal vein?
options: Anterior to the uncinate process
Behind the neck of the pancreas
Within the hepatoduodenal ligament
On the anterior surface of the third part of the duodenum
Superior to the celiac trunk
correctOption: Behind the neck of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The superior mesenteric vein passes anterior to the uncinate process of the pancreas, but the actual union with the splenic vein occurs more superiorly.
The neck of the pancreas is the definitive landmark for the formation of the portal vein, where the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein converge.
The portal vein travels within the hepatoduodenal ligament (part of the lesser omentum) after its formation, but it is formed more inferiorly behind the pancreas.
The superior mesenteric vein passes in front of the third part of the duodenum, but it does not form the portal vein until it reaches the pancreatic neck.
The portal vein formation is inferior to the celiac trunk; the celiac trunk arises from the aorta at T12, while the portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck (L1 level).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The portal vein is about 2 in. (5 cm) long and forms behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

category: Identify the borders, surfaces and Impressions of spleen
coreConcept: Splenic Hilum and Peritoneal Ligament Contents
statement: A surgeon is performing an emergency splenectomy following a blunt force trauma. While ligating the vessels within the splenorenal ligament, which anatomical structure must be carefully identified and preserved to avoid postoperative enzymatic autolysis?
options: The fundus of the stomach
The left suprarenal gland
The left colic flexure
The phrenicocolic ligament
The tail of the pancreas
correctOption: The tail of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The fundus of the stomach is connected to the spleen via the gastrosplenic omentum, not the splenorenal ligament.
The left suprarenal gland is retroperitoneal and superior to the kidney; it is not a content of the splenorenal ligament.
The left colic flexure is an anterior relation but is not found within the splenorenal ligament.
The phrenicocolic ligament is a peritoneal fold that supports the splenic flexure and prevents downward splenic enlargement but does not contain the splenic vessels or pancreas.
The tail of the pancreas is contained within the splenorenal ligament and reaches the hilum of the spleen. Damage to it during splenectomy can release pancreatic enzymes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The peritoneum also passes to the left kidney as the splenorenal ligament (carrying the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas).

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
statement: A 16-year-old female presents with severe postprandial nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain. Imaging reveals that the third part of her duodenum is being compressed against the vertebral column by an overlying vessel. Which vessel is most likely responsible for this compression, given its relationship to the duodenum's anterior surface?
options: Left renal vein
Portal vein
Superior mesenteric artery
Inferior mesenteric artery
Celiac artery
correctOption: Superior mesenteric artery
optionExplanations: While the left renal vein passes between the SMA and Aorta, it is usually the vessel being compressed (Nutcracker syndrome), not the one causing duodenal obstruction.
The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas, superior to the third part of the duodenum.
The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) crosses the third part of the duodenum anteriorly; an acute angle between the SMA and the aorta can compress the duodenum.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises at L3 but is located much further down and does not cross the anterior surface of the duodenum.
The celiac artery arises at T12, far superior to the third part of the duodenum which lies at L3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Anteriorly: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine, the superior mesenteric vessels contained within it, and coils of the jejunum.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of splenic trauma and splenomegaly
statement: A clinician is palpating a patient with suspected chronic myeloid leukemia and finds a large mass in the left upper quadrant. The mass is found to have a distinctively notched edge and is moving downward and medially during inspiration. Which anatomical factor primarily dictates the medial direction of this organ's enlargement?
options: The attachment of the falciform ligament to the diaphragm
The restrictive presence of the left colic flexure and phrenicocolic ligament
The proximity of the tail of the pancreas in the splenorenal ligament
The orientation of the long axis along the 10th rib
The traction of the gastrosplenic omentum
correctOption: The restrictive presence of the left colic flexure and phrenicocolic ligament
optionExplanations: The falciform ligament is a hepatic attachment and has no anatomical relationship with the splenic fossa or its enlargement patterns.

The left colic flexure and its supporting phrenicocolic ligament form a structural floor in the left hypochondrium, which physically blocks the spleen from enlarging directly downward, forcing it toward the umbilicus.
The tail of the pancreas is related to the splenic hilum but does not influence the gross direction of splenic expansion in splenomegaly.
The long axis along the 10th rib is the normal anatomical position; however, during enlargement, the constraints of the pelvic/colic structures override this initial orientation.
The gastrosplenic omentum connects the spleen to the stomach but does not provide the structural resistance that forces the spleen medially during hypertrophy.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A pathologically enlarged spleen extends downward and medially. The left colic flexure and the phrenicocolic ligament prevent a direct downward enlargement of the organ.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
statement: What is the specific name given to the two-layered fold of peritoneum that connects the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first inch of the duodenum to the liver?
options: Mesentery
Gastrosplenic ligament
Greater omentum
Lesser omentum
Falciform ligament
correctOption: Lesser omentum
optionExplanations: The term 'mesentery' specifically refers to the two-layered folds connecting parts of the intestines (like the jejunum and ileum) to the posterior abdominal wall.
The gastrosplenic ligament (or omentum) connects the upper part of the greater curvature of the stomach specifically to the hilum of the spleen.
The greater omentum connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon and hangs down like an apron over the small intestine.
The lesser omentum is a specific peritoneal fold consisting of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments, connecting the liver to the lesser curvature and proximal duodenum.
The falciform ligament is a peritoneal fold that connects the liver to the diaphragm and the anterior abdominal wall, rather than connecting viscera to viscera.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lesser omentum suspends the lesser curvature of the stomach and the proximal duodenum from the fissure of the ligamentum venosum and the porta hepatis on the undersurface of the liver.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of splenic trauma and splenomegaly
statement: The development of the spleen is unique among abdominal organs. From which embryological structure does the spleen primarily originate?
options: Mesenchyme in the dorsal mesentery
Ectodermal thickening of the body wall
Septum transversum
Neural crest cells
Entodermal bud from the foregut
correctOption: Mesenchyme in the dorsal mesentery
optionExplanations: The spleen is a mesodermal organ that develops from the mesenchyme between the layers of the dorsal mesogastrium (dorsal mesentery).
The spleen is not an ectodermal derivative; it is lymphoid and mesenchymal in origin.
The septum transversum contributes to the liver and the diaphragm.
Neural crest cells form the adrenal medulla, not the spleen.
The liver and pancreas develop from entodermal buds; the spleen does not.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen develops as a thickening of the mesenchyme in the dorsal mesentery.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
statement: In surface anatomy, where is the base of the vermiform appendix typically located relative to the anterior abdominal wall landmarks?
options: At the midpoint of the intertubercular plane
One-third of the way up the line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
Two inches inferior to the right ninth costal cartilage
At the intersection of the right vertical line and the subcostal plane
Halfway between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus in the linea alba
correctOption: One-third of the way up the line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
optionExplanations: The intertubercular plane is lower (L5 level) and used to divide the abdomen into regions, not to locate the appendix.
McBurney’s point is the surface projection of the base of the appendix, defined as one-third the distance from the right ASIS to the umbilicus.
This location corresponds more closely to the fundus of the gallbladder (near the 9th costal cartilage), not the appendix.
The intersection of the subcostal plane and the right vertical line is usually in the right hypochondrium, often associated with the liver or gallbladder.
This describes the epigastric region or the site for an epigastric hernia, far superior to the location of the appendix.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In relation to the anterior abdominal wall, its base is situated one third of the way up the line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus (McBurney’s point).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
statement: The pancreas is an elongated organ that lies across the posterior abdominal wall. Which of its parts is correctly described as lying on the transpyloric plane?
options: Body
Head
Neck
Tail
Uncinate process
correctOption: Neck
optionExplanations: The body is described as being situated above and to the left of the transpyloric plane.
The head of the pancreas is situated below and to the right of the transpyloric plane.
The neck of the pancreas is the specific anatomical portion that crosses the transpyloric plane (L1 level).
The tail lies above and to the left of the transpyloric plane, usually reaching the level of the hila of the kidneys.
The uncinate process is the lowest part of the head and lies well below the transpyloric plane.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pancreas lies across the transpyloric plane. The head lies below and to the right, the neck lies on the plane, and the body and tail lie above and to the left.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
statement: A 70-year-old male with a history of chronic gallstones presents with small bowel obstruction. A large gallstone is found impacted at the ileocecal junction. Based on the anatomical relations of the gallbladder, through which structure did the stone most likely ulcerate to enter the gastrointestinal tract?
options: The tail of the pancreas
The transverse colon
The right kidney
The second part of the duodenum
The fundus of the stomach
correctOption: The second part of the duodenum
optionExplanations: The tail of the pancreas is located on the left side of the abdomen and is not in contact with the gallbladder.
While gallstones can ulcerate into the transverse colon, this usually results in the stone being passed in the stool rather than causing a high-grade small bowel obstruction.
The right kidney is a posterior relation of the liver and gallbladder, but stones ulcerating into the urinary system is not a standard mechanism for bowel obstruction.

The gallbladder body lies in close posterior relation to the first and second parts of the duodenum. Ulceration into the duodenum allows a large stone to enter the small intestine, where it often becomes trapped at the narrowest point—the ileocecal junction (Gallstone Ileus).
The stomach is a posterior relation, but the duodenum is more commonly involved in the formation of cholecysto-enteric fistulas leading to obstruction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Gallstones may ulcerate through the gallbladder wall into the transverse colon or the duodenum. In the former case, they are passed naturally per the rectum, but in the latter case, they may be held up at the ileocecal junction, producing intestinal obstruction.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
statement: A 19-year-old male presents with periumbilical pain that has migrated to the right iliac fossa over 8 hours. His WBC is 14,000/mm³. On physical exam, there is no rebound tenderness in the RLQ, but the patient experiences intense pain when the clinician performs a digital rectal exam and palpates the right side of the rectovesical pouch. Which appendiceal position most likely accounts for these findings?
options: Subcecal, lying on the iliacus muscle
Pre-ileal, anterior to the mesenteric vessels
Pelvic, hanging against the right pelvic wall
Retrocecal, lying in the retrocecal recess
Paracecal, lateral to the ascending colon
correctOption: Pelvic, hanging against the right pelvic wall
optionExplanations: A subcecal appendix is too high to be easily palpated or to cause focal tenderness in the deep pelvic pouches via a rectal exam.
Pre-ileal appendices are anterior and would typically cause very localized, early anterior abdominal wall tenderness.

A pelvic appendix hangs into the pelvic cavity and sits near the rectum/bladder. Its inflammation irritates the pelvic peritoneum, causing pain on rectal exam while sparing the anterior abdominal wall.
A retrocecal appendix often lacks RLQ tenderness but would not typically produce tenderness localized to the rectovesical pouch on a rectal exam.
A paracecal appendix is lateral and superior; it would cause flank or high RLQ pain, not tenderness accessible via the rectum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An appendix hanging down in the pelvis may result in absent abdominal tenderness in the right lower quadrant... Rectal or vaginal examination may reveal tenderness of the peritoneum in the pelvis on the right side.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
statement: In a patient with gastric cancer, the celiac lymph nodes are identified as the terminal destination of the disease's lymphatic spread. Around which major anatomical landmark are these celiac nodes precisely located?
options: The bifurcation of the aorta at the L4 level.
The root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall.
The anterior surface of the gallbladder fundus.
The hilum of the right kidney only.
The superior border of the symphysis pubis.
correctOption: The root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall.
optionExplanations: The bifurcation of the aorta at L4 marks the origin of the common iliac arteries, where iliac nodes are located, not the celiac nodes.
The celiac nodes are clustered at the origin (root) of the celiac artery from the abdominal aorta, situated at the T12/L1 level on the posterior abdominal wall.
The gallbladder fundus is located at the ninth costal cartilage; while cystic nodes are nearby, the terminal celiac nodes are deeper on the posterior wall.
The right kidney hilum contains renal lymph nodes; while these drain to para-aortic nodes, they are not the specific terminal station for gastric lymph.
The symphysis pubis is a pelvic landmark; no visceral gastric lymph nodes are located in this inferior position.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": All lymph from the stomach eventually passes to the celiac nodes located around the root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
statement: Clinical examination of a patient with a suspected perforated duodenal ulcer reveals tenderness and guarding that has shifted from the epigastrium to the right iliac fossa. Which anatomical feature explains this diagnostic contrast in the spread of inflammatory fluid?
options: The retrocecal recess providing a direct channel to the lesser sac.
The transverse colon directing fluid into the right lateral paracolic gutter.
The attachment of the mesoappendix to the ascending colon.
The phrenicocolic ligament directing fluid into the left paracolic gutter.
The sigmoid mesocolon sequestering fluid in the pelvic cavity.
correctOption: The transverse colon directing fluid into the right lateral paracolic gutter.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The retrocecal recess is a pocket behind the cecum and does not connect the duodenum to the right iliac fossa in this manner.

Correct. Fluid from a perforated duodenal ulcer is physically directed by the transverse colon into the right lateral paracolic gutter, where it travels down to the right iliac fossa, mimicking appendicitis.
Incorrect. The mesoappendix is a mesentery for the appendix and does not act as a primary channel for fluid spread from the duodenum.
Incorrect. The phrenicocolic ligament is on the left side and usually restricts fluid spread from the splenic flexure region.
Incorrect. The sigmoid mesocolon is in the left lower quadrant and would not explain the shift to the right iliac fossa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An ulcer of the anterior wall of the first inch of the duodenum may perforate into the upper part of the greater sac, above the transverse colon. The transverse colon directs the escaping fluid into the right lateral paracolic gutter and thus down to the right iliac fossa.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
coreConcept: Posterior Relations of the Bile Duct
statement: During a surgical dissection, a resident is identifying the three parts of the bile duct. Which structure is the primary posterior relation of the second part of the bile duct as it descends?
options: The portal vein
The gastroduodenal artery
The right margin of the pancreatic head
The first part of the duodenum
The inferior vena cava
correctOption: The inferior vena cava
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The portal vein lies posterior to the first part of the bile duct in the free margin of the lesser omentum.
Incorrect. The gastroduodenal artery lies to the left of the second part of the bile duct, not posterior to it.
Incorrect. The head of the pancreas is a medial and inferior relation to the second part of the duct; the duct enters the pancreatic groove in its third part.
Incorrect. The first part of the duodenum is an anterior relation to the second part of the bile duct, not a posterior one.
Correct. In its second part, behind the duodenum, the bile duct is related posteriorly to the inferior vena cava.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the second part of its course, it is situated behind the first part of the duodenum... to the right of the gastroduodenal artery. [Earlier section notes] Posteriorly: Inferior vena cava.

category: Describe the anatomical basis for Sigmoidoscopy, rectal prolapse, rectal examination, rectal cancer and hemorrhoids
statement: During the development of internal hemorrhoids, which physiological factor facilitates the reversal of blood flow from the portal system to the systemic venous system in the anal canal?
options: The low pressure within the portal venous system compared to the systemic system
The high oxygen content of portal blood
The presence of one-way valves in the portal vein
The contraction of the internal anal sphincter
The lack of valves in the portal vein and its tributaries
correctOption: The lack of valves in the portal vein and its tributaries
optionExplanations: In the case of portal hypertension, the pressure in the portal system is higher than the systemic system, which is what drives the blood into the systemic veins.
The portal vein carries deoxygenated blood rich in nutrients from the GI tract; its oxygen content is not the driver of shunting or hemorrhoid development.
The portal venous system is unique because it lacks valves, meaning blood can flow in reverse if pressure gradients change, which is the opposite of a one-way valve system.
The internal anal sphincter is a smooth muscle that regulates defecation; its contraction does not facilitate the portal-systemic shunting of blood.

The portal vein and its tributaries (like the superior rectal vein) do not have valves. When portal hypertension occurs (e.g., due to cirrhosis), blood is forced backward into collateral routes, such as the anorectal anastomosis, leading to hemorrhoids.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Should the portal vein become obstructed (e.g., in cirrhosis of the liver), portal hypertension develops, resulting in dilatation and varicosity of the portal–systemic anastomoses.

category: Describe the formation of superficial and deep inguinal rings and conjoint tendon
statement: Which of the following layers of the anterolateral abdominal wall is directly responsible for the formation of the deep inguinal ring?
options: Extraperitoneal fascia
Internal oblique muscle
Parietal peritoneum
External oblique aponeurosis
Transversalis fascia
correctOption: Transversalis fascia
optionExplanations: The extraperitoneal fascia is a fatty layer deep to the transversalis fascia; it does not form the margins of the ring.
The internal oblique muscle contributes to the roof and the cremasteric fascia, but it does not form the deep ring.
The parietal peritoneum is the deepest layer; while it evaginates as the processus vaginalis, the 'ring' itself is defined by the transversalis fascia.
The external oblique aponeurosis forms the superficial inguinal ring, not the deep ring.
The deep inguinal ring is a specific anatomical defect or opening within the transversalis fascia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The deep inguinal ring, an oval opening in the transversalis fascia, lies about 0.5 in. (1.3 cm) above the inguinal ligament

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
coreConcept: Pathophysiological Mechanism of Obstructive Jaundice in Pancreatic Head Tumors
statement: A 62-year-old patient presents with a progressive, painless yellowish discoloration of the sclera and skin. Imaging reveals a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which anatomical relationship best explains the development of obstructive jaundice in this specific pathology?
options: The uncinate process of the head of the pancreas extends to the left, anterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
The main pancreatic duct joins the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla in the third part of the duodenum.
The head of the pancreas is surrounded by the first, second, and third parts of the duodenum on its lateral and inferior borders.
The bile duct lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas before entering the duodenum.
The head of the pancreas lies anterior to the portal vein and the beginning of the superior mesenteric artery.
correctOption: The bile duct lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas before entering the duodenum.
optionExplanations: The uncinate process lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels, not anteriorly, and its compression of these vessels would cause vascular or intestinal issues rather than jaundice.
The ducts typically join in the second (descending) part of the duodenum, not the third (horizontal) part.
While the duodenum's concavity houses the pancreatic head, this anatomical wrap-around describes the head's general position rather than the specific mechanism of biliary compression.

The common bile duct passes through a groove (or sometimes a tunnel) on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic head. Consequently, any enlargement of the head, such as a carcinoma, easily compresses the duct, leading to bile stasis and jaundice.
While the neck of the pancreas lies anterior to the portal vein, this relationship does not directly explain biliary obstruction unless the tumor is massive.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the third part of its course, it [the bile duct] lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (see Fig. 7.29). ... Because of the close relation of the head of the pancreas to the bile duct, cancer of the head of the pancreas often causes obstructive jaundice.

category: Identify the borders, surfaces and Impressions of spleen
statement: Which specific abdominal organ lies in direct contact with the medial border of the spleen, situated between the stomach and the left kidney in the splenic visceral impressions?
options: The left colic flexure
The transverse colon
The left suprarenal gland
The tail of the pancreas
The left psoas muscle
correctOption: The tail of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The left colic flexure is related to the lower part of the spleen's anterior surface.
The transverse colon is related anteriorly and inferiorly, but not specifically the medial border.
The left suprarenal gland is in the retroperitoneal space and while nearby, it is not listed as the primary medial border contact compared to the kidney and pancreas.
The tail of the pancreas is one of the three major anterior/visceral relations and specifically sits between the stomach and kidney impressions at the hilum/medial area.
The left psoas muscle is a posterior abdominal wall structure, not a visceral relation of the spleen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Anteriorly: The stomach, tail of the pancreas, and left colic flexure. The left kidney lies along its medial border.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
statement: A 24-year-old male with a history of rapid weight loss presents with symptoms of high intestinal obstruction. Imaging suggests the third part of the duodenum is being compressed between two major vascular structures. Which vessels are involved in this compression?
options: Portal vein and the Hepatic artery
Gastroduodenal artery and the Hepatic artery
Inferior mesenteric artery and the Aorta
Celiac trunk and the Inferior Vena Cava
Superior mesenteric artery and the Aorta
correctOption: Superior mesenteric artery and the Aorta
optionExplanations: The portal vein and hepatic artery are located in the lesser omentum superior to the first part of the duodenum, not involved with the third part's relations.
The gastroduodenal artery lies posterior to the first part of the duodenum, not the third part.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises at the L3 level but is located much lower than the site of duodenal passage and does not cross over the duodenum to create a compression point.
The celiac trunk is located at the level of T12, significantly superior to the third part of the duodenum which lies at L3.

The third part of the duodenum runs horizontally between the aorta (posteriorly) and the superior mesenteric artery/vein (anteriorly) within the root of the mesentery. Significant weight loss can reduce the mesenteric fat cushion, causing the SMA to compress the duodenum against the aorta.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Anteriorly: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine, the superior mesenteric vessels contained within it... Posteriorly: The right ureter, the right psoas muscle, the inferior vena cava, and the aorta.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of splenic trauma and splenomegaly
statement: A newborn is found to have three small, accessory masses of splenic tissue located near the hilum of the primary spleen. What is the developmental basis for these 'supernumerary spleens'?
options: Herniation of the midgut loop into the umbilicus
Abnormal budding from the foregut entoderm
Atrophy of the vitelline duct during the fifth week
Partial rotation of the ventral mesentery
Failure of mesenchymal masses to fuse in the dorsal mesentery
correctOption: Failure of mesenchymal masses to fuse in the dorsal mesentery
optionExplanations: The midgut loop is involved in the development of the intestines, not the spleen, which is a foregut-associated mesenchymal organ.
The spleen is mesodermal/mesenchymal in origin, unlike the liver and pancreas, which are entodermal outgrowths of the gut tube.
The vitelline duct is associated with the midgut and Meckel's diverticulum, and it has no role in splenic development.
The ventral mesentery gives rise to the liver and its ligaments, whereas the spleen develops entirely within the dorsal mesentery.
The spleen develops from several mesenchymal masses in the dorsal mesentery. If these masses fail to fuse completely with the main organ, they remain as accessory or supernumerary spleens.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the earliest stages, the spleen consists of a number of mesenchymal masses that later fuse. The notches along its anterior border are permanent and indicate that the mesenchymal masses never completely fuse.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice, clay-colored stools, and significant weight loss. Physical examination reveals a palpable, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign). Imaging confirms a malignant mass in the head of the pancreas. Which anatomical relationship best explains the development of obstructive jaundice in this patient?
options: Compression of the portal vein as it forms behind the neck of the pancreas
The bile duct passing through a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head
The body of the pancreas obstructing the left renal vein
The tail of the pancreas compressing the splenic hilum
Obstruction of the accessory duct at the minor duodenal papilla
correctOption: The bile duct passing through a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreatic head
optionExplanations: Compression of the portal vein would lead to portal hypertension (splenomegaly, ascites, etc.), not direct obstructive jaundice and clay-colored stools.

The bile duct travels behind the first part of the duodenum and then occupies a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic head. A mass in the head easily compresses the duct, leading to bile backup and jaundice.
While the body of the pancreas is anterior to the left kidney and renal vein, its compression would cause venous congestion, not obstructive jaundice.
The tail of the pancreas is related to the spleen; its involvement would not cause biliary obstruction or jaundice.
The accessory duct only drains a small portion of the pancreas; its obstruction does not affect the main biliary flow from the liver to the duodenum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the third part of its course, it lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas... Because of the close relation of the head of the pancreas to the bile duct, cancer of the head of the pancreas often causes obstructive jaundice.

category: Identify the borders, surfaces and Impressions of spleen
statement: The long axis of the spleen is most closely aligned with which of the following skeletal structures?
options: The shaft of the 9th rib
The spine of the 12th thoracic vertebra
The shaft of the 11th rib
The shaft of the 10th rib
The transpyloric plane
correctOption: The shaft of the 10th rib
optionExplanations: The 9th rib covers the upper part of the spleen but does not define its long axis.
The spleen is related to the ribs, not the thoracic spines directly, and is located more laterally.
The 11th rib covers the lower part of the spleen.
Anatomically, the spleen's long axis is tilted and runs parallel to the 10th rib on the left side.
The transpyloric plane (L1) is related to the hila of the kidneys and the pancreas, but the spleen is higher and more lateral.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen is situated in the left upper quadrant and lies under cover of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs. Its long axis corresponds to that of the 10th rib.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Autonomic Control of the Pyloric Sphincter
statement: A medical student is asked to demonstrate the physiological control of the pyloric sphincter on a cadaveric specimen. Which statement accurately describes the autonomic and local regulation of this anatomic feature?
options: The pyloric sphincter receives motor fibers from the sympathetic system and inhibitory fibers from the vagi.
Hormonal control is absent, as the sphincter is regulated exclusively by myenteric reflexes.
Sympathetic fibers from the celiac plexus provide inhibitory signals to the sphincter.
The circular muscle of the pylorus is thinner than the longitudinal layer to facilitate rapid emptying.
The vagus nerves provide motor fibers that cause the sphincter to contract.
correctOption: The pyloric sphincter receives motor fibers from the sympathetic system and inhibitory fibers from the vagi.
optionExplanations: Regulation of the pyloric sphincter is a balance where sympathetic nerves cause contraction (motor) and parasympathetic (vagal) nerves cause relaxation (inhibitory), allowing coordinated gastric emptying.
Hormonal control is significant; for instance, gastrin from the antrum can influence the sphincter's tone, and local stretching also plays a role through the myenteric plexus.
The sympathetic system provides motor innervation to the sphincter, promoting its contraction and delaying gastric emptying; it does not provide inhibitory signals.
The circular muscle layer at the pylorus is significantly thickened to form the anatomical sphincter; it is much thicker than the longitudinal layer.
The vagus nerves (parasympathetic) are actually inhibitory to the pyloric sphincter, meaning they promote relaxation and allow chyme to pass into the duodenum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pyloric sphincter receives motor fibers from the sympathetic system and inhibitory fibers from the vagi.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Appendicular Base
statement: During an emergency laparotomy for suspected appendicitis, the surgeon successfully identifies the cecum but cannot immediately visualize the vermiform appendix. Which anatomical feature serves as the most reliable surgical landmark to locate the base of the appendix?
options: The convergence of the three teniae coli
The termination of the ileocolic artery's inferior branch
The superior margin of the ileocecal valve
The lateral border of the mesoappendix
The junction of the right colic and ileocolic flexures
correctOption: The convergence of the three teniae coli
optionExplanations: The teniae coli are three distinct bands of longitudinal muscle that run along the length of the large intestine. On the cecum, these bands invariably converge at the exact point where the appendix originates, making them the gold-standard surgical landmark for locating the base.

While the ileocolic artery provides the blood supply, its terminal branches are variable and often obscured by inflammatory fat or adhesions, making them unreliable landmarks compared to muscle bands.
The ileocecal valve is located superior to the appendicular orifice. While it is a landmark for the terminal ileum, it does not directly lead to the base of the appendix as reliably as the teniae.

The mesoappendix is a peritoneal fold carrying the appendicular artery. In cases of inflammation or variable tip positions (like retrocecal), the mesoappendix can be distorted or hidden, whereas the teniae are structural parts of the cecal wall.
The right colic flexure (hepatic flexure) is located much higher in the right upper quadrant and is unrelated to the immediate anatomical search for the appendicular base in the right iliac fossa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Inside the abdomen, the base of the appendix is easily found by identifying the teniae coli of the cecum and tracing them to the base of the appendix, where they converge to form a continuous longitudinal muscle coat

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
coreConcept: Greater Omentum and Localization of Infection
statement: A 22-year-old male with a 48-hour history of untreated appendicitis presents with a palpable, tender mass in the right iliac fossa. A surgeon explains that the body has 'localized' the infection. Which structure is primarily responsible for this manifestation via the formation of peritoneal adhesions?
options: The gastrosplenic ligament
The greater omentum
The falciform ligament
The parietal peritoneum of the paracolic gutter
The mesentery of the jejunum
correctOption: The greater omentum
optionExplanations: The gastrosplenic ligament is a specific connection between the stomach and spleen and does not have the generalized protective role of the greater omentum.
The greater omentum is mobile and known as the 'abdominal policeman' because it migrates to and wraps around inflamed viscera to localize infection.
The falciform ligament is a fixed structure connecting the liver to the anterior wall; it does not move to 'wrap' infections.
The parietal peritoneum is fixed and cannot wrap itself around an organ to form a localized mass.
The mesentery is attached to the small intestine and is not typically the structure that 'polices' the abdomen and wraps distant organs like the appendix.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The greater omentum... in an acutely inflamed appendix, for example, the inflammatory exudate causes the omentum to adhere to the appendix and wrap itself around the infected organ. By this means, the infection is often localized to a small area of the peritoneal cavity.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
statement: A 70-year-old patient with a history of long-standing gallstones presents with symptoms of small-bowel obstruction. Imaging reveals a large gallstone lodged in the terminal ileum. Anatomically, which relationship explains how a gallstone could directly enter the intestinal tract without passing through the bile duct?
options: The cystic duct lies anterior to the superior mesenteric vein.
The gallbladder fundus is in contact with the sigmoid colon.
The gallbladder body and neck are in close contact with the transverse colon and the duodenum.
The gallbladder lies in the fissure for the ligamentum teres.
The gallbladder is suspended by the transverse mesocolon.
correctOption: The gallbladder body and neck are in close contact with the transverse colon and the duodenum.
optionExplanations: The cystic duct relation to the superior mesenteric vein does not facilitate the formation of a fistula for stone passage into the intestinal lumen.
The fundus is near the anterior abdominal wall and the transverse colon, but the sigmoid colon is a pelvic organ, distant from the gallbladder.
Because the gallbladder lies directly against the duodenum and transverse colon, chronic inflammation can lead to fistulae, allowing stones to enter the gut (gallstone ileus).
The gallbladder lies in its own fossa on the visceral surface of the liver, not in the fissure for the ligamentum teres (which contains the round ligament).
The gallbladder is not suspended by the mesocolon; it is attached to the liver and suspended from the stomach by the lesser omentum via its ducts.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Posteriorly: The transverse colon and the first and second parts of the duodenum... Gallstones may ulcerate through the gallbladder wall into the transverse colon or the duodenum.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
statement: When an individual is in a fasting state (not actively digesting food), what is the physiological state of the biliary tree components?
options: The sphincter of Oddi is closed and bile is diverted into the gallbladder.
The cystic duct is constricted by the spiral valve to prevent storage.
Bile flows continuously into the duodenum through an open ampulla.
The hepatic ducts stop secreting bile until CCK is released.
The gallbladder is contracting and the sphincter of Oddi is open.
correctOption: The sphincter of Oddi is closed and bile is diverted into the gallbladder.
optionExplanations: Correct. During fasting, the sphincter of Oddi is closed, causing bile secreted by the liver to back up through the cystic duct into the gallbladder for storage.
Incorrect. The spiral valve (valve of Heister) in the cystic duct functions to keep the lumen open, not to constrict it.
Incorrect. If bile flowed continuously, the gallbladder would not be able to store and concentrate it between meals.
Incorrect. The liver secretes bile at a constant rate (~40 mL/hour) regardless of the digestive state; it is stored, not stopped.
Incorrect. This describes the state during digestion (stimulated by CCK).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": When digestion is not taking place, the sphincter of Oddi remains closed, and bile is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder.

category: Identify the borders, surfaces and Impressions of spleen
statement: A radiologist is reviewing a CT scan of the abdomen and identifies the spleen. They note the relationships of the visceral surface. Which structure would the radiologist expect to see located immediately medial to the hilum of the spleen, creating a deep longitudinal impression?
options: The abdominal aorta
The descending colon
The left kidney
The left suprarenal gland
The right lobe of the liver
correctOption: The left kidney
optionExplanations: The abdominal aorta is a midline structure and is separated from the spleen by the left kidney and the tail of the pancreas.
The descending colon is inferior to the spleen; the left colic flexure is the structure that touches the lower pole.
The left kidney is the primary medial relation of the spleen, creating the renal impression on the visceral surface between the hilum and the posterior border.
While the left suprarenal gland is near the kidney, it does not typically create a distinct, large impression on the spleen like the kidney does.
The right lobe of the liver is on the opposite side of the abdomen and does not relate to the spleen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The left kidney lies along its medial border (see Figs. 7.5 and 7.11).

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
statement: A 52-year-old female undergoes a rectal examination. The physician considers the peritoneal relations of the rectum. Which statement accurately describes the peritoneal covering of the middle third of the rectum?
options: It is covered by peritoneum on its anterior and lateral surfaces.
It is completely covered by peritoneum and has a short mesentery.
It is covered by peritoneum only on its posterior surface.
It is covered by peritoneum only on its anterior surface.
It is entirely retroperitoneal with no peritoneal covering.
correctOption: It is covered by peritoneum only on its anterior surface.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes the upper third of the rectum.
Incorrect. The rectum does not have a mesentery; only the sigmoid colon does.
Incorrect. The rectum is never covered posteriorly by peritoneum as it lies against the sacrum.
Correct. Classically, the upper third is covered anteriorly and laterally, the middle third only anteriorly, and the lower third is entirely subperitoneal.
Incorrect. The rectum is not entirely devoid of peritoneum; its upper parts are covered.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", The rectum occupies the posterior part of the pelvic cavity... Note that the regions are, in reality, a single, continuous space... [Chapter 9 details omitted, but Page 809/812 sections describe omenta and retroperitoneal organs].

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
statement: In a vertical (sagittal) trace of the peritoneal reflections, which structure is identified as a two-layered fold that suspends the lesser curvature of the stomach and the proximal duodenum from the liver?
options: Falciform ligament
Greater omentum
Transverse mesocolon
Gastrosplenic ligament
Lesser omentum
correctOption: Lesser omentum
optionExplanations: The falciform ligament is a reflection that connects the anterior and superior surfaces of the liver to the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall, rather than the stomach.
The greater omentum is a four-layered reflection that hangs from the greater curvature and attaches to the transverse colon, not the liver.
The transverse mesocolon is a reflection of the posterior abdominal wall that suspends the transverse colon.
The gastrosplenic ligament is a horizontal reflection connecting the stomach's greater curvature to the splenic hilum.
The lesser omentum is a primary vertical reflection connecting the lesser curvature and proximal duodenum to the liver's visceral surface.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lesser omentum suspends the lesser curvature of the stomach and the proximal duodenum from the fissure of the ligamentum venosum and the porta hepatis on the undersurface of the liver.

category: Describe the formation, tributaries and drainage of hepatic-portal vein
statement: A 62-year-old female is diagnosed with a tumor of the gallbladder that has invaded the portal system. Considering the drainage of the gallbladder, how does the majority of its venous blood enter the portal circulation?
options: Via the cystic veins into the left gastric vein.
Via the cystic veins into the inferior mesenteric vein.
Via the cystic veins into the portal vein or directly into the liver.
Via the cystic veins into the superior mesenteric vein.
Via the cystic veins directly into the splenic vein.
correctOption: Via the cystic veins into the portal vein or directly into the liver.
optionExplanations: The left gastric vein drains the lesser curvature of the stomach and is not involved in the drainage of the gallbladder.
The inferior mesenteric vein is far removed from the gallbladder, as it drains the hindgut and enters the splenic vein behind the pancreas.

Venous drainage of the gallbladder is primarily through the cystic veins. These veins may either enter the liver directly (through the gallbladder bed into liver sinusoids) or join the main trunk of the portal vein near the porta hepatis.
While the cystic veins are in the general region of the SMV's terminus, they are primarily described as entering the main portal vein trunk or the liver sinusoids directly.

The cystic veins do not typically drain into the splenic vein, as the gallbladder is located on the right side and its drainage is more closely associated with the porta hepatis or the liver substance itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Cystic veins: These veins either drain the gallbladder directly into the liver or join the portal vein

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Pancreatic Head
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. Imaging confirms a mass in the pancreas obstructing the common bile duct. Based on the anatomical relations, which part of the pancreas is most likely involved?
options: Head of the pancreas
Uncinate process
Body of the pancreas
Tail of the pancreas
Neck of the pancreas
correctOption: Head of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-loop of the duodenum and is traversed posteriorly or grooved by the bile duct; tumors in this location frequently compress the duct, leading to jaundice and Courvoisier's sign (palpable gallbladder).
