statement: When distinguishing between various sites of portosystemic anastomosis, which systemic vessels at the 'anorectal junction' are responsible for receiving portal blood during hypertension?
options: Inferior mesenteric vein via sigmoidal branches
Lumbar and phrenic veins via retroperitoneal organs
Internal and external iliac veins via middle and inferior rectal veins
Superior rectal veins
Paraumbilical veins via the ligamentum teres
correctOption: Internal and external iliac veins via middle and inferior rectal veins
optionExplanations: The inferior mesenteric vein is the portal trunk that gives rise to the superior rectal vein; it is not the systemic recipient at this junction.
Lumbar and phrenic veins participate in the retroperitoneal portosystemic anastomotic sites (Retzius), not the anorectal site.

The middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal/internal iliac) veins are the systemic vessels that receive the diverted blood from the portal superior rectal vein.
The superior rectal vein is the portal component of this anastomosis, not the systemic recipient of the shunted blood.
Paraumbilical veins are involved in the umbilical anastomosis, not the anorectal one.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Halfway down the anal canal, the superior rectal veins (portal tributary) draining the upper half of the anal canal anastomose with the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic tributaries), which are tributaries of the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins, respectively.

category: Describe the origin, course, branches (tributaries in case of veins) and distribution of the blood vessels of GIT
statement: A 72-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe periumbilical pain. Physical examination shows a soft, non-distended abdomen with only minimal tenderness, representing a 'pain out of proportion to exam' clinical picture. Considering the vascular distribution of the midgut, which vessel is most likely occluded by an embolus?
options: Gastroduodenal artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Celiac trunk
Common iliac artery
Inferior mesenteric artery
correctOption: Superior mesenteric artery
optionExplanations: The gastroduodenal artery supplies the stomach and duodenum but is too small a vessel to cause the generalized midgut ischemia described in this severe clinical presentation.
The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) supplies the entire midgut. Embolic occlusion is a common cause of acute mesenteric ischemia, characterized by sudden severe pain and few physical findings.
Occlusion of the celiac trunk would primarily affect the foregut (stomach, liver, spleen), which typically presents with epigastric rather than periumbilical pain.
Occlusion of a common iliac artery would primarily cause lower limb ischemia (pulselessness, coldness, pain), not the visceral abdominal ischemia typical of SMA syndrome.
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut (distal transverse colon to rectum); its occlusion is less likely to present with sudden periumbilical pain and 'pain out of proportion'.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The superior mesenteric artery, a branch of the abdominal aorta, supplies an extensive territory of the gut, from halfway down the second part of the duodenum to the left colic flexure.

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
statement: A senior registrar is explaining the final pathway of lymphatic clearance for the stomach. Which group of lymph nodes serves as the ultimate collection point through which all gastric lymph eventually passes before reaching the cisterna chyli?
options: Celiac lymph nodes
Superior mesenteric nodes
Splenic lymph nodes
Hepatic nodes
Left gastric nodes
correctOption: Celiac lymph nodes
optionExplanations: The celiac lymph nodes, situated at the root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall, represent the final common pathway for all lymphatic channels originating from the stomach, including those from the gastric and gastroepiploic groups.

Superior mesenteric nodes primarily drain the midgut, from the lower duodenum to the distal transverse colon; while they communicate with celiac nodes, they are not the primary terminal for the stomach.

Splenic nodes receive drainage from the fundus and upper greater curvature via short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels, but they are an intermediate station that eventually drains into the celiac group.
Hepatic nodes receive lymph from the liver and gallbladder and drain into the celiac nodes; they do not serve as the terminal collection point for the entire stomach's lymphatic system.

Left gastric nodes are regional nodes located along the lesser curvature; while they receive a significant portion of gastric lymph, they must further drain into the celiac nodes for terminal clearance.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": All lymph from the stomach eventually passes to the celiac nodes located around the root of the celiac artery on the posterior abdominal wall.

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Anatomical Basis of Referred Pain in Appendicitis
statement: A 15-year-old boy presents with a 6-hour history of vague periumbilical pain. Following the physiological mechanism of visceral pain referral, why does early appendiceal inflammation present at this specific anatomical location?
options: The phrenic nerve carries referred pain from the mesoappendix to the dermatome of the umbilicus.
Afferent pain fibers from the appendix enter the spinal cord at the T7 level.
The appendix and the umbilicus share a common somatic nerve supply from the obturator nerve.
The appendix is anatomically situated directly posterior to the umbilical scar.
Visceral afferents from the appendix accompany sympathetic nerves to the T10 spinal segment.
correctOption: Visceral afferents from the appendix accompany sympathetic nerves to the T10 spinal segment.
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) carries sensation from the central diaphragmatic peritoneum to the shoulder (C3-C4 dermatomes), not the umbilicus (T10). Jointly, the mesoappendix is innervated by sympathetic plexuses, not the phrenic nerve.
T7 is the dermatome for the xiphoid process, not the umbilicus. Pain from the foregut, such as the stomach, is referred to the epigastrium (T7-T9).
The umbilicus receives somatic innervation from the T10 spinal nerve. The obturator nerve (L2-L4) supplies the pelvic wall and parietal peritoneum in the pelvis, not the umbilicus.
The base of the appendix is located at McBurney's point (one third of the way up the line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus), not directly behind the umbilicus.

Visceral pain from the midgut (including the appendix) is carried by afferents that follow sympathetic nerves back to the T10 spinal segment. Because the T10 dermatome encompasses the umbilicus, the pain is referred there.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Afferent nerve fibers concerned with the conduction of visceral pain from the appendix accompany the sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at the level of the 10th thoracic segment.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
coreConcept: Vascular Supply of the Esophageal Junction
statement: A surgeon is performing a partial gastrectomy and needs to ligate the arterial supply to the abdominal portion of the esophagus. Which vessel must be carefully identified as the primary source of blood for this segment?
options: Short gastric arteries
Left gastric artery
Splenic artery
Celiac trunk
Right gastric artery
correctOption: Left gastric artery
optionExplanations: The short gastric arteries supply the fundus of the stomach; they arise from the splenic artery and do not provide the primary supply to the abdominal esophagus.

The left gastric artery is a branch of the celiac trunk that ascends to the esophageal hiatus, where it gives off esophageal branches to supply the abdominal esophagus before descending along the lesser curvature.
The splenic artery supplies the pancreas, spleen, and the greater curvature of the stomach via short gastric and left gastroepiploic branches, but not the abdominal esophagus.
The celiac trunk is the parent vessel, but the specific branches to the abdominal esophagus arise specifically from the left gastric artery, not the trunk itself.
The right gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach but originates from the hepatic artery and does not supply the esophagus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The arteries [to the abdominal esophagus] are branches from the left gastric artery.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: A clinician is preparing to insert a Sengstaken–Blakemore balloon for a patient with massive variceal bleeding. Based on anatomical averages, what is the approximate distance from the incisor teeth to the stomach in an adult?
options: 24 inches (60 cm)
10 inches (25 cm)
12.5 inches (32 cm)
16 inches (41 cm)
20 inches (50 cm)
correctOption: 16 inches (41 cm)
optionExplanations: 24 inches is excessive for reaching the stomach entry, although the tube might eventually reach the pylorus at this length.
10 inches is too short; this would barely reach the mid-esophagus and would not ensure the gastric balloon is within the stomach.
12.5 inches is insufficient; it would likely sit in the distal esophagus, risking rupture if the gastric balloon is inflated there.
The average anatomical distance from the incisors to the cardiac orifice of the stomach is 16 inches (41 cm), a critical measurement for correct tube placement.
20 inches is significantly longer than the average distance to the cardia; the tube would be coiled within the stomach.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the average adult... the distance between the incisor teeth and the stomach is 16 in. (41 cm).

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy Limits of the Spleen
statement: Under normal physiological conditions in a healthy adult, what is the anterior-most extent of the spleen relative to the surface landmarks of the abdomen?
options: The midclavicular line
The left vertical line
The midaxillary line
The anterior axillary line
The linea alba
correctOption: The midaxillary line
optionExplanations: If the spleen reaches the midclavicular line, it has usually enlarged to about twice its normal size, making it easily palpable.
The left vertical line passes through the midpoint between the ASIS and symphysis pubis; the normal spleen remains lateral to this line in the hypochondrium.
In a healthy adult, the spleen is tucked away in the left hypochondrium and does not extend anterior to the midaxillary line, which is why it is not palpable.
The anterior axillary line is too far forward; the normal spleen is located more posteriorly.
The linea alba is the midline of the abdomen; the spleen is a lateral organ and only reaches the midline in extreme splenomegaly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Its long axis corresponds to that of the 10th rib, and in the adult, it does not normally project forward in front of the midaxillary line.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Internal Features: Muscularis Externa of the Stomach
statement: During a dissection of the stomach wall, three distinct layers of smooth muscle are identified. Which of the following describes the unique arrangement of the innermost muscular layer compared to the typical layers found in the rest of the gastrointestinal tract?
options: It consists of circular fibers that thicken to form the cardiac sphincter.
It is a thickened circular layer that functions only as a physiologic valve.
It consists of longitudinal fibers concentrated at the curvatures.
It consists of skeletal muscle fibers for voluntary control of the fundus.
It consists of oblique fibers that are absent in most other parts of the gut.
correctOption: It consists of oblique fibers that are absent in most other parts of the gut.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Circular fibers form the middle layer of the stomach and thicken significantly at the pylorus, not the cardia, to form an anatomic sphincter.
Incorrect. The oblique fibers are the innermost layer; the thickened circular layer forms the pyloric sphincter, which is an anatomic, not just physiologic, sphincter.
Incorrect. Longitudinal fibers are the outermost layer of the stomach, not the unique innermost layer.
Incorrect. The stomach wall consists entirely of smooth muscle under autonomic control, not skeletal muscle.

Correct. Unlike the rest of the GI tract which typically has two layers (inner circular and outer longitudinal), the stomach has a unique third, innermost layer of oblique fibers which assist in the complex churning and mixing of food.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The muscular wall of the stomach contains longitudinal fibers, circular fibers, and oblique fibers.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Lesser Curvature
statement: A student identifying the arterial supply of the stomach on a cadaver notes an artery arising from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus. This vessel, which runs to the left along the lesser curvature, is the:
options: Left gastric artery
Left gastroepiploic artery
Short gastric artery
Right gastroepiploic artery
Right gastric artery
correctOption: Right gastric artery
optionExplanations: The left gastric artery arises directly from the celiac artery and descends from the cardiac end toward the right along the lesser curvature.
The left gastroepiploic artery originates from the splenic artery and runs along the greater curvature, not the lesser curvature.
The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and supply the fundus, not the lesser curvature.
The right gastroepiploic artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery and runs along the greater curvature from right to left.

The right gastric artery is a branch of the hepatic artery (or sometimes its branches). It begins at the pylorus and runs toward the left along the lesser curvature to anastomose with the left gastric artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus and runs to the left along the lesser curvature.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of splenic trauma and splenomegaly
coreConcept: Vulnerability of the Splenic Parenchyma to Blunt Trauma
statement: An 18-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department following a high-velocity blunt impact to the left upper quadrant during a rugby match. Radiographs reveal fractures of the 9th and 10th ribs on the left side. Given the anatomical relations, which feature of the spleen most significantly contributes to its susceptibility to laceration in this scenario?
options: The tortuosity of its arterial supply
Its attachment to the phrenicocolic ligament
Its soft and friable consistency
The presence of a notched anterior border
Its location deep to the costal margin
correctOption: Its soft and friable consistency
optionExplanations: The tortuosity of the splenic artery is a normal physiological feature to accommodate stomach distension and does not contribute to the organ's friability or traumatic risk.
The phrenicocolic ligament supports the spleen and prevents direct downward enlargement, but it does not directly increase the organ's risk of laceration from rib fractures.

The spleen is described as a soft, friable mass. This mechanical property makes it highly susceptible to parenchymal tearing and fragmentation when compressed against the vertebral column or struck by rib fragments.
The notched anterior border is a developmental remnant of mesenchymal fusion and is a diagnostic landmark for palpation, but it is not a structural weakness relevant to trauma.
While the spleen is located deep to the left costal margin, this is generally a protective feature; injury occurs when the protective ribs are fractured and driven into the organ.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The liver is a soft, friable structure enclosed in a fibrous capsule... automobile accidents of the crushing or run-over type commonly produce laceration of the spleen.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
statement: Which anatomical relationship is correct regarding the uncinate process of the pancreas?
options: It extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
It is a superior projection of the pancreatic tail.
It lies anterior to the stomach within the lesser sac.
It lies posterior to the inferior vena cava and the aorta.
It is separated from the head by the splenic artery.
correctOption: It extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
optionExplanations: The uncinate process specifically hooks behind the superior mesenteric artery and vein as they pass in front of the pancreas and duodenum.
The uncinate process is part of the head of the pancreas, not the tail.
The uncinate process is retroperitoneal and lies posterior to the stomach, not anterior.
The uncinate process lies anterior to the aorta and inferior vena cava, while it is posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the body and tail, not between the head and uncinate process.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A part of the head extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels and is called the uncinate process.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
coreConcept: Vascular Formations behind the Pancreatic Neck
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with weight loss and an abdominal CT showing a malignant mass at the neck of the pancreas. Anatomically, which vascular structure is most likely to be compressed or invaded because it is formed directly behind this constricted part of the gland?
options: The portal vein
The inferior vena cava
The common iliac vein
The left renal vein
The inferior mesenteric vein
correctOption: The portal vein
optionExplanations: The junction of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein occurs behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein, making this vein highly susceptible to neck tumors.
The IVC is situated behind the head and to the right of the midline, but the portal vein's specific formation occurs directly behind the neck.
The common iliac veins form at the L5 level, well below the anatomical position of the pancreas.
The left renal vein passes behind the body of the pancreas and the SMA, but it does not form at the neck; the portal vein is the most immediate posterior relation to the neck.
The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein behind the body of the pancreas, not the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The portal vein is about 2 in. (5 cm) long and forms behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

category: Discuss the sites and vessels contributing in portosystemic anastomosis
statement: At the gastroesophageal junction, which specific portal and systemic veins anastomose to form a clinically significant portosystemic link?
options: Short gastric veins and the superior vena cava
Right gastric vein and the accessory hemiazygos vein
Left gastric vein and the esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Paraumbilical veins and the internal thoracic vein
Left gastroepiploic vein and the left phrenic vein
correctOption: Left gastric vein and the esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
optionExplanations: Short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and join the splenic vein; while they are portal, they do not form the specific esophageal anastomosis with the superior vena cava directly.
The right gastric vein drains the lesser curvature but does not provide the primary esophageal branches involved in the distal esophageal anastomosis with the hemiazygos system.

This is the classic gastroesophageal anastomosis. The left gastric vein (a direct tributary of the portal vein) meets the esophageal veins that drain into the azygos/hemiazygos system (systemic), leading to varices in portal hypertension.
The paraumbilical veins are involved in the umbilical portosystemic site, not the gastroesophageal site.
The left gastroepiploic vein is a tributary of the splenic vein (portal), and while it drains the greater curvature, it is not involved in the submucosal esophageal venous plexuses.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": At the lower third of the esophagus, the esophageal branches of the left gastric vein (portal tributary) anastomose with the esophageal veins draining the middle third of the esophagus into the azygos veins (systemic tributary).

category: Draw and label a diagram illustrating the lymphatic drainage of Stomach
statement: According to the anatomical description of the stomach's lymphatic system, which of the following is NOT listed as a primary regional node group receiving vessels directly from the stomach wall?
options: Left gastric nodes
Lateral aortic nodes
Left gastroepiploic nodes
Short gastric nodes
Right gastric nodes
correctOption: Lateral aortic nodes
optionExplanations: Left gastric nodes are a primary regional group mentioned as following the left gastric artery.
Correct. Lateral aortic (para-aortic) nodes drain the kidneys, gonads, and posterior wall, but are not listed as the primary regional nodes for the stomach wall.
Left gastroepiploic nodes are part of the gastroepiploic group mentioned as following the gastroepiploic arteries.
Short gastric nodes are a primary regional group mentioned as draining the fundus.
Right gastric nodes are a primary regional group mentioned as following the right gastric artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lymph vessels follow the arteries into the left and right gastric nodes, the left and right gastroepiploic nodes, and the short gastric nodes (Fig. 7.23).

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
coreConcept: Referred Pain Pathways in Hepato-biliary Disease
statement: A 50-year-old woman with a history of gallstones presents with sharp pain referred to her right shoulder. Applying knowledge of the diaphragmatic relations and nerve supply of the liver and gallbladder, what is the most likely neuro-anatomical pathway for this referred pain?
options: Direct compression of the axillary nerve by the enlarged right lobe of the liver.
Reflex spasm of the serratus anterior muscle via the long thoracic nerve.
Irritation of the visceral peritoneum of the gallbladder by the greater splanchnic nerves.
Irritation of the central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum (C3-C5) and referred pain via the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4).
Irritation of the peripheral diaphragmatic peritoneum supplied by the lower intercostal nerves (T7-T11).
correctOption: Irritation of the central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum (C3-C5) and referred pain via the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4).
optionExplanations: The liver does not anatomically contact or compress the axillary nerve, which is located in the upper limb/axilla.
Shoulder pain in this context is a sensory referral (dermatomal), not a motor reflex involving the long thoracic nerve.
Visceral peritoneum irritation usually presents as dull, poorly localized epigastric pain, not sharp shoulder pain.

Inflammatory processes of the liver or gallbladder that irritate the central part of the diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum transmit impulses via the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). The brain interprets this as coming from the C3-C4 dermatomes (shoulder) supplied by the supraclavicular nerves.
Irritation of the peripheral diaphragm leads to pain referred to the lower ribs or abdominal wall (T7-T11), not the shoulder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Involvement of the central diaphragmatic parietal peritoneum, which is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), can give rise to referred pain over the shoulder because the supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) innervate the skin in this area.

category: Define the following hernias: umbilical, epigastric, incisional, Spigelian, lumbar, femoral, internal and inguinal
coreConcept: Congenital Pathogenesis of Indirect Inguinal Hernia
statement: What is the primary anatomical mechanism responsible for the development of an indirect inguinal hernia?
options: Failure of the conjoint tendon to reinforce the superficial inguinal ring.
Protrusion of peritoneum through the Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery.
Generalized weakness of the abdominal muscles in elderly patients.
Dilation of the femoral ring due to increased intra-abdominal pressure during parturition.
Persistence of the processus vaginalis forming a preformed congenital sac.
correctOption: Persistence of the processus vaginalis forming a preformed congenital sac.
optionExplanations: The conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall behind the superficial inguinal ring to prevent direct hernias. While its weakness is relevant to direct hernias, it is not the primary cause of indirect hernias.
Protrusion medial to the inferior epigastric artery through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal defines a direct inguinal hernia, not an indirect one.
Generalized muscle weakness is the characteristic predisposing factor for direct inguinal hernias, which are typically acquired in older males, whereas indirect hernias are congenital.
Dilation of the femoral ring relates to the pathogenesis of femoral hernias, which occur below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, distinct from the inguinal canal's rings.

The processus vaginalis is an embryonic diverticulum of peritoneum. If it fails to obliterate, it provides a preformed path for abdominal contents to enter the inguinal canal, defining an indirect hernia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An indirect inguinal hernia is caused by a congenital persistence of a sac formed from the lining of the abdomen. This sac has a narrow neck, and its cavity remains in free communication with the abdominal cavity.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Posterior Stomach Wall
statement: A 55-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain that radiates to his back. A gastroscopy confirms a deep, chronic ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach body. Given the anatomical relations of the posterior surface of the stomach, which structure is at the highest risk of erosion and subsequent life-threatening hemorrhage?
options: Right gastric artery in the lesser omentum
Superior mesenteric artery behind the neck of the pancreas
Splenic artery along the upper border of the pancreas
Inferior vena cava in the retroperitoneal space
Hepatic artery in the porta hepatis
correctOption: Splenic artery along the upper border of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The right gastric artery is on the lesser curvature (right/anterior relation) and is not at risk from a posterior wall ulcer erosion in the stomach body.
The superior mesenteric artery is posterior to the neck of the pancreas but is lower and more midline than the typical location of the stomach body's posterior wall.
The splenic artery travels horizontally along the superior border of the pancreas, which forms the posterior 'stomach bed'; a posterior ulcer can easily erode into it.
The inferior vena cava is located to the right of the midline and is separated from the posterior wall of the stomach by the lesser sac and liver.
The hepatic artery is located within the lesser omentum and porta hepatis, anterior and to the right, and is not directly behind the stomach body.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas, and erosion of this artery may produce fatal hemorrhage.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
statement: A surgeon is dissecting the structures within the porta hepatis. From posterior to anterior, what is the standard anatomical arrangement of the three major structures entering or leaving the liver hilum?
options: Bile duct, Hepatic artery, Portal vein
Hepatic artery, Bile duct, Portal vein
Portal vein, Bile duct, Hepatic artery
Hepatic artery, Portal vein, Bile duct
Portal vein, Hepatic artery, Bile duct
correctOption: Portal vein, Hepatic artery, Bile duct
optionExplanations: The bile duct is the most anterior structure on the right, not the most posterior.
The hepatic artery is not the most posterior structure; that position is held by the portal vein.
While the portal vein is posterior, the bile duct is anterior to the hepatic artery, making this sequence incorrect.
The hepatic artery is anterior to the portal vein, not posterior to it.

In the porta hepatis, the standard relationship from posterior to anterior is: 1) Portal vein (most posterior), 2) Hepatic artery (intermediate), and 3) Hepatic ducts/Bile duct (most anterior). This is often remembered as V-A-D (Vein, Artery, Duct) from back to front.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In it [porta hepatis] lie the right and left hepatic ducts, the right and left branches of the hepatic artery, the portal vein, and sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibers.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
statement: A surgeon performs a truncal vagotomy to reduce gastric acid secretion in a patient with recurrent ulcers. This procedure targets the anterior and posterior vagal trunks. Which physiological change in the stomach is specifically expected due to the loss of these parasympathetic fibers?
options: Hypertrophy of the rugae within the fundus.
Inhibition of the secretomotor activity of the gastric glands.
Contraction of the pyloric sphincter.
Immediate relaxation of the gastroesophageal physiologic sphincter.
Increased production of gastrin by the antral mucosa.
correctOption: Inhibition of the secretomotor activity of the gastric glands.
optionExplanations: Rugae are mucosal folds that flatten with distension; their size is not increased by vagal denervation.
The vagus nerve is secretomotor; its sectioning inhibits the glands that produce acid and pepsin, which is the primary goal of the surgery.
The vagus nerves are inhibitory to the pyloric sphincter; their loss (vagotomy) would result in failure of relaxation, not a targeted therapeutic contraction.
The gastroesophageal sphincter is under vagal control, but vagotomy is not used to cause immediate relaxation there; it's used for acid reduction.
Vagotomy aims to reduce acid; gastrin production is a separate hormonal mechanism, though partially vagally influenced, the primary effect is on gland secretion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The parasympathetic vagal fibers are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the muscular wall of the stomach.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
statement: A 32-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents with sudden, sharp midline abdominal pain following a severe coughing fit. Physical examination reveals a tender, non-pulsatile mass confined within the right rectus sheath below the umbilicus. Based on the anatomical contents of the sheath, which structure is the most likely source of hemorrhage?
options: Subcostal nerve (T12)
Superior epigastric artery
Inferior epigastric vein
Paraumbilical veins
Deep circumflex iliac artery
correctOption: Inferior epigastric vein
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While the subcostal nerve is a content, it is a nervous structure; damage would cause sensory or motor loss rather than an acutely tender mass (hematoma).
Incorrect. The superior epigastric artery supplies the upper part of the sheath and is less commonly involved in lower rectus hematomas.
Correct. The inferior epigastric vein is more frequently the source of bleeding in rectus sheath hematomas, especially when stretched during pregnancy or heavy coughing.
Incorrect. Paraumbilical veins are involved in portal-systemic anastomoses but are not the primary vessels causing rectus sheath hematomas from trauma or stretching.
Incorrect. The deep circumflex iliac artery supplies the lateral abdominal wall, not the contents of the rectus sheath.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The source of the bleeding is the inferior epigastric vein or, more rarely, the inferior epigastric artery. These vessels may be stretched during a severe bout of coughing or in the later months of pregnancy, which may predispose to the condition.

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
statement: The lesser omentum is a specialized two-layered fold of peritoneum that plays a crucial role in suspending the stomach. Which anatomical structures serve as the specific attachment points for this fold?
options: Descending duodenum and the right kidney
Lesser curvature of the stomach and the undersurface of the liver
Fundus of the stomach and the left hemidiaphragm
Stomach hilum and the hilum of the spleen
Greater curvature of the stomach and the transverse colon
correctOption: Lesser curvature of the stomach and the undersurface of the liver
optionExplanations: The descending duodenum is retroperitoneal and does not serve as an attachment point for the lesser omentum; there is no peritoneal fold connecting it directly to the kidney in this context.
The lesser omentum extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum to the liver at the porta hepatis and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum.
This describes the gastrophrenic ligament, which connects the stomach to the diaphragm.
This describes the gastrosplenic ligament (or omentum), which connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the splenic hilum.
This describes the attachments of the greater omentum, not the lesser omentum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lesser omentum suspends the lesser curvature of the stomach and the proximal duodenum from the fissure of the ligamentum venosum and the porta hepatis on the undersurface of the liver.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Pancreas in Splenectomy
statement: A 34-year-old woman undergoes an emergency splenectomy following a blunt trauma to the left hypochondrium. Postoperatively, she develops severe epigastric pain and an elevated serum amylase. The surgeon suspects an accidental injury to the pancreas during the clamping of the splenic hilum. Given the anatomical relations, which part of the pancreas was most likely damaged?
options: Tail
Uncinate process
Neck
Head
Body
correctOption: Tail
optionExplanations: Correct. The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament and is in close contact with the splenic hilum, making it vulnerable to accidental trauma during splenectomy.
The uncinate process is an extension of the head on the right/midline and is not related to the spleen.
The neck of the pancreas is a midline structure, not involved in the splenic hilum.
The head of the pancreas is located on the right side of the vertebral column, far from the splenic hilum.
While the body is related to the splenic artery, it is not contained within the ligament that is clamped during hilum ligation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The presence of the tail of the pancreas in the splenorenal ligament sometimes results in its damage during splenectomy. The damaged pancreas releases enzymes that start to digest surrounding tissues, with serious consequences.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
statement: A 48-year-old female presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, jaundice, and clay-colored stools. Laboratory tests reveal significantly elevated serum amylase and lipase. A gallstone is suspected to be causing these symptoms. Anatomically, where is the most likely site of impaction to cause both biliary obstruction and pancreatitis?
options: The neck of the gallbladder
The junction of the right and left hepatic ducts
The cystic duct at the spiral valve
The middle of the common hepatic duct
The hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
correctOption: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater)
optionExplanations: A stone in the neck of the gallbladder would lead to cholecystitis but would not cause jaundice or pancreatitis, as the main biliary and pancreatic flow remains patent.

Impaction at the junction of the hepatic ducts would cause obstructive jaundice (blocking bile from both lobes) but would not affect the pancreas as it is far proximal to the pancreatic duct junction.

A stone in the cystic duct would cause biliary colic and potentially cholecystitis, but bile can still flow from the liver to the duodenum via the hepatic and bile ducts, and the pancreas would be unaffected.
Obstruction in the common hepatic duct causes jaundice by blocking bile flow from the liver, but it occurs before the cystic duct and pancreatic duct join, so it would not cause pancreatitis.

The hepatopancreatic ampulla is the common channel for both bile and pancreatic secretions. Impaction here blocks bile (causing jaundice) and can cause reflux of bile or increased pressure in the pancreatic duct, leading to pancreatitis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The impaction of a stone in the ampulla of Vater may result in the passage of infected bile into the pancreatic duct, producing pancreatitis.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: A 30-year-old woman complains of difficulty swallowing both liquids and solids, often feeling that food is 'stuck' in her chest. A barium swallow reveals a 'bird's beak' appearance at the lower end of the esophagus. What is the most likely microscopic finding in the esophageal wall of this patient?
options: Metaplasia of squamous cells to columnar cells
Absence of the longitudinal muscle layer
Infiltration of the mucosa by eosinophils
Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus
Hyperplasia of the stratified squamous epithelium
correctOption: Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus
optionExplanations: Squamous to columnar metaplasia is Barrett's esophagus, a complication of GERD, not achalasia.
Achalasia involves a failure of both muscle layers (longitudinal and circular) to coordinate, not the absence of the longitudinal layer itself.
Eosinophilic infiltration is characteristic of eosinophilic esophagitis, not classic achalasia.
The 'bird's beak' appearance on imaging is classic for achalasia, which is caused by the degeneration of the ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.
Hyperplasia is not the primary mechanism of achalasia; the pathology is neurological/plexus-based.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Achalasia... The cause is unknown, but it is associated with a degeneration of the parasympathetic plexus (Auerbach plexus) in the wall of the esophagus.

category: Demonstrate the various positions of appendix
coreConcept: Physical Exam Challenges in Retrocecal Appendicitis
statement: In a patient with suspected appendicitis, the clinician finds that palpation in the right iliac fossa does not elicit significant tenderness, even though the patient has a high-grade fever and typical visceral symptoms. Why might a retrocecal position of the appendix lead to this clinical finding?
options: The appendix lies behind a gas-distended cecum.
The appendix is protected by the pelvic brim.
The appendix is located medial to the terminal ileum.
The appendix has no contact with the parietal peritoneum.
The appendix is covered by the greater omentum only.
correctOption: The appendix lies behind a gas-distended cecum.
optionExplanations: Option B is correct. A retrocecal appendix is located posteriorly to the cecum; if the cecum contains gas, it can act as a cushion or barrier, masking the signs of localized peritonitis from palpation.
Option A is incorrect because protection by the pelvic brim is characteristic of the pelvic position, not the retrocecal position.
Option C is incorrect because an appendix medial to the ileum is in the pre-ileal or post-ileal position, which usually presents with localized anterior tenderness.

Option E is incorrect because an inflamed retrocecal appendix will irritate the parietal peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall (psoas fascia), but it is just difficult to palpate through the anterior wall.
Option D is incorrect because the greater omentum can wrap around any inflamed appendix regardless of position, and its presence usually localizes pain rather than masking it entirely.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A retrocecal appendix, for example, may lie behind a cecum distended with gas, and thus it may be difficult to elicit tenderness on palpation in the right iliac region.

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: During the insertion of a nasogastric tube, a clinician must be aware of the anatomical sites where the esophagus is normally narrowed. At what distance from the incisor teeth is the first narrowing, caused by the cricoid cartilage, typically encountered?
options: 7.2 inches (18 cm)
11.2 inches (28 cm)
20 inches (50 cm)
3 inches (7.5 cm)
17.2 inches (44 cm)
correctOption: 7.2 inches (18 cm)
optionExplanations: 7.2 inches (18 cm) is the standard anatomical measurement for the first narrowing at the cricopharyngeus muscle/cricoid cartilage.
11.2 inches (28 cm) corresponds to the second narrowing where the left bronchus and aortic arch cross the esophagus.
20 inches exceeds the total length of the esophagus and would place the tube well into the gastric body.
3 inches is too shallow and corresponds roughly to the oral cavity rather than the esophageal inlet.
17.2 inches (44 cm) corresponds to the third narrowing where the esophagus pierces the diaphragm to enter the stomach.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Three sites of esophageal narrowing may offer resistance to the nasogastric tube—at the beginning of the esophagus behind the cricoid cartilage (7.2 in. [18 cm])

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
statement: A surgeon is performing a mobilising procedure in the upper abdomen. Which segment of the duodenum must be handled with the understanding that it is the only part partially covered with peritoneum both anteriorly and posteriorly?
options: The fourth part held by the suspensory ligament of Treitz
The third part running horizontally on the subcostal plane
The entire second part containing the major duodenal papilla
The first inch of the duodenum immediately distal to the pylorus
The distal three inches of the first part
correctOption: The first inch of the duodenum immediately distal to the pylorus
optionExplanations: The fourth part is retroperitoneal until it reaches the duodenojejunal flexure, where it is held by the suspensory ligament of Treitz.
The third part is retroperitoneal, passing in front of the aorta and inferior vena cava.
The second part of the duodenum is strictly retroperitoneal, lying in front of the hilum of the right kidney.
The first inch of the duodenum is unique because it is covered by peritoneum on both sides, making it mobile and similar to the stomach; the rest is retroperitoneal.
Only the first inch of the first part is intraperitoneal; the remainder of the first part is retroperitoneal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The first inch (2.5 cm) of the duodenum resembles the stomach in that it is covered on its anterior and posterior surfaces with peritoneum... The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, being only partially covered by peritoneum.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
statement: A 70-year-old female presents with signs of intestinal obstruction, including vomiting, distension, and high-pitched bowel sounds. An abdominal radiograph reveals the presence of air within the biliary tree (pneumobilia). Based on the anatomical relations of the gallbladder, what is the most likely cause of this condition?
options: Retrograde infection from the ileum has ascended through the bile duct into the gallbladder.
A congenital choledochal cyst has spontaneously perforated into the lesser sac.
Rupture of the cystic duct has allowed intestinal gases to enter the portal circulation.
A gallstone has ulcerated through the gallbladder wall into the transverse colon.
A large gallstone has ulcerated through the gallbladder wall into the first or second part of the duodenum.
correctOption: A large gallstone has ulcerated through the gallbladder wall into the first or second part of the duodenum.
optionExplanations: Infections can cause gas-forming cholecystitis, but the primary cause of pneumobilia combined with mechanical intestinal obstruction is a fistula (gallstone ileus).
A choledochal cyst perforation would lead to bile peritonitis rather than a mechanical small-bowel obstruction with air in the biliary tree.
The cystic duct does not communicate with the portal circulation in a way that allows air to enter the biliary tree from the intestine.
Ulceration into the transverse colon allows the stone to be passed through the rectum without causing a small bowel obstruction, although pneumobilia would still occur.

The gallbladder lies in close contact with the duodenum. A large stone can cause pressure necrosis, creating a cholecystoduodenal fistula. The stone then enters the small bowel and often lodges at the narrow ileocecal junction, causing obstruction. Air from the gut then enters the biliary tree.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Gallstones may ulcerate through the gallbladder wall into the transverse colon or the duodenum. In the former case, they are passed naturally per the rectum, but in the latter case, they may be held up at the ileocecal junction, producing intestinal obstruction.

category: Identify the borders, surfaces and Impressions of spleen
statement: The visceral surface of the spleen is characterized by impressions from various abdominal organs. Which of the following organs does NOT leave a permanent impression on the spleen's visceral surface?
options: Left kidney
Left colic flexure
Descending colon
Stomach
Tail of the pancreas
correctOption: Descending colon
optionExplanations: The renal impression is located on the visceral surface, specifically along the medial and posterior aspect, where it meets the left kidney.
The colic impression is located at the lower pole of the spleen where it rests on the left colic (splenic) flexure.
The descending colon begins after the left colic flexure and passes inferiorly; it does not reach the spleen to leave an impression.
The gastric impression is the largest on the spleen's visceral surface, located anterior to the hilum.
The tail of the pancreas leaves a small pancreatic impression at the hilum between the gastric and colic areas.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Relations Anteriorly: The stomach, tail of the pancreas, and left colic flexure. The left kidney lies along its medial border (see Figs. 7.5 and 7.11).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
coreConcept: Neuroanatomical Basis of Referred Appendiceal Pain
statement: A 19-year-old medical student presents with a vague, dull pain in the periumbilical region that started 4 hours ago. According to the anatomical basis of referred pain, which spinal cord segment is responsible for this early manifestation of acute appendicitis?
options: L2
T7
L1
optionExplanations: T12 is incorrect; the subcostal nerve (T12) supplies the skin of the suprapubic region and the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall, not the periumbilical area.
L2 is incorrect; this segment typically supplies the skin of the anterior and medial thigh via the femoral and genitofemoral nerves, not the mid-abdominal region or appendix visceral afferentsPHL .
T7 is incorrect; this dermatome is located in the epigastrium over the xiphoid process and typically receives referred pain from foregut structures like the stomach.
T10 is correct; the visceral afferent fibers from the appendix travel with the sympathetic nerves to the T10 spinal segment, causing referred pain in the T10 dermatome (umbilicus).
L1 is incorrect; the first lumbar nerve (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) supplies the skin just above the inguinal ligament and the symphysis pubis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Afferent nerve fibers concerned with the conduction of visceral pain from the appendix accompany the sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at the level of the 10th thoracic segment.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
statement: A 62-year-old male with chronic cirrhosis and massive ascites presents for paracentesis. The clinician chooses a lateral approach in the flank. To avoid hemorrhage, the cannula must be placed lateral to which specific vascular landmark?
options: The paraumbilical veins
The inferior epigastric artery
The testicular artery
The superior epigastric artery
The deep circumflex iliac artery
correctOption: The inferior epigastric artery
optionExplanations: Paraumbilical veins may be distended (caput medusae) in cirrhosis but are not the deep arterial landmark used to define the safe zone for lateral cannula insertion.
The inferior epigastric artery runs within the rectus sheath; placing the cannula lateral to this vessel avoids a high-pressure arterial bleed from the rectus sheath contents.
The testicular artery is located deeper on the posterior abdominal wall and is not typically at risk during a superficial anterior/lateral paracentesis approach through the abdominal wall muscles.
The superior epigastric artery is located in the upper abdomen and is not at risk during a standard lower quadrant flank paracentesis.
The deep circumflex iliac artery is a boundary to stay above, but the primary medial boundary that must be avoided in the lateral approach is the epigastric system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": If the cannula is inserted in the flank lateral to the inferior epigastric artery and above the deep circumflex artery, it will pass through the following: skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia (very thin), aponeurosis or muscle of external oblique, internal oblique muscle, transversus abdominis muscle, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal connective tissue (fatty), and parietal peritoneum.

category: Describe relations, functions, blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of Gallbladder
statement: During a cholecystectomy, the cystic artery is typically identified within the calot's triangle. From which vessel does the cystic artery usually arise?
options: Superior mesenteric artery
Gastroduodenal artery
Left hepatic artery
Right hepatic artery
Common hepatic artery
correctOption: Right hepatic artery
optionExplanations: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut; the gallbladder is a foregut structure supplied by the celiac trunk via the hepatic system.
The gastroduodenal artery passes behind the first part of the duodenum and supplies the stomach and pancreas; it does not typically supply the gallbladder.
The left hepatic artery primarily supplies the left lobe and is not the standard origin for the cystic artery.
In standard anatomy, the cystic artery is a branch of the right hepatic artery, providing the primary oxygenated blood supply to the gallbladder.
The common hepatic artery gives rise to the hepatic artery proper and gastroduodenal artery, but the cystic artery specifically branches from the right hepatic artery proper.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery... supplies the gallbladder.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
statement: Which pathophysiological mechanism explains why particulate matter or infected fluid in the lower peritoneal cavity can rapidly reach the subphrenic spaces?
options: The presence of the transverse mesocolon which acts as an absolute physical barrier.
The localized secretion of viscous mucus by the omental appendices.
The gravity-dependent flow of fluid into the pelvic cavity during upright posture.
Continuous upward movement of fluid aided by the respiratory excursions of the diaphragm.
The static nature of peritoneal fluid which prevents the spread of infection.
correctOption: Continuous upward movement of fluid aided by the respiratory excursions of the diaphragm.
optionExplanations: The transverse mesocolon is a barrier that may 'hinder' movement, but it does not completely prevent the continuous upward flow toward the diaphragm.
Omental appendices are fatty tags on the colon and do not secrete the volume of fluid responsible for this circulation mechanism.
While gravity affects fluid collection in the pelvis, the question asks how it reaches the subphrenic spaces (upward movement).
Correct. Respiratory movements create a pressure gradient and mechanical pump effect that moves fluid toward the subphrenic spaces for lymphatic absorption.
Peritoneal fluid is not static; it moves constantly due to diaphragmatic and peristaltic activity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Intraperitoneal movement of fluid toward the diaphragm appears to be continuous (see Fig. 7.14), and there it is quickly absorbed into the subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries. This can be explained on the basis that the area of peritoneum is extensive in the region of the diaphragm and the respiratory movements of the diaphragm aid lymph flow in the lymph vessels.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
statement: The posterior vagal trunk, after entering the abdomen through the esophageal hiatus, provides which of the following distributions?
options: Gives off a large hepatic branch that passes directly to the liver.
Provides motor innervation only to the pyloric sphincter to cause contraction.
Distributes branches to the celiac plexus and the intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
Supplies only the anterior surface of the stomach and the fundus.
Terminates exclusively within the lesser omentum to supply the gallbladder.
correctOption: Distributes branches to the celiac plexus and the intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
optionExplanations: The large hepatic branch is a derivative of the anterior vagal trunk, not the posterior.
Vagal fibers are generally inhibitory to the pyloric sphincter (causing relaxation), while sympathetic fibers are motor (causing contraction).

The posterior vagal trunk (primarily from the right vagus) enters behind the esophagus. It supplies the posterior gastric wall and sends a large celiac branch to the plexuses, extending parasympathetic supply to the midgut.
The anterior vagal trunk (primarily from the left vagus) supplies the anterior surface; the posterior trunk supplies the posterior surface.
The vagus supply is extensive and covers the stomach, pancreas, and intestines; it is not limited to the lesser omentum or gallbladder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A large branch passes to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas.

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
statement: A surgeon is performing a left-sided nephrectomy and notes the relationship of the spleen to the left kidney. Where is the left kidney located relative to the spleen?
options: Lateral to the spleen
Along the medial border of the spleen
In front of the notched border
Superior to the spleen
Anterior to the spleen
correctOption: Along the medial border of the spleen
optionExplanations: The spleen itself is the most lateral organ in the LUQ; nothing except the rib cage and diaphragm is lateral to it.
The spleen has a visceral surface that is molded by surrounding organs; the left kidney is situated medially and slightly posteriorly to the spleen.
The notched border is the anterior border; the kidney is related to the hilum on the medial surface, not the anterior border.
The diaphragm is superior to the spleen. Both the spleen and the kidney are located in the upper abdomen, but the spleen 'caps' the lateral aspect of the kidney.
The stomach and the tail of the pancreas are the primary structures located anterior to the spleen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The left kidney lies along its medial border

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
coreConcept: Visceral Pain Referral in Biliary Colic
statement: A patient presents with sharp, stabbing pain in the epigastric region that radiates to the back below the inferior angle of the scapula. The clinician suspects biliary colic. Which anatomical pathway explains this specific referral of visceral pain?
options: Afferent fibers traveling with sympathetic nerves to the T7-T9 spinal segments.
Afferent fibers from the gallbladder wall traveling through the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
Afferent fibers traveling with the phrenic nerve to the C3-C5 spinal segments.
Somatic fibers from the skin of the back traveling with the dorsal rami of T12.
Parasympathetic fibers traveling with the vagus nerve to the medulla oblongata.
correctOption: Afferent fibers traveling with sympathetic nerves to the T7-T9 spinal segments.
optionExplanations: Biliary colic is a visceral pain where afferent fibers accompany sympathetic nerves through the celiac plexus/greater splanchnic nerves to the T7-T9 segments, referring pain to the epigastrium and back.
Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) supply pelvic viscera; the gallbladder is an upper abdominal organ supplied by the celiac plexus and splanchnic nerves.
The phrenic nerve mediates referred pain to the shoulder (C3-C5) when the parietal peritoneum of the diaphragm is irritated, not the initial visceral pain of colic.
T12 dermatomes are located in the lower abdomen and flank; the biliary system is primarily associated with the upper thoracic segments.
While the vagus nerve carries visceral sensations, pain sensation from the abdominal viscera predominantly travels via sympathetic pathways to the spinal cord.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Afferent nerve fibers ascend through the celiac plexus and the greater splanchnic nerves to the thoracic segments of the spinal cord. Referred pain is felt in the right upper quadrant or the epigastrium (T7 to 9 dermatomes).

category: Describe the anatomical basis for Sigmoidoscopy, rectal prolapse, rectal examination, rectal cancer and hemorrhoids
coreConcept: Anatomical Support of the Pelvic Viscera
statement: A 70-year-old female presents with a 'mass' protruding through the anal canal during straining. Anatomical assessment suggests a full-thickness rectal prolapse. Which of the following provides the primary structural support that, when weakened, facilitates the descent of the rectum through the pelvic floor?
options: The transverse mesocolon
The pelvic floor and fascial linings
The phrenicocolic ligament
The gastrohepatic ligament
The falciform ligament
correctOption: The pelvic floor and fascial linings
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The transverse mesocolon suspends the transverse colon, not the rectum.

Correct. The integrity of the pelvic floor and the continuity of the fascial linings (transversalis and pelvic fascia) are essential for supporting the pelvic viscera against intra-abdominal pressure.
Incorrect. The phrenicocolic ligament supports the splenic flexure of the colon, preventing its downward movement, but it does not support the rectum.
Incorrect. This is part of the lesser omentum connecting the stomach and liver.
Incorrect. The falciform ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pelvic floor below... The pelvic inlet marks the anatomically arbitrary (but descriptively useful) boundary line that demarcates the upper abdominal cavity from the lower pelvic cavity.

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
statement: The pancreas is known to cross which horizontal anatomical plane of the abdomen, with its neck lying specifically on this plane?
options: Intercristal plane
Subcostal plane
Intertubercular plane
Transpyloric plane
Transthoracic plane
correctOption: Transpyloric plane
optionExplanations: The intercristal plane is at L4, used for lumbar punctures, not pancreatic landmarks.
The subcostal plane is at L3, which corresponds to the third part of the duodenum, below the main mass of the pancreas.
The intertubercular plane passes through the iliac tubercles at L5, far below the pancreas.
The transpyloric plane (L1) is the primary level for the neck of the pancreas and the hila of the kidneys.
The transthoracic plane refers to the chest and is not used for abdominal visceral landmarks.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The pancreas lies across the transpyloric plane. The head lies below and to the right, the neck lies on the plane, and the body and tail lie above and to the left.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
coreConcept: Anatomical layers of the midline abdominal wall
statement: During a midline abdominal paracentesis performed to relieve massive ascites, which of the following anatomical structures is pierced immediately after the thin layer of deep fascia but prior to reaching the transversalis fascia?
options: Extraperitoneal fat
Linea alba
Rectus abdominis muscle
Medial umbilical ligament
Pyramidalis muscle
correctOption: Linea alba
optionExplanations: Extraperitoneal fat (or extraperitoneal connective tissue) is located immediately deep to the transversalis fascia and superficial to the parietal peritoneum.

Correct. In the midline of the abdomen, the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles fuse to form the fibrous linea alba, which lies between the deep fascia and the transversalis fascia.

The rectus abdominis muscle is located lateral to the midline; a true midline paracentesis passes through the linea alba, which is the fusion of the aponeuroses, thereby bypassing the muscle fibers of the rectus abdominis.
The medial umbilical ligament is a remnant of the fetal umbilical artery found in the extraperitoneal tissue, which is deeper than the transversalis fascia.

The pyramidalis is a small, often absent muscle that lies in front of the lower part of the rectus abdominis, within the rectus sheath, and would not be traversed in a precise midline puncture of the linea alba.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": If the cannula is inserted in the midline (Fig. 6.44), it will pass through the following anatomic structures: skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia (very thin), linea alba (virtually bloodless), transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal connective tissue (fatty), and parietal peritoneum.

category: Describe the gross anatomical features of the following: Mesentery, Omentum, Peritoneal ligaments, Peritoneal fold, Peritoneal sac, Recesses, Spaces and Gutters
statement: During the upward movement of peritoneal fluid towards the diaphragm, what physiological mechanism primarily facilitates its absorption into the subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries?
options: The rhythmic peristaltic waves of the descending and sigmoid colon.
The negative pressure created by the secretion of bile into the duodenum.
The respiratory movements of the diaphragm and the extensive area of the peritoneum in that region.
The tonic contraction of the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
The hydrostatic pressure generated by the accumulation of fluid in the paracolic gutters.
correctOption: The respiratory movements of the diaphragm and the extensive area of the peritoneum in that region.
optionExplanations: While peristalsis moves fluid locally, it is not the primary driver for lymphatic absorption at the diaphragmatic level.
Bile secretion is a digestive function and does not create the pressure gradients necessary for peritoneal fluid absorption.
The diaphragm's movement acts as a pump, and the large surface area of the diaphragmatic peritoneum is specialized for rapid fluid and particulate clearance into the lymphatics.
The sphincter of Oddi regulates bile and pancreatic juice flow; it has no role in the dynamics of the peritoneal cavity's serous fluid.
Paracolic gutters are anatomical pathways for fluid travel, but they do not provide the mechanism for trans-peritoneal absorption into the lymphatic system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": This can be explained on the basis that the area of peritoneum is extensive in the region of the diaphragm and the respiratory movements of the diaphragm aid lymph flow in the lymph vessels.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
coreConcept: Internal Features of the Gastric Mucosa
statement: Upon internal inspection of a stomach cadaveric specimen that has been incised along the greater curvature, numerous longitudinal folds of mucous membrane are observed. What is the correct clinical name for these features and their physiological behavior during gastric distention?
options: Villi; they increase in height when the stomach is full
Rugae; they flatten out when the stomach is distended
Haustra; they facilitate the storage of chyme
Plicae circulares; they remain permanent regardless of volume
Teniae coli; they contract to decrease surface area
correctOption: Rugae; they flatten out when the stomach is distended
optionExplanations: Villi are microscopic projections found in the small intestine, not the stomach; they do not change height with distention.
Rugae are mucosal folds that allow the stomach to expand; they are prominent in an empty stomach and disappear as the organ distends with food.
Haustra are the sacculations of the large intestine (colon) caused by the teniae coli, not found in the stomach.
Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds found in the small intestine, primarily the duodenum and jejunum, unlike gastric rugae.
Teniae coli are three bands of longitudinal muscle found on the colon, not the stomach.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The mucous membrane of the stomach is thick and vascular and is thrown into numerous folds, or rugae, that are mainly longitudinal in direction. The folds flatten out when the stomach is distended.

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the structures that enter or leave the liver at the porta hepatis. Which of the following is NOT typically found within the porta hepatis?
options: Portal vein
Hepatic veins
Right and left hepatic ducts
Right and left branches of the hepatic artery
Hepatic lymph nodes
correctOption: Hepatic veins
optionExplanations: The portal vein is the largest structure in the porta hepatis, carrying 70% of the blood supply into the organ.
Hepatic veins are the drainage vessels that emerge from the posterior surface of the liver to enter the IVC; they do not pass through the porta hepatis.
Hepatic ducts are the exit route for bile and are essential components of the portal triad at the porta hepatis.
The hepatic artery enters the liver at the porta hepatis and divides into its primary right and left branches there.
Hepatic lymph nodes are located at the porta hepatis to drain lymph from the liver and gallbladder towards the celiac nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In it [porta hepatis] lie the right and left hepatic ducts, the right and left branches of the hepatic artery, the portal vein, and sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibers.

category: Describe the location of abdominal surgical incisions
statement: During the closure of a transverse abdominal incision, the surgeon notes that the ends of the rectus abdominis muscles were not sutured. Based on surgical anatomy, why is this omission generally acceptable?
options: The tendinous intersections act as natural anchors to prevent muscle retraction.
Repair of the fibrous rectus sheaths provides sufficient wound strength.
The rectus abdominis is a non-essential stabilizer of the trunk.
Transverse incisions are only performed above the costal margin where the muscle is absent.
The muscle fibers regenerate rapidly across the surgical gap.
correctOption: Repair of the fibrous rectus sheaths provides sufficient wound strength.
optionExplanations: Tendinous intersections are attached to the anterior sheath, but they do not prevent the muscle from retracting significantly if the sheath itself is not repaired properly.

The strength of the abdominal wall repair in the rectus region comes from the aponeurotic sheaths. If these are securely sutured, the underlying muscle will heal within the envelope without needing direct suturing.
The rectus abdominis is an essential muscle for trunk flexion and stabilization of the pelvis; it is not considered non-essential.
Transverse incisions are commonly made above or below the umbilicus, well within the region where the rectus abdominis is the primary vertical muscle of the anterior wall.
Skeletal muscle fibers do not significantly regenerate across a large surgical gap; they typically heal with fibrous scar tissue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It is unnecessary to suture the cut ends of the rectus muscles, provided that the sheaths are carefully repaired.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of spleen
coreConcept: Peritoneal Coverage and the Splenic Hilum
statement: The spleen is located in the left upper quadrant and is entirely covered by peritoneum except at one specific site. What is this site?
options: The diaphragmatic surface
The lower pole
The gastric impression
The hilum
The anterior notched border
correctOption: The hilum
optionExplanations: The diaphragmatic surface is a smooth, convex surface entirely covered by visceral peritoneum.
The lower pole is the pointed inferior extremity of the organ and is fully invested in peritoneum.
The gastric impression is a large concave area on the visceral surface, all of which is covered by visceral peritoneum.
Correct. The hilum is the 'bare' area of the spleen where the peritoneal reflections (ligaments) attach and where vessels/nerves enter and leave.
The notched anterior border is covered by peritoneum; the notches are a developmental remnant.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen is surrounded by the peritoneum (see Figs. 7.6 and 7.61), which passes from it at the hilum as the gastrosplenic omentum (ligament)...

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: Which specific anatomical landmark corresponds to the point where the esophagus pierces the diaphragm to enter the abdominal cavity?
options: The median arcuate ligament at the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra
The psoas major fascia at the level of the 1st lumbar vertebra
The right crus of the diaphragm at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra
The central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra
The left crus of the diaphragm at the level of the 8th thoracic vertebra
correctOption: The right crus of the diaphragm at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The aorta enters the abdomen behind the diaphragm at the level of T12, passing through the aortic hiatus formed by the median arcuate ligament.
Incorrect. This level corresponds to the origin of the renal arteries and the kidneys, well below the esophageal entry into the abdomen at T10.
Correct. The esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus, which is formed by the fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm, typically at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra.

Incorrect. While T10 is the correct vertebral level, the esophageal hiatus is located in the muscular part of the diaphragm (right crus), not the central tendon. The central tendon is pierced by the Vena Cava at T8.
Incorrect. The hepatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava which pierces the central tendon at T8, but the esophagus uses the esophageal hiatus at T10.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The esophagus is a muscular, collapsible tube about 10 in. (25 cm) long that joins the pharynx to the stomach. . . The esophagus enters the abdomen through an opening in the right crus of the diaphragm

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
coreConcept: Relationship Between the Bile Duct and the Pancreatic Head
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, and clay-colored stools. Imaging reveals a solid mass in the pancreas compressing the bile duct as it descends in a groove on its posterior surface. Based on the anatomical course of the bile duct, which pancreatic part is most likely involved?
options: Neck
Body
Tail
Uncinate process
Head
correctOption: Head
optionExplanations: The neck is medial to the bile duct's descent and sits anterior to the vascular junctions, not the biliary tract.
The body is to the left of the common bile duct and is separated from it by the neck and the gastroduodenal artery.
The tail is the lateral-most part and is not involved in biliary obstruction.
The uncinate process is posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels but is usually inferior to the main biliary descent into the pancreatic head.

The bile duct descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum and then enters a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas before reaching the duodenum. Tumors here cause obstructive jaundice.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the third part of its course, it lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (see Fig. 7.29).

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
statement: A researcher is studying the pathophysiology of gastric acid regulation. Which anatomical region of the stomach is correctly matched with its specific mucosal secretion and regulatory function?
options: Pyloric antrum: Major source of protective hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor
Body: Principal site for the secretion of hydrochloric acid and pepsin
Pyloric canal: Primary region for the neurogenic stimulation of pepsinogen
Lesser curvature: Exclusive site for the production of somatostatin
Fundus: Predominant site of gastrin and alkaline mucus production
correctOption: Body: Principal site for the secretion of hydrochloric acid and pepsin
optionExplanations: The pyloric antrum secretes gastrin and a weakly alkaline mucus to protect the distal stomach and prepare the chyme for the duodenum; it does not produce hydrochloric acid, which is the role of the proximal stomach.

The mucosa of the body and fundus contains parietal cells and chief cells, making these regions the primary sites for hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen secretion, essential for the chemical digestion of proteins.
The pyloric canal is largely involved in the mechanical control of gastric emptying via the pyloric sphincter; pepsinogen secretion is concentrated in the fundic and body regions.
While somatostatin is produced by D-cells in the gastric mucosa, these cells are distributed throughout the stomach (especially the antrum) and are not limited to the lesser curvature.
The fundus, along with the body, is actually involved in acid and pepsin production. Gastrin is primarily produced by the G-cells in the antral mucosa, not the fundus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The mucous membrane of the body of the stomach and, to a lesser extent, that of the fundus produces acid and pepsin . The secretion of the antrum and pyloric canal is mucous and weakly alkaline

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
statement: In a patient diagnosed with diverticulosis of the colon, what is the anatomical basis for the typical site of mucosal herniation through the muscular coat?
options: Herniation occurs where the circular muscle is weakest at the points of blood vessel penetration.
Herniation occurs between the teniae coli where the longitudinal muscle layer is naturally absent.
Herniation occurs through the teniae coli due to excessive pressure during peristalsis.
Herniation occurs only in the sigmoid colon because it lack appendices epiploicae.
Herniation occurs at the mesenteric border where the vasa recta enter the bowel wall.
correctOption: Herniation occurs where the circular muscle is weakest at the points of blood vessel penetration.
optionExplanations: Correct. The text states that herniation occurs through the circular muscle between the teniae coli at points where the blood vessels pierce the muscle, which are the weakest areas.
