If the anterior abdominal wall remains stationary or contracts inward when the chest expands, the parietal peritoneum is probably inflamed...

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
statement: What is the primary arterial supply and venous drainage for the abdominal portion of the esophagus?
options: Right gastric artery and azygos vein directly
Celiac artery and inferior vena cava directly
Superior mesenteric artery and superior mesenteric vein
Splenic artery and splenic vein
Left gastric artery and left gastric vein
correctOption: Left gastric artery and left gastric vein
optionExplanations: The right gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature near the pylorus. The azygos vein receives drainage from the thoracic esophagus, but the abdominal portion primarily drains to the left gastric vein.
While the left gastric is a branch of the celiac, the venous drainage is into the portal system, not directly into the IVC.
The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut (distal duodenum to mid-transverse colon), not the esophagus.
The splenic artery supplies the spleen and parts of the stomach (short gastrics/left gastroepiploic), but not the esophagus.
Correct. The abdominal esophagus receives arterial blood from the left gastric artery (from the celiac trunk) and drains into the left gastric vein, which leads to the portal vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Blood Supply [of the esophagus]: The arteries are branches from the left gastric artery... The veins drain into the left gastric vein, a tributary of the portal vein.

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Perforation vs Appendicitis
statement: In the clinical presentation of appendicitis, the pain often begins as a vague discomfort in the umbilical region before shifting to the right iliac fossa. How does the anatomical presentation of a perforated gastric ulcer differ regarding pain localization?
options: Pain is initially umbilical but shifts to the right upper and lower quadrants if the fluid tracks down the right paracolic gutter.
It is always localized to the left iliac fossa due to the position of the descending colon.
It remains strictly localized to the shoulder due to phrenic nerve irritation.
It presents as severe suprapubic pain only, mimicking a pelvic appendix.
The pain is referred only to the back via the splenic artery sympathetic plexus.
correctOption: Pain is initially umbilical but shifts to the right upper and lower quadrants if the fluid tracks down the right paracolic gutter.
optionExplanations: Fluid from a perforated ulcer (especially duodenal or anterior gastric) tracks down the right paracolic gutter, causing localized pain in the right quadrants, which mimics appendicitis.
Gastric/duodenal contents typically track down the right side, not the left, due to the anatomical barriers provided by the mesentery.
Shoulder pain is a referred somatic symptom of diaphragmatic irritation, but it is not the only localization; abdominal somatic pain is primary.
While pelvic tracking can occur, the primary clinical concern described is the tracking to the right iliac fossa via the paracolic gutter.
Back pain is specific to posterior wall penetration involving the pancreas; anterior perforations involve the greater sac and tracking fluid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The transverse colon directs the escaping fluid into the right lateral paracolic gutter and thus down to the right iliac fossa. The differential diagnosis between a perforated duodenal ulcer and a perforated appendix may be difficult.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
statement: A 10-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of intermittent, inconsolable crying episodes where he draws his knees to his chest. Between episodes, the infant is lethargic. Physical examination reveals a palpable 'sausage-shaped' mass in the right upper quadrant and 'red currant jelly' stool on rectal exam. Given the anatomical basis of this condition, what is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism?
options: Herniation of the mucosa through the circular muscle at the site of vascular penetration.
Torsion of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery leading to venous stasis.
Failure of the midgut loop to rotate 270 degrees counterclockwise during return to the abdomen.
Telescoping of the ileum into the lumen of the cecum due to violent peristalsis of the ileal wall.
Compression of the third part of the duodenum by the superior mesenteric artery.
correctOption: Telescoping of the ileum into the lumen of the cecum due to violent peristalsis of the ileal wall.
optionExplanations: This describes the pathogenesis of diverticulosis, where mucosa herniates through weak points in the circular muscle layer where blood vessels pierce the wall.
This describes volvulus, which is a rotation of the bowel around its mesentery, common in the sigmoid colon of adults, not the 'telescoping' seen in infants with intussusception.
Malrotation of the midgut can lead to volvulus or internal herniation but does not describe the telescoping mechanism characteristic of intussusception.

Intussusception in children often involves the telescoping of the ileum into the cecum (ileocolic). It may be triggered by swollen Peyer patches, which act as a lead point for peristalsis to pull the proximal segment into the distal lumen.
This describes Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) syndrome, which causes duodenal obstruction, not the telescoping of one bowel segment into another.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Intussusception is the telescoping of a proximal segment of the bowel into the lumen of an adjoining distal segment... Ileocolic, colocolic, and ileoileal forms do occur, but ileocolic is the most common.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Histology and Gross Structure of the Gastric Wall
statement: The muscular wall of the stomach is uniquely adapted for its role in churning food into chyme. Which of the following correctly identifies the orientation of the smooth muscle layers found in the stomach wall, from superficial to deep?
options: Oblique, Circular, Longitudinal
Circular, Longitudinal, Oblique
Longitudinal, Oblique, Circular
Circular, Oblique, Longitudinal
Longitudinal, Circular, Oblique
correctOption: Longitudinal, Circular, Oblique
optionExplanations: The oblique layer is the deepest (innermost), not the most superficial.
The circular layer is the middle layer, not the most superficial.
The oblique layer is deep to the circular layer, not vice versa.
The longitudinal layer is the most superficial, followed by the circular, and finally the oblique.
In the standard anatomical arrangement of the stomach, the muscularis externa consists of an outer longitudinal layer, a middle circular layer, and an inner oblique layer.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The muscular wall of the stomach contains longitudinal fibers, circular fibers, and oblique fibers.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
statement: A patient with generalized peritonitis is advised to be 'nursed in the inclined position' (Fowler's position), sitting up at a 45-degree angle. What is the anatomical rationale for this management strategy?
options: It stretches the greater omentum, allowing it to more effectively wrap around the site of primary perforation.
It forces infected fluid into the lesser sac, where it is easily accessible for percutaneous drainage.
It facilitates the drainage of inflammatory exudate toward the pelvic cavity where toxin absorption is slower.
It promotes the movement of infected fluid toward the subphrenic spaces for faster lymphatic absorption.
It prevents the accumulation of fluid in the paracolic gutters, thereby protecting the retroperitoneal kidneys.
correctOption: It facilitates the drainage of inflammatory exudate toward the pelvic cavity where toxin absorption is slower.
optionExplanations: Option D is incorrect as the positioning is about fluid dynamics and absorption rates, not the mechanical stretching of the omentum, which moves primarily in response to peristaltic activity.

Option B is incorrect as the lesser sac is a relatively closed space behind the stomach; fluid does not naturally gravitate into it from the greater sac unless the epiploic foramen is specifically involved.

Option C is correct. The pelvic peritoneum has a slower absorption rate for toxins compared to the diaphragmatic peritoneum. Gravity is used to move the 'pool' of infection away from the highly absorbent subphrenic area.

Option A is incorrect because promoting movement to subphrenic spaces is dangerous; the large surface area and active respiratory movement of the diaphragm lead to very rapid absorption of toxins into the lymphatics, worsening sepsis.

Option E is incorrect because the paracolic gutters act as conduits; fluid will naturally move through them, but the goal is the final destination (pelvis vs. diaphragm), not merely 'protecting' the retroperitoneal organs.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In this position, the infected peritoneal fluid tends to gravitate downward into the pelvic cavity, where the rate of toxin absorption is slow (see Fig. 7.15).

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
statement: A 19-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He has localized tenderness and bruising over the left posterior-lateral thoracic wall. A radiograph reveals fractures of the left 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs. Based on anatomical positioning, which space is most likely to be primarily involved in the resulting hemorrhage?
options: The lesser sac
The right subphrenic space
The retroperitoneal space
The left upper quadrant (greater sac)
The pelvic cavity
correctOption: The left upper quadrant (greater sac)
optionExplanations: While the spleen forms the left boundary of the lesser sac, splenic hemorrhage from rib trauma typically spills into the main peritoneal cavity (greater sac) in the left upper quadrant first.
The right subphrenic space is associated with the liver; the trauma described is localized to the left side.
The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ, not a retroperitoneal one; hemorrhage would be intraperitoneal unless the injury is to the posterior renal structures.

The spleen lies directly deep to the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant of the greater sac; fractures here commonly lacerate the splenic parenchyma, leading to intraperitoneal bleeding.
Bleeding may eventually gravitate to the pelvic cavity if the patient is upright, but the primary and immediate site of hemorrhage is the left upper quadrant where the organ resides.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen is situated in the left upper quadrant and lies under cover of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
statement: A surgeon is performing a Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy). To mobilize the head of the pancreas, they must identify the 'uncinate process.' What is the anatomical relation of this process to the major abdominal vessels?
options: It extends to the left, behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
It is situated anterior to the body of the stomach.
It lies superior to the origin of the celiac trunk.
It extends to the right, anterior to the inferior vena cava.
It lies anterior to the superior mesenteric artery and vein.
correctOption: It extends to the left, behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
optionExplanations: The uncinate process is a hook-like extension of the lower part of the pancreatic head that passes medially to the left, specifically behind the superior mesenteric artery and superior mesenteric vein.
The pancreas is posterior to the stomach; no part of it is anterior to the gastric body.
The uncinate process is at the inferior part of the pancreatic head, whereas the celiac trunk arises above the pancreatic neck/body.
While it is in the vicinity of the IVC, its primary defining relation in surgical anatomy is its extension behind the superior mesenteric artery and vein.
The uncinate process lies posterior (behind) the superior mesenteric vessels, not anteriorly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": A part of the head extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels and is called the uncinate process.

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
statement: Pancreatic secretions are delivered into the duodenum via two distinct routes. Which of the following correctly describes the anatomical destination of the accessory pancreatic duct?
options: The major duodenal papilla, alongside the bile duct
The first part of the duodenum, near the pylorus
The hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater)
The third part of the duodenum, behind the superior mesenteric vessels
The minor duodenal papilla, situated above the major papilla
correctOption: The minor duodenal papilla, situated above the major papilla
optionExplanations: The major duodenal papilla is the opening for the main pancreatic duct and the common bile duct, not the accessory duct.
The first part of the duodenum is smooth-walled and does not contain the papillae for ductal drainage.
The hepatopancreatic ampulla is the dilated junction of the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct, not the accessory duct.
The third part of the duodenum is horizontal and does not receive the primary or accessory pancreatic secretions; these occur in the second (descending) part.

The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) drains the upper portion of the head and opens into the second part of the duodenum at the minor duodenal papilla, which is located approximately 0.75 inches (2 cm) superior to the major papilla.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The accessory duct of the pancreas, when present, drains the upper part of the head and then opens into the duodenum a short distance above the main duct on the minor duodenal papilla.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic alcoholism and liver cirrhosis presents to the emergency department with massive hematemesis. On examination, he has caput medusae and splenomegaly. The bleeding is suspected to be from a portal-systemic anastomosis. Which specific veins are involved in this esophageal anastomosis?
options: Left gastric vein and the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins
Superior mesenteric vein and the portal vein
Short gastric veins and the splenic vein
Paraumbilical veins and the epigastric veins
Right gastric vein and the inferior vena cava
correctOption: Left gastric vein and the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins
optionExplanations: At the lower third of the esophagus, the left gastric vein (portal) anastomoses with the azygos system (systemic), leading to varices in portal hypertension.
The superior mesenteric and portal veins are both parts of the portal system; an anastomosis requires a systemic partner like the azygos or renal veins.
Short gastric veins drain the fundus into the splenic vein (portal), but they are not the primary site of systemic anastomosis in the lower esophagus.
Paraumbilical and epigastric veins form the anastomosis at the umbilicus (caput medusae), not the esophageal site causing hematemesis.
The right gastric vein drains into the portal vein, but it does not form the primary esophageal anastomosis with the systemic circulation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": the esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (which drains into the portal vein) anastomose with the esophageal tributaries of the azygos veins (systemic veins).

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
coreConcept: Peritoneal Relations of Ascending and Descending Colon
statement: The peritoneal relations of the colon are important for surgical mobilization. Which statement accurately describes the peritoneal status of the ascending and descending colon?
options: They are completely surrounded by peritoneum and suspended by a mesocolon.
They are retroperitoneal, with peritoneum covering only their front and sides.
They have no peritoneal covering whatsoever on any surface.
They are entirely extraperitoneal and located in the prevesical space.
They are intraperitoneal organs like the stomach and spleen.
correctOption: They are retroperitoneal, with peritoneum covering only their front and sides.
optionExplanations: Only the transverse and sigmoid colons are typically suspended by a mesocolon; the ascending and descending parts are fixed.
The ascending and descending colon are secondary retroperitoneal; the peritoneum covers their anterior and lateral surfaces, binding them to the posterior wall.
All abdominal viscera have some relationship with the peritoneum; they are covered on at least one surface.
The prevesical space is in the pelvis anterior to the bladder; the colons are on the posterior abdominal wall.
Intraperitoneal organs are nearly entirely covered and are mobile; these colon segments are relatively fixed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The peritoneum covers the front and the sides of the ascending colon, binding it to the posterior abdominal wall.

category: Trace the horizontal and vertical peritoneal reflections
statement: Tracing the reflections of the greater omentum, how does its posterior layer interact with the transverse colon during development to form the adult horizontal reflection?
options: It remains entirely separate from the transverse colon, allowing the omental bursa to open into the greater sac inferiorly.
It fuses with the visceral peritoneum of the liver to form the right triangular ligament.
It reflects upward to form the falciform ligament on the anterior abdominal wall.
It obliterates the transverse mesocolon completely, making the transverse colon a retroperitoneal organ.
It fuses with the transverse mesocolon and becomes attached to the anterior surface of the transverse colon.
correctOption: It fuses with the transverse mesocolon and becomes attached to the anterior surface of the transverse colon.
optionExplanations: In the adult, the posterior layers of the greater omentum are fused with the transverse mesocolon, which typically obliterates the inferior-most part of the lesser sac recess.
The coronary and triangular ligaments are derivatives of the ventral mesentery related to the liver, not the dorsal mesentery from which the greater omentum arises.
The falciform ligament is a vertical reflection derived from the ventral mesentery, connecting the liver to the anterior wall, and is unrelated to the omental reflections.
The transverse colon remains an intraperitoneal organ because it is suspended by the transverse mesocolon, even after the greater omentum fuses with it.

During development, the descending apron of the greater omentum (dorsal mesentery) folds back and its posterior layer fuses with the mesentery of the transverse colon (transverse mesocolon), creating the adult attachment to the transverse colon.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Later, the posterior layer of the omentum fuses with the transverse mesocolon. As a result, the greater omentum becomes attached to the anterior surface of the transverse colon (see Fig. 7.19D).

category: Discuss the anatomical basis of esophageal varices, achalasia and Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
coreConcept: Hormonal Regulation of the Gastroesophageal Sphincter
statement: The closure of the gastroesophageal physiologic sphincter is a complex process modulated by various neuro-hormonal factors. Which of the following substances acts to increase the tonicity of this sphincter, thereby preventing reflux?
options: Cholecystokinin
Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide
Glucagon
Gastrin
Secretin
correctOption: Gastrin
optionExplanations: Cholecystokinin acts to reduce the closure of the sphincter, contrary to the action needed to prevent GERD.
Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) typically acts as a relaxant of smooth muscle in the GI tract, which would decrease sphincteric tone.
Glucagon reduces the tonicity of the sphincter and is sometimes used clinically to relax the esophagus for foreign body removal.
Gastrin increases or augments the tonic contraction of the lower esophageal sphincter, helping to keep it closed.
Secretin is known to reduce the pressure and tonicity of the gastroesophageal sphincter, which can potentially facilitate reflux.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The closure of the sphincter is under vagal control, and this can be augmented by the hormone gastrin and reduced in response to secretin, cholecystokinin, and glucagon.

category: Describe components of Biliary tree- hepatic duct and bile duct
statement: In the third part of its course, the bile duct demonstrates a critical relationship with the pancreas which explains why tumors in that organ often cause jaundice. Which statement describes this relationship correctly?
options: The duct remains entirely lateral to the uncinate process without touching it
The duct runs along the superior border of the body of the pancreas
The duct lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas
The duct passes anterior to the neck of the pancreas
The duct is embedded within the tail of the pancreas in the splenorenal ligament
correctOption: The duct lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas
optionExplanations: The uncinate process is part of the head of the pancreas, and the bile duct is closely associated with the head; it does not avoid the head of the pancreas.
The splenic artery, not the bile duct, runs along the superior border of the body of the pancreas.

In its distal descent, the bile duct is intimately related to the head of the pancreas, usually lying in a groove on its posterior surface. This proximity allows pancreatic head tumors to easily compress the duct, causing obstructive jaundice.
The bile duct descends behind the first part of the duodenum and head of the pancreas; it does not pass anterior to the neck.
The tail of the pancreas relates to the hilum of the spleen and is far from the bile duct's course, which is localized to the head and neck regions of the pancreas.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the third part of its course, it lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas.

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
statement: During a cadaveric dissection, the notched border of the spleen is identified. In correct anatomical positioning, this specific characteristic border is oriented in which direction?
options: Posterior
Inferior
Superior
Medial
Anterior
correctOption: Anterior
optionExplanations: The posterior border of the spleen is smooth and rounded, situated between the diaphragm and the kidney.
The inferior extremity (or pole) of the spleen is a blunt area related to the phrenicocolic ligament, but it is not the 'notched border' itself.
The superior aspect of the spleen is generally smooth and rounded, molded to the diaphragm.
The medial aspect of the spleen is the location of the hilum and renal impression; it is not described as a notched border.
The anterior border of the spleen is characteristically notched, a feature resulting from the incomplete fusion of the mesenchymal masses during embryonic development.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It is oval shaped and has a notched anterior border .

category: Describe the gross anatomical features, peritoneal relations, blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of cecum ascending and descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum and anal canal
statement: A 70-year-old female presents with severe abdominal pain, absolute constipation, and massive distension. An X-ray reveals a 'coffee-bean' sign, suggesting sigmoid volvulus. Which anatomical feature of the sigmoid colon predisposes it to this rotational torsion?
options: The lack of teniae coli compared to the ascending colon
Its direct attachment to the psoas muscle without intervening fascia
The absence of appendices epiploicae in the pelvic segment
Its fixed retroperitoneal position on the posterior pelvic wall
The presence of a long, mobile mesentery called the sigmoid mesocolon
correctOption: The presence of a long, mobile mesentery called the sigmoid mesocolon
optionExplanations: The sigmoid colon does possess teniae coli; their presence or absence is not the primary factor in torsion.
The sigmoid is separated from the posterior structures by the peritoneum and mesentery, not directly attached to the psoas.
The sigmoid colon actually has numerous appendices epiploicae (fatty tags), which are characteristic of the large intestine.
The sigmoid colon is not fixed retroperitoneally; its mobility is what allows it to twist.
The sigmoid colon is suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon, a fan-shaped fold that provides significant mobility, which can lead to volvulus (twisting).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Because of its extreme mobility, the sigmoid colon sometimes rotates around its mesentery. This may correct itself spontaneously, or the rotation may continue until the blood supply of the gut is cut off completely.

category: Identify the parts of the pancreas
statement: When examining the ductal anatomy of the pancreas, the accessory pancreatic duct (if present) serves to drain which specific portion of the gland?
options: The neck and proximal body
The upper part of the head
The entire pancreas into the major papilla
The uncinate process and lower head
The tail and distal body
correctOption: The upper part of the head
optionExplanations: The neck and body are part of the drainage area of the main pancreatic duct.
Correct. The accessory duct specifically drains the superior portion (upper part) of the pancreatic head.
The accessory duct opens on the minor papilla, not the major papilla; the main duct opens on the major papilla.
The main pancreatic duct typically receives drainage from the uncinate process and the lower part of the head via the ventral bud derivatives.
The tail and body are primarily drained by the main pancreatic duct, which runs the length of the gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The accessory duct of the pancreas, when present, drains the upper part of the head and then opens into the duodenum a short distance above the main duct on the minor duodenal papilla (see Figs. 7.51 and 7.58).

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
statement: A surgeon exploring the floor of the inguinal canal identifies a structural transition where the inguinal ligament's medial fibers extend backward and upward. What is the specific name of this medial extension?
options: Fascia lata
Reflected ligament
Conjoint tendon
Pectineal ligament
Lacunar ligament
correctOption: Lacunar ligament
optionExplanations: Fascia lata is the deep fascia of the thigh that attaches to the inferior rounded border of the inguinal ligament, essentially pulling it downwards, not an extension of the ligament itself.
The reflected inguinal ligament consists of fibers that pass upward from the lacunar ligament toward the linea alba, rather than the primary posterior-upward extension from the medial end.
The conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) is formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses and reinforces the posterior wall, not the floor.
The pectineal ligament (of Cooper) is a thickening of the periosteum on the pectineal line that becomes continuous with the lacunar ligament, rather than being the direct primary extension.
The lacunar ligament is a triangular extension of the medial end of the inguinal ligament that attaches to the pectineal line and forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lacunar ligament extends backward and upward from the medial end of the inguinal ligament to the pectineal line on the superior ramus of the pubis.

category: Identify and demonstrate the parts, external and internal features of stomach on anatomical model and cadaver
statement: When classifying the stomach into its anatomical subdivisions, which landmark on the lesser curvature is used to demarcate the body from the pyloric antrum?
options: Greater curvature notch
Fundus boundary
Pyloric sphincter
Cardiac orifice
Incisura angularis
correctOption: Incisura angularis
optionExplanations: The greater curvature is much longer and more variable; the standard landmark for this division is on the lesser curvature.
The fundus is the dome above the level of the cardiac orifice; it does not demarcate the antrum.
The pyloric sphincter is the anatomical end of the stomach, located at the junction with the duodenum.
The cardiac orifice is the superior entry point of the esophagus, defining the start of the body, not its distal transition.
The incisura angularis is a constant notch on the lesser curvature that serves as the clinical and anatomical boundary between the stomach body and the pyloric antrum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Body: This extends from the level of the cardiac orifice to the level of the incisura angularis, a constant notch in the lower part of the lesser curvature.

category: Describe related clinical correlates- gall stones, biliary colic, cholecystectomy, gallbladder gangrene
statement: A patient with suspected biliary pathology describes a vague, dull ache in the epigastrium that eventually shifts to a sharp, precise pain in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnostic contrast between these two types of pain?
options: The dull pain is somatic, while the sharp pain is visceral from the cystic duct.
The initial dull ache is caused by gallbladder gangrene, while the sharp pain is a sign of recovery.
The shift in pain indicates the stone has moved from the gallbladder into the common bile duct.
The sharp pain is due to referred pain via the phrenic nerve to the C3-C5 dermatomes.
The dull pain represents biliary colic (visceral), while the sharp pain indicates parietal peritoneal irritation (somatic).
correctOption: The dull pain represents biliary colic (visceral), while the sharp pain indicates parietal peritoneal irritation (somatic).
optionExplanations: Visceral pain is dull and poorly localized; somatic pain is sharp and precise. This option reverses the standard definitions.
Gangrene is a complication of advanced inflammation; it would not be represented by an initial dull ache followed by sharp pain in a manner suggesting recovery.
Ductal stones (choledocholithiasis) often cause jaundice and similar visceral pain, but the transition to sharp, localized pain is specifically a marker of peritoneal inflammation.
Phrenic nerve involvement results in referred pain to the shoulder, not sharp localized pain in the right upper quadrant itself.

Visceral pain (biliary colic) is mediated by autonomic fibers and felt vaguely in the midline/epigastrium. Once inflammation (cholecystitis) involves the parietal peritoneum, the pain becomes somatic and localized.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Afferent nerve fibers... enter the spinal cord at the thoracic segments... Referred pain is felt in the right upper quadrant or the epigastrium... Later, the pain shifts to where the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum. Here the pain is precise, severe, and localized

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
statement: On an anatomical model of the small intestine, which feature is specifically found in the mucous membrane of the lower ileum and serves as a key identifier?
options: Peyer's patches
Brunner's glands
Teniae coli
Major duodenal papilla
Spiral valve
correctOption: Peyer's patches
optionExplanations: Peyer's patches are aggregations of lymphoid tissue characteristic of the ileum, particularly the distal portion.
Brunner's glands are found in the submucosa of the duodenum to neutralize acid, not in the lower ileum.
Teniae coli are longitudinal muscle bands found on the large intestine, not the small intestine.
The major duodenal papilla is the opening for the bile and pancreatic ducts in the second part of the duodenum.
The spiral valve (of Heister) is a feature of the cystic duct in the biliary system, not the ileum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Aggregations of lymphoid tissue (Peyer patches) are present in the mucous membrane of the lower ileum along the antimesenteric border.

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
coreConcept: Orientation and axis of the spleen
statement: When demonstrating the surface anatomy of the spleen, the long axis of the organ is said to correspond with which of the following structures?
options: Shaft of the 11th rib
Subcostal plane
Shaft of the 10th rib
Transpyloric plane
Shaft of the 9th rib
correctOption: Shaft of the 10th rib
optionExplanations: The 11th rib covers the inferior part of the spleen but, like the 9th, does not define the central long axis.
The subcostal plane (L3) is located far inferior to the spleen's normal position in the upper quadrants.
The spleen is oriented obliquely such that its long axis runs parallel to the shaft of the 10th rib in the left hypochondrium.
The transpyloric plane (L1) is related to the hila of the kidneys and the pancreas, but the spleen's long axis is oblique and posterior.
The 9th rib covers the superior part of the spleen, but it does not represent the primary long axis of the organ.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The long axis lies along the shaft of the 10th rib, and its lower pole extends forward only as far as the midaxillary line

category: Identify and demonstrate the Parts and external features of small and large intestines on anatomical model and cadaver
statement: During a cadaveric dissection of the posterior abdominal wall, an examiner points to three distinct, flat longitudinal bands of smooth muscle on the outer surface of the ascending colon. Which of the following anatomical terms correctly identifies these structures?
options: Appendices epiploicae
Haustra
Teniae coli
Villi
Plicae circulares
correctOption: Teniae coli
optionExplanations: Appendices epiploicae (or omental appendices) are small pouches of peritoneum filled with fat that hang from the colon, not muscle bands.
Haustra (or sacculations) are the pouches or bags formed in the wall of the large intestine due to the teniae coli being shorter than the gut itself, not the muscle bands themselves.

Teniae coli are the three specific longitudinal muscle bands (mesocolic, omental, and free) that characterize the large intestine and are essential landmarks for identifying the colon and locating the appendix.
Villi are microscopic finger-like projections of the mucosa found in the small intestine to increase surface area for absorption; they are not visible as gross external muscle bands.
Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds of the mucous membrane characteristic of the small intestine, specifically prominent in the jejunum, rather than external muscle bands on the colon.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the large intestine (with the exception of the appendix), the longitudinal muscle is collected into three bands, the teniae coli

category: Describe the relationship of viscera to the peritoneum
statement: Which of the following structures is classified as a retroperitoneal organ, being only partially covered by visceral peritoneum?
options: Spleen
Stomach
Sigmoid colon
Ascending colon
Ileum
correctOption: Ascending colon
optionExplanations: The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ located in the left upper quadrant, enclosed by peritoneum and attached by ligaments.
The stomach is intraperitoneal, almost entirely enclosed in visceral peritoneum and attached by omenta.
The sigmoid colon is intraperitoneal; it is suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon and hangs into the pelvic cavity.
The ascending colon is fixed against the posterior abdominal wall and is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its front and sides.
The ileum is intraperitoneal and suspended by the mesentery of the small intestine, providing it with great mobility.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Retroperitoneal organs lie behind the peritoneum and are only partially covered with visceral peritoneum. The pancreas and the ascending and descending parts of the colon are examples of retroperitoneal organs.

category: Give the formation and extent of inguinal ligament
coreConcept: Bony Attachments of the Inguinal Ligament
statement: The inguinal ligament extends between which two bony landmarks?
options: Posterior superior iliac spine and pubic crest
Anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis
Iliac crest and pectineal line
Anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
Anterior inferior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
correctOption: Anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The posterior spine is located on the back; the inguinal ligament is an anterior structure.
Incorrect. While the symphysis is nearby, the specific medial attachment point for the inguinal ligament is the pubic tubercle.
Incorrect. These are related areas but not the primary extent of the inguinal ligament.
Correct. The inguinal ligament spans from the ASIS laterally to the pubic tubercle medially.
Incorrect. The attachment is to the superior spine (ASIS), not the inferior spine (AIIS).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lower border of the aponeurosis is folded backward on itself between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, forming the inguinal ligament

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of pancreas
statement: In the physiological delivery of exocrine secretions, the main pancreatic duct must traverse the pancreatic head to reach the duodenum. Which anatomical structure typically regulates the final passage of both bile and pancreatic juice into the intestinal lumen?
options: The Sphincter of Oddi
The Spiral valve
The Plicae circulares
The Valve of Heister
The Ligament of Treitz
correctOption: The Sphincter of Oddi
optionExplanations: The Sphincter of Oddi is a complex of circular smooth muscle that surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla (Ampulla of Vater), controlling the release of both bile and pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum.
The spiral valve is another name for the mucosal folds in the cystic duct and is unrelated to the terminal pancreatic orifice.
Plicae circulares are permanent mucosal folds in the small intestine that increase surface area for absorption but do not regulate ductal flow.
The Valve of Heister (spiral valve) is located in the cystic duct and helps maintain its patency, not the terminal pancreatic duct.
The Ligament of Treitz (suspensory muscle of the duodenum) holds the duodenojejunal flexure in place and is not involved in the pancreatic ductal system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The terminal parts of both ducts and the ampulla are surrounded by circular muscle, known as the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (sphincter of Oddi).

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of spleen
statement: A patient is undergoing a lymph node biopsy for suspected lymphoma. If a primary malignancy is located in the spleen, to which group of nodes would the lymph first drain as it follows the splenic artery?
options: Internal iliac nodes
Celiac nodes
Inferior mesenteric nodes
Superior mesenteric nodes
Para-aortic nodes at L3
correctOption: Celiac nodes
optionExplanations: The internal iliac nodes drain pelvic viscera, which are anatomically distant from the spleen.
Correct. The spleen, being a foregut derivative in terms of its vascular and lymphatic territory, drains through nodes at the hilum and then along the splenic artery to the celiac nodes.
The inferior mesenteric nodes drain the hindgut derivatives, not the spleen.
The superior mesenteric nodes drain the midgut derivatives, not the spleen.
While the celiac nodes are a type of para-aortic node, they are located at the level of T12/L1 (the celiac trunk), not L3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The lymph vessels emerge from the hilum and pass through a few lymph nodes along the course of the splenic artery and then drain into the celiac nodes .

category: Describe location, lobes, important relations, peritoneal ligaments, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, related clinical correlates of liver and subphrenic spaces
statement: A 60-year-old patient with portal hypertension due to liver cirrhosis shows signs of caput medusae. Which specific venous anastomosis at the liver's surface is involved in the formation of these distended umbilical veins?
options: Splenic vein and renal vein
Esophageal veins and azygos veins
Paraumbilical veins and superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall
Left gastric vein and esophageal tributaries
Superior rectal and middle rectal veins
correctOption: Paraumbilical veins and superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall
optionExplanations: This describes the splenorenal shunt, which is often a surgical intervention or a retroperitoneal anastomosis.
This describes the gastroesophageal anastomosis, leading to esophageal varices.
The paraumbilical veins (portal) anastomose with superficial epigastric veins (systemic), resulting in caput medusae under hypertension.
This is another description of the esophageal portal-systemic connection.
This describes the anorectal anastomosis, leading to hemorrhoids.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The paraumbilical veins connect the left branch of the portal vein with the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall (systemic tributaries).

category: Demonstrate the correct anatomical positioning of spleen
coreConcept: Diagnostic Features of the Splenic Border
statement: The spleen possesses a specific feature along its anatomical borders that allows a clinician to distinguish it from an enlarged kidney during palpation of a mass in the left hypochondrium. What is this feature?
options: A horizontal long axis
A pulsating medial hilum
A notched anterior border
A smooth posterior border
A rounded inferior pole
correctOption: A notched anterior border
optionExplanations: The long axis is oblique (along the 10th rib), not horizontal.
The hilum contains vessels, but pulsation is not a distinguishing border feature palpated during physical exams.
The notches on the anterior border are a unique developmental remnant of the spleen's mesenchymal origin and are a classic clinical sign of splenomegaly.
Both the kidney and spleen have relatively smooth posterior surfaces/borders.
The spleen has an 'expanded upper end' and a 'narrow lower end' (tail), but the notched border is the pathognomonic feature.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": It is oval shaped and has a notched anterior border .

category: Describe the clinical presentation and the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Carcinoma of stomach and peptic ulcers
coreConcept: Anatomical Pathway of Peritoneal Fluid Migration
statement: A patient presents with a perforated ulcer in the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Based on the anatomical arrangement of the peritoneal gutters, where is the escaped fluid most likely to migrate and potentially cause mistaken diagnostic signs?
options: The right iliac fossa via the right lateral paracolic gutter
The superior duodenal recess
The left iliac fossa via the left lateral paracolic gutter
The lesser sac via the epiploic foramen
The rectovesical or recto-uterine pouch directly
correctOption: The right iliac fossa via the right lateral paracolic gutter
optionExplanations: The transverse colon acts as a barrier that directs the fluid from a perforated anterior duodenal ulcer into the right lateral paracolic gutter. The fluid then tracks down to the right iliac fossa, where it may mimic the presentation of acute appendicitis.
Recesses like the superior duodenal recess are small peritoneal pockets; they do not accommodate the large volumes of fluid associated with a free perforation.
The fluid from a duodenal ulcer (on the right) is prevented from moving to the left by the attachment of the mesentery and the position of the stomach.
The lesser sac is located posterior to the stomach; an anterior duodenal perforation opens into the greater sac, not the lesser sac.
While fluid may eventually reach the pelvic pouches, it must first navigate the paracolic gutters; the migration to the right iliac fossa is the most immediate clinical 'mimic' mentioned in the text.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An ulcer of the anterior wall of the first inch of the duodenum may perforate into the upper part of the greater sac, above the transverse colon. The transverse colon directs the escaping fluid into the right lateral paracolic gutter and thus down to the right iliac fossa.

category: Describe the location, position, parts, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of duodenum, Jejunum & Ileum (Small Intestine)
coreConcept: Relations of the First Part of the Duodenum
statement: Which of the following structures is found immediately posterior to the first part of the duodenum, making it susceptible to erosion by a posterior duodenal ulcer?
options: Psoas major muscle
Superior mesenteric artery
Inferior vena cava
Gastroduodenal artery
Right kidney hilum
correctOption: Gastroduodenal artery
optionExplanations: The psoas muscle is a posterior relation of the third and fourth parts of the duodenum.
The SMA is anterior to the third part of the duodenum, not posterior to the first part.
The IVC is posterior to the 1st part but is further removed than the gastroduodenal artery and bile duct.
The gastroduodenal artery descends immediately behind the first part of the duodenum; its erosion leads to massive hemorrhage.
The hilum of the right kidney is a posterior relation of the second part, not the first part of the duodenum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": An ulcer of the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum may penetrate the wall and erode the relatively large gastroduodenal artery.

category: Describe the extent, formation and contents of rectus sheath
coreConcept: Clinical Diagnosis of Rectus Sheath Hematoma
statement: A 29-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe midline abdominal pain after a vigorous coughing fit. Physical examination reveals a tender, non-reducible, firm mass in the right lower quadrant that does not change in position with the patient's movement. Her vitals show mild tachycardia but stable blood pressure. Given the anatomical contents of the rectus sheath, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute appendicitis with localized peritonitis
Strangulated indirect inguinal hernia
Volvulus of the sigmoid colon
Torsion of the greater omentum
Rupture of the inferior epigastric artery within the rectus sheath
correctOption: Rupture of the inferior epigastric artery within the rectus sheath
optionExplanations: Appendicitis causes severe RLQ pain, but it rarely presents as a discrete, firm mass within the abdominal wall layers immediately following a cough; it is an intra-abdominal inflammatory process.
While an indirect inguinal hernia presents in the groin, it would typically be lateral to the rectus sheath and pass through the inguinal canal, whereas this mass is confined to the rectus sheath.
Sigmoid volvulus involves the large intestine and typically presents with significant abdominal distention and signs of bowel obstruction, not a localized abdominal wall mass.
Omental torsion can cause severe pain and a mass, but the specific association with the rectus sheath and the coughing trigger in pregnancy makes a hematoma far more probable anatomically.

Correct. The clinical picture of a sudden, tender mass in the rectus sheath following a cough in a pregnant patient is the classic presentation of a rectus sheath hematoma due to inferior epigastric vessel rupture.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Hematoma of the rectus sheath... occurs most often below the level of the umbilicus. The source of the bleeding is the inferior epigastric vein or, more rarely, the inferior epigastric artery. These vessels may be stretched during... the later months of pregnancy... An acutely tender mass confined to one rectus sheath is diagnostic.

category: Describe the extent of esophagus, its constrictions, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage
statement: A clinician is preparing to insert a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube to manage massive variceal bleeding. According to anatomical standards in an average adult, what is the expected distance from the external orifices of the nose to the stomach?
options: 10 inches (25 cm)
20 inches (50 cm)
16 inches (41 cm)
17.2 inches (44 cm)
12.5 inches (32 cm)
correctOption: 17.2 inches (44 cm)
optionExplanations: 10 inches is the approximate total length of the esophagus itself, not the distance from the nose to the stomach.
20 inches (50 cm) is the approximate length of the umbilical cord at term, which is unrelated to esophageal anatomy.
16 inches (41 cm) is the average distance from the incisor teeth to the stomach, not from the nose.
The clinical standard for nasogastric or esophageal tubes via the nasal route is 17.2 inches (44 cm) to reach the stomach.
32 cm is too short for a nasogastric tube to reach the gastric lumen in an average adult.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In the average adult, the distance between the external orifices of the nose and the stomach is 17.2 in. (44 cm)

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
coreConcept: Peritoneal Fluid Dynamics and Nursing Care
statement: A patient with generalized peritonitis is nursed in bed with the back at a 45-degree angle. What is the anatomical rationale for this specific positioning?
options: It encourages the fluid to collect in the right lateral paracolic gutter to relieve pressure on the bladder.
It promotes the movement of particulate matter toward the subphrenic spaces for faster lymphatic absorption.
It allows infected fluid to gravitate into the pelvic cavity where toxin absorption is slower.
It prevents the greater omentum from adhering to the small intestine.
It keeps the stomach empty to prevent chemical irritation of the lesser omentum.
correctOption: It allows infected fluid to gravitate into the pelvic cavity where toxin absorption is slower.
optionExplanations: Fluid in the paracolic gutters often tracks toward the subphrenic spaces or pelvis; the goal of the 45-degree tilt is pelvic pooling specifically, not bladder pressure relief.
Moving fluid toward subphrenic spaces is undesirable in peritonitis because the rate of toxin absorption is very rapid near the diaphragm.

The pelvic cavity has a slower rate of absorption than the subphrenic regions. By sitting the patient at 45 degrees (Fowler's position), infected fluid pools in the pelvis, reducing systemic toxicity.
Positioning does not prevent the omentum from adhering; the omentum's adhesions are generally beneficial for localizing infection regardless of posture.
While an empty stomach is good for comfort, the 45-degree angle's primary anatomical purpose in peritonitis is managing the gravity-dependent flow of infected exudate.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": In this position, the infected peritoneal fluid tends to gravitate downward into the pelvic cavity, where the rate of toxin absorption is slow (see Fig. 7.15).

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following: Peritonitis and ascites, Peritoneal adhesions (and adhesiostomy), Abdominal paracentesis
statement: Describe the physiological loop governing the movement and absorption of peritoneal fluid within the abdominal cavity.
options: Fluid is produced by the parietal layer and absorbed primarily by the pelvic peritoneum via the obturator vein.
Fluid is sequestered in the lesser sac and drains into the portal vein through the epiploic foramen.
Fluid circulates from the cisterna chyli into the peritoneal cavity to lubricate the visceral peritoneum.
Fluid moves continuously toward the diaphragm and is absorbed into the subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries.
Fluid moves laterally into the paracolic gutters and is absorbed by the pararenal fat for renal filtration.
correctOption: Fluid moves continuously toward the diaphragm and is absorbed into the subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries.
optionExplanations: While the pelvic peritoneum can absorb fluid, the primary, continuous physiological circulation of the fluid is toward the diaphragm.
The lesser sac is a small posterior space; it is not the primary site of absorption, and the fluid does not drain directly into the portal vein.
The cisterna chyli is a collection point for lymph and is the 'destination' after absorption, not the source of peritoneal fluid lubrication.
Peristalsis and diaphragmatic movement create a continuous upward flow of peritoneal fluid toward the diaphragm, where it is absorbed by subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries into the thoracic duct.
The paracolic gutters are pathways for movement, but the fat is not an absorbent organ; the fluid must reach the lymphatics for removal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": Intraperitoneal movement of fluid toward the diaphragm appears to be continuous (see Fig. 7.14), and there it is quickly absorbed into the subperitoneal lymphatic capillaries.

category: Describe the anatomical basis and manifestations of the following conditions: Duodenal Ulcers, Ileal diverticulum, Diverticulosis, Large bowel cancer, Appendicitis, Volvulus, Intussusception
statement: A senior surgeon is demonstrating the identification of the vermiform appendix during a difficult laparotomy where the cecum is obscured by inflammatory adhesions. Which anatomical feature of the large intestine serves as the most reliable landmark for finding the base of the appendix?
options: The position of the right lateral paracolic gutter.
The location of the ileocecal valve in the medial wall.
The presence of appendices epiploicae at the cecal fundus.
The termination of the ileocolic artery at the ileocecal junction.
The convergence of the three teniae coli on the posteromedial surface.
correctOption: The convergence of the three teniae coli on the posteromedial surface.
optionExplanations: The paracolic gutters are peritoneal recesses that guide fluid flow; while the appendix can be located near the right gutter, its position is highly variable (retrocecal, pelvic, etc.), making the gutter an unreliable landmark for the base.

The ileocecal valve is an internal horizontal fold of mucous membrane. While the appendix is attached below it, the valve cannot be used as an external surgical landmark to find the appendix base during laparotomy.
Appendices epiploicae (omental appendices) are fatty tags characteristic of the colon but are notably absent from the appendix and cecal base, making them an unreliable landmark for localization.

The ileocolic artery provides the blood supply, but its branching pattern is variable and requires dissection. The teniae coli are visible on the surface of the cecum without dissection, providing a more immediate landmark.

The teniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands on the colon that converge exactly at the base of the appendix, where they become a continuous longitudinal muscle layer. This is the definitive surgical landmark.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": the base of the appendix is easily found by identifying the teniae coli of the cecum and tracing them to the base of the appendix, where they converge to form a continuous longitudinal muscle coat

category: Describe the location, position, parts, external and internal structure, relations, vascular and nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of stomach
coreConcept: Gross Anatomy and Divisions of the Stomach
statement: Which of the following correctly describes the anatomical boundaries and divisions of the stomach?
options: The stomach is divided into the fundus, body, pyloric antrum, and pylorus
The fundus is the region between the incisura angularis and the pylorus
The lesser omentum attaches to the greater curvature of the stomach
The greater curvature forms the right border of the stomach
The cardiac orifice is protected by an anatomical smooth muscle sphincter
correctOption: The stomach is divided into the fundus, body, pyloric antrum, and pylorus
optionExplanations: This is the standard anatomical division of the stomach as described in clinical texts.
Incorrect; the region between the incisura and the pylorus is the pyloric antrum and canal.
Incorrect; the lesser omentum attaches to the lesser curvature; the greater omentum attaches to the greater curvature.
Incorrect; the greater curvature forms the left and inferior border; the lesser curvature forms the right border.
Incorrect; while a physiologic sphincter exists at the cardia, there is no discrete anatomical sphincter visible on dissection.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The stomach is divided into the following parts: Fundus... Body... Pyloric antrum... Pylorus

category: Describe the location, surfaces, peritoneal reflections, relations, neurovascular supply and lymphatic drainage of spleen
coreConcept: Peritoneal Coverings and the Splenic Hilum
statement: The spleen is almost entirely covered by visceral peritoneum. Which area of the spleen lacks this serous covering where structures enter and leave the organ?
options: The renal impression
The notched anterior border
The lower pole
The diaphragmatic surface
The hilum on the medial surface
correctOption: The hilum on the medial surface
optionExplanations: The renal impression is part of the visceral surface and is covered by peritoneum except at the point of ligamentous attachment near the hilum.
The notched anterior border is covered by visceral peritoneum.
The lower pole is smooth and covered by peritoneum.
The diaphragmatic surface is the convex surface of the spleen and is completely covered by peritoneum.

The hilum is the only part of the spleen not covered by visceral peritoneum, as it is the site where the peritoneal reflections (gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments) attach and where neurovascular structures enter/exit.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions": The spleen is surrounded by the peritoneum (see Figs. 7.6 and 7.61), which passes from it at the hilum as the gastrosplenic omentum (ligament)...
